en_revised: Fourteen or fifteen *li* to the southwest of the great city, one reaches the old city of Śākala (奢羯羅故城). Although the walls are ruined, the foundations remain solid. It is over twenty *li* in circumference. Within it, a smaller city has been built, six or seven *li* in circumference, where the inhabitants are wealthy; this is the former capital of this country. Several hundred years ago, there was a king named Mihirakula (摩醯邏矩羅) (translated as "Great Clan" in Chinese), who made this city his capital and ruled over all of India. He possessed talent and wisdom, and his nature was brave and fierce; there was no neighboring country that did not submit to him. During his leisure from state affairs, he wished to study the Buddha-dharma and ordered the monks to recommend a person of outstanding virtue. At that time, the monks dared not respond to the order, for they were few in desire and practiced non-action, not seeking fame or status; those who were learned and brilliant feared his majesty. At that time, there was a former servant of the royal household who had long worn the dyed robes (i.e., was a monk), whose rhetoric was refined and elegant, and whose speech was eloquent and quick; the assembly collectively recommended him to respond to the order. The King said, "I respect the Buddha-dharma and have sought out famous monks from afar, yet the assembly recommends this menial to engage in discussion with me. I always thought that among the monks, the wise and brilliant were comparable; now that I know this, what is there to respect?" Thereupon, he issued a decree throughout the five regions of India that from then on, the Buddha-dharma was to be utterly destroyed, and all monks were to be expelled until not a single one remained. King Bālāditya (婆羅阿迭多) (translated as "Young Sun" in Chinese) of the country of Magadha (摩揭陀國) revered the Buddha-dharma and loved his people; because of King Mihirakula’s excessive punishments and tyrannical rule, he guarded his own borders and did not offer the customary tribute. At that time, King Mihirakula mobilized his troops, intending to punish him. When King Bālāditya (幼日王) learned of this news, he told his ministers, "I hear the invaders are coming, but I cannot bear to let my soldiers engage in battle. I hope my officials and the common people will forgive me for this, and I shall take this humble body and hide in the marshes and wilderness." Having finished speaking, he left the palace and took refuge in the mountains and forests. Several tens of thousands of people in the country, moved by gratitude and admiration, followed him and hid on islands in the sea. King Mihirakula (大族王) entrusted his troops to his younger brother and sailed across the sea to attack him. King Bālāditya guarded the strategic passes and sent light cavalry to lure the enemy into battle; at the first sound of the gongs and drums, ambushers rose from all sides, capturing Mihirakula alive and leading him forward with his hands tied behind his back. King Mihirakula, ashamed of his failure, covered his face with his garment. King Bālāditya sat upon his lion throne, surrounded by his officials, and ordered his attendants to say to Mihirakula, "Uncover your face, for I have words for you." Mihirakula replied, "The positions of subject and master have been reversed, and we look upon each other as enemies; since we are not on friendly terms, what is the use of speaking face to face?" Though they urged him again and again, he would not comply. Thereupon, the King issued a proclamation enumerating his crimes, saying, "The Three Jewels are a field of merit upon which the four forms of birth depend. You have acted like a jackal or wolf, destroying these noble works. Fortune has not protected you, and you have been captured by me. Your crimes are unpardonable, and you must face the penalty of the law." At that time, the mother of King Bālāditya was widely learned and possessed a keen memory, and she was highly skilled in physiognomy. Hearing that he was about to execute Mihirakula, she hurriedly told King Bālāditya, "I have heard that Mihirakula possesses an extraordinary appearance and great wisdom; I wish to see him once." King Bālāditya ordered that Mihirakula be led into his mother's palace. The mother of Bālāditya (幼日王) said, "Alas, Mihirakula (大族), I pray you do not feel ashamed! The world is impermanent, and honor and disgrace alternate. I am like a mother to you, and you are like a son to me; you should remove the cloth covering your face and speak to me face to face."  Mihirakula said, "Formerly the ruler of a hostile state, I am now a captive prisoner. Having ruined the royal enterprise and extinguished the ancestral sacrifices, I am ashamed before the spirits of my ancestors above and the common people below; I am truly disgraced to show my face. Looking up and down between heaven and earth, I cannot bear the loss of myself, and that is why I cover my face."  The king's mother said, "Rise and fall follow the times; existence and extinction have their destiny. If you use the mind to equalize things, then gain and loss are both forgotten; if you use things to equalize the mind, then praise and blame arise in turn. You should believe in karmic retribution and move along with the times. Remove your covering and speak; perhaps you may preserve your life."  Mihirakula thanked her, saying, "Being a man of no talent, I inherited the royal throne, yet my governance strayed from the Way, leading to the ruin of my kingdom. Although I am now in bonds, I still cling to the hope of living for a little longer. I dare to accept your great kindness and will uncover my face to thank you for your profound grace."  Thereupon, he removed the cloth and revealed his face. The king's mother said, "Take care of yourself, for you shall live out your natural lifespan."  Soon after, she told King Bālāditya, "The ancient scriptures contain the teaching to forgive transgressions and cherish life. Although King Mihirakula has accumulated evil for a long time, his remaining merit is not yet exhausted. If you kill this man, for twelve years there will be famine and suffering. However, he possesses the energy of a restoration; he will not ultimately be a king of a great country, but he shall occupy the north and possess a small territory." King Bālāditya, obeying his compassionate mother's command and pitying the sovereign who had lost his kingdom, gave him a young daughter in marriage and treated him with extraordinary courtesy; he assembled the king's remaining troops and provided additional guards before they had even left the island. The younger brother of King Mihirakula returned to his country and established himself as ruler; having lost his throne, Mihirakula fled to hide in the mountains and wilderness, eventually seeking refuge in the north in the kingdom of Kaśmīra (迦濕彌羅國). The King of Kaśmīra treated him with great courtesy and, pitying him for the loss of his kingdom, granted him a territory as a fief. After some time had passed, he led his townspeople, treacherously killed the King of Kaśmīra, and established himself as ruler. Taking advantage of the prestige of his victory, he attacked the kingdom of Gandhāra (健馱邏國) to the west; by deploying hidden troops and an ambush, he killed its king and completely exterminated the royal clan and the high ministers. He destroyed one thousand six hundred stūpas and sanghārāmas. Beyond those killed in battle, there were nine hundred million people whom he intended to execute, leaving no survivors. At that time, his assistants all remonstrated, saying, "The Great King has intimidated powerful enemies and, without engaging in battle, has executed the chief culprits. What fault have the common people committed? We wish to offer our own humble bodies to die in their stead." The King replied, "You believe in the Buddha-dharma, value merit in the afterlife, aspire to attain the fruit of Buddhahood, and speak extensively on the Jātakas; do you wish to transmit my evil deeds to future generations? You should return to your positions and speak no more of this." Thereupon, he took three hundred million of the upper-class families and had them killed at the bank of the Sindhu (信度) River; three hundred million of the middle-class families were drowned and killed in the Sindhu River; and three hundred million of the lower-class families were distributed among the soldiers. Having seized the wealth of the ruined state, he gathered his troops and returned. Before a year had passed, he suddenly died. At that time, clouds and fog grew dark and gloomy, the great earth shook, and violent winds raged. A person who had attained the fruit (of the path) felt pity and sighed, saying, "By unjustly killing the innocent and destroying the Buddha-dharma, he has fallen into the Avīci hell, to transmigrate without end."  In the old city of Śākala (奢羯羅故城), there is a monastery (saṃghārāma) with more than one hundred monks, all of whom study the Hīnayāna teachings. The Bodhisattva Vasubandhu (世親) formerly composed the *Paramārthasaptati* (勝義諦論) here. Beside it is a stūpa over two hundred feet high, where the four past Buddhas preached the Dharma. There is also a site with traces of the four Buddhas walking in meditation. Five or six li to the northwest of the monastery is a stūpa over two hundred feet high, built by King Aśoka (無憂王), which is the place where the four past Buddhas preached the Dharma. More than ten li to the northeast of the new capital city, one reaches a stone stūpa over two hundred feet high, built by King Aśoka, which is the place where the Tathāgata halted midway while traveling north to spread his teachings. The *Account of India* (印度記) says, "There are many relics within the stūpa, and on days of fasting, it sometimes emits light."

en_revised: Traveling eastward from here for more than five hundred li, one arrives at the country of Cīnabhukti (至那僕底國) (within the borders of North India). The country of Cīnabhukti is more than two thousand li in circuit. The capital city is fourteen or fifteen li in circuit. The crops are lush and abundant, but fruit trees are sparse. The households are settled in their occupations, and the national resources are plentiful. The climate is warm and hot; the customs of the people are timid and weak. Their studies encompass both the true and the conventional, and their faith includes both the heterodox and the orthodox. There are ten saṃghārāmas and eight deva temples.  In the past, during the reign of King Kaniṣka (迦膩色迦王), his reputation shook neighboring countries and his might extended to distant lands; the border tribes west of the river feared his power and sent hostages. Once King Kaniṣka had obtained the hostages, he treated them with great generosity and favor, changing their residences according to the three seasons and providing guards from the four branches of the military. This country was his winter residence, and therefore it is called Cīnabhukti (which in the language of the Tang means "Han Fief"). Because it was the place where the hostages resided, it became the name of the country.  From this region onward, as far as the various parts of India, the land had no pears or peaches. They were planted by the hostages, and thus peaches are called *cīnānī* (至那爾) (which in the language of the Tang means "brought from Han"), and pears are called *cīnarājaputra* (至那羅闍弗呾邏) (which in the language of the Tang means "Han Prince"). Therefore, the people of this country deeply revere the eastern lands, and they point to one another and say, "These are the people from the original country of our former king."

en_revised: Traveling more than five hundred *li* to the southeast of the great city, one arrives at the Tamasavana Monastery (答秣蘇伐那僧伽藍) (in the Tang language, "Dark Forest"). There are more than three hundred monks who study the Sarvāstivāda school; their deportment is solemn and their moral conduct is lofty, and they are particularly well-versed in the studies of the Lesser Vehicle. The thousand Buddhas of the Bhadrakalpa all gathered assemblies of gods and humans in this place to preach the profound and wonderful Dharma. In the three-hundredth year after the Nirvāṇa of the Tathāgata Śākyamuni, the master Kātyāyana (formerly called Jiazhanyan [迦旃延], which is erroneous) composed the *Jñānaprasthāna-śāstra* here. Within the Tamasavana Monastery, there is a stūpa over two hundred feet high, which was built by King Aśoka. Beside it are the sites of the seats and walking paths of the four past Buddhas. Small stūpas and various large stone chambers stand facing one another like the scales of a fish, in numbers too many to detail; these are all places where the various sages who have attained fruition since the beginning of the *kalpa* have entered into extinction, and it is difficult to enumerate them all, though their teeth and bones still remain. The monasteries surrounding the mountain cover a circuit of twenty *li*, and there are hundreds of thousands of stūpas containing the Buddha’s relics, with their corners connected and their shadows touching.

en_revised: From here, traveling northeast for one hundred forty or fifty li, one arrives at the country of Jālaṃdhara (闍爛達羅國) (in the territory of North India). The country of Jālaṃdhara is over one thousand li from east to west and over eight hundred li from north to south. The capital city of the country is twelve or thirteen li in circumference. It is suitable for grain crops, with an abundance of non-glutinous rice; the forests and trees are lush and spreading, and flowers and fruits are abundant. The climate is warm and hot; the customs of the people are fierce and unyielding, their appearance is coarse and ugly, and their households are wealthy and prosperous. There are more than fifty saṃghārāmas and over two thousand monks, who study both the Great and Lesser Vehicles. There are three Deva temples, and more than five hundred followers of non-Buddhist paths, all of whom are of the sect that smears themselves with ash.  A former king of this country revered non-Buddhist paths, but later he met an arhat, heard the Dharma, and attained faith and enlightenment. Therefore, the king of Mid-India, recognizing his pure faith, entrusted to him the sole supervision of the affairs of the Three Jewels throughout the five Indias. He made no distinction between this and that, forgot preferences and aversions, supervised the monks, and thoroughly discerned the virtuous and the wicked. Thus, those whose moral character was renowned were honored with utmost sincerity, while those who violated the precepts were severely punished. At all sites of sacred traces, he erected memorials, whether stūpas or saṃghārāmas, and there is no place within the territory of India where these are not found.

en_revised: From here, traveling northeast, crossing steep ridges, traversing deep valleys, passing over perilous routes, and wading through dangerous paths for more than seven hundred *li*, one reaches the country of Kulūta (屈露多國) (屈 is read 居勿反) (within the borders of North India). The country of Kulūta is more than three thousand *li* in circuit, with mountains surrounding its four borders. The capital city of the country is fourteen or fifteen *li* in circuit. The land is fertile, grain is sown in its season, flowers and fruits are abundant, and plants and trees flourish. As it borders the Snow Mountains (Himālaya), it is rich in precious medicinal herbs and produces gold, silver, red copper, as well as fire-pearls and rain-stones. The climate is extremely cold, and frost and snow fall lightly. The people are coarse and ugly in appearance, and are prone to goiters and swollen feet; their nature is fierce and impetuous, and they value spirit and courage. There are more than twenty *saṃghārāmas* (伽藍) with over one thousand monks, most of whom study the Great Vehicle (Mahāyāna), while few practice the various schools (Hīnayāna). There are fifteen *deva* temples, where followers of different paths live together. Relying on cliffs and occupying ridges, stone chambers are situated at intervals, some being dwellings of *arhats* and others being places where *ṛṣis* (仙人) have stayed. In the country there is a *stūpa* built by King Aśoka (無憂王). In the past, the Tathāgata came to this country, preached the Dharma to save people, and this record remains of his traces.

en_revised: From here, traveling east more than five hundred *li*, one arrives at the country of Mathurā (秣菟羅國) (within the borders of Central India). The country of Mathurā is more than five thousand *li* in circuit. The capital city of the country is more than twenty *li* in circuit. The land is fertile and rich, and the people are devoted to agriculture. Every household plants mango trees to form groves; although they share the same name, there are two varieties: the small ones are green when raw and yellow when ripe, while the large ones remain green from beginning to end. The country produces fine striped cotton cloth and gold. The climate is hot, and the customs are honest and compliant; the people delight in cultivating merit for the afterlife, and they revere virtue and value learning. There are more than twenty monasteries and over two thousand monks, who study both the Great and Lesser Vehicles with equal diligence. There are five *deva* temples, where followers of various heterodox sects live together. There are three *stūpas* that were all built by King Aśoka. There are many traces of the four past Buddhas. There are *stūpas* containing the relics of the holy disciples of the Śākya Tathāgata, namely: Śāriputra (formerly called Shelizi or Shelifu, which are erroneous abbreviations), Maudgalyāyana (formerly called Mujianlian, which is erroneous), Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra (called Manci Zi in the Tang language; formerly called Miduoluonizi, which is an erroneous abbreviation), Upāli, Ānanda, Rāhula (formerly called Luohou or Luoyun, both of which are erroneous abbreviations), and Mañjuśrī (called Miaojixiang [妙吉祥] in the Tang language; formerly called Rushou [濡首], also Wenshushili [文殊師利], or sometimes Manshushili [曼殊尸利], translated as 'Wonderful Virtue' [妙德], which is erroneous), and the stūpas of the various Bodhisattvas. During the three long fast months of every year and the six fast days of every month, the members of the Saṅgha compete with one another, leading those of like mind to bring offerings and prepare many rare curiosities, presenting them before the images of their respective patrons. Those who study the Abhidharma make offerings to Śāriputra; those who practice meditation make offerings to Maudgalyāyana; those who recite and uphold the Sūtras make offerings to Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra; those who study the Vinaya make offerings to Upāli; the various bhikṣuṇīs make offerings to Ānanda; those who have not yet received the full ordination make offerings to Rāhula; and those who study the Mahāyāna make offerings to the various Bodhisattvas. On these days, the various stūpas compete in performing offerings; pearl-adorned banners are arrayed in rows, precious canopies are lined up, smoke from incense is like clouds, and flowers are scattered like rain, obscuring the sun and moon and shaking the valleys. The king and his ministers make the cultivation of merit their primary duty.

issues: note （去聲） on 昏 (read in the departing tone) dropped
en_revised: Traveling more than one hundred li to the south of the city, one arrives at the Gukhunda (俱昏荼) (昏 in the departing tone) monastery. Multi-storied pavilions have connected roof ridges, and terraced platforms stand interspersed between them. The community of monks is pure and disciplined, and their deportment is calm and elegant.

en_revised: From here, traveling northeast for more than four hundred li, one arrives at the country of Srughna (窣祿勤那國) (within the borders of Central India). The country of Srughna is over six thousand li in circuit; it borders the Ganges (gaṅgā) river to the east, rests against great mountains to the north, and the Yamunā river flows through the middle of its territory. The capital city of the country is over twenty li in circuit; it borders the Yamunā river to the east. Although it is very desolate, its foundations remain firm. The produce of the land and the suitability of the climate are the same as in the country of Sthāneśvara (薩他泥濕伐羅國). The people are honest and simple by nature, and they revere and believe in non-Buddhist paths. They value the arts and sciences, and esteem both merit and wisdom. There are five monasteries with over one thousand monks, most of whom study the Lesser Vehicle (Hīnayāna), while few study other schools. They deliberate on subtle doctrines and engage in pure, profound discussions; talented scholars from distant regions come here to investigate doctrines and resolve doubts. There are one hundred Deva temples, and the non-Buddhist sects are very numerous. To the southeast of the great city, on the west bank of the Yamunā river and outside the eastern gate of a large monastery, there is a stūpa built by King Aśoka. In the past, the Tathāgata once preached the Dharma here to save people. Beside it is another stūpa, which contains the hair and nails of the Tathāgata. Surrounding it on the left and right are several dozen stūpas containing the hair and nails of the arhats Śāriputra (舍利子) and Maudgalyāyana (沒特伽羅). After the Tathāgata entered extinction, this country was misled by various non-Buddhists; they accepted and followed erroneous teachings and abandoned correct views. The five monasteries that exist today were built at the sites where masters from other countries held debates and emerged victorious over various non-Buddhists and Brahmins.

en_revised: Crossing the river to the east bank, one arrives at the country of Matipura (秣底補羅國) (within the borders of Central India). The country of Matipura is over six thousand li in circuit. The capital city of the country is over twenty li in circuit. It is suitable for grain and wheat, and there are many flowers and fruits. The climate is harmonious and pleasant, and the customs are simple and honest. The people esteem learning and the arts, and are deeply skilled in magical incantations. Those who believe in heterodox paths and those who believe in the orthodox path are about equal in number. The king is of the Śūdra caste; he does not believe in the Buddha-Dharma and reverently serves the heavenly deities. There are more than ten monasteries with over eight hundred monks, most of whom study the Sarvāstivāda school of the Lesser Vehicle teachings. There are more than fifty temples to the heavenly deities, where followers of different paths live together. Four or five li to the south of the great city, one reaches a small monastery with over fifty monks. In the past, the master of treatises Guṇaprabha (in the Tang language, "Virtue-Light") composed the *Tattvavibhaṅga* (辯真) and other treatises here, totaling over one hundred works. The master of treatises was heroic and outstanding in his youth, and broad-minded and quick-witted in his maturity; he was widely learned and possessed a retentive memory, being a scholar of great erudition. Originally, he studied the Mahayana, but not having exhausted its profound mysteries, he read the *Vibhāṣā-śāstra* and subsequently abandoned his former studies to learn the Lesser Vehicle. He composed several dozen treatises, refuting the principles of the Mahayana and establishing the attachments of the Lesser Vehicle. He also produced several dozen secular books, criticizing and rejecting the canonical treatises composed by his predecessors. He pondered the Buddhist scriptures deeply, but there were over ten points he could not resolve; though he studied them with refinement for a long time, his doubts remained. At that time, there was an arhat named Devasena (in the Tang language, "Heavenly Army") who traveled back and forth to the Tuṣita Heaven. Guṇaprabha wished to see Maitreya to resolve his doubts and request further instruction. Devasena, using his supernatural powers, took him up to the heavenly palace. Upon seeing Maitreya (慈氏 - *Maitreya*), he merely made a long bow and did not prostrate. Devasena said to him, "Maitreya Bodhisattva is the next to succeed to the Buddha’s throne; why are you so arrogant that you dare not show him respect? You are seeking to receive instruction, so how can you not humble yourself?" Guṇaprabha (德光 - *Guṇaprabha*) replied, "Venerable one, your words are indeed a guide. However, I am a fully ordained bhikṣu and a monastic disciple, while Maitreya Bodhisattva enjoys the bliss of heavenly rewards and is not a member of the monastic order; I fear it would be inappropriate for me to pay him homage." The Bodhisattva, knowing that his pride was deeply rooted and that he was not a vessel fit to hear the Dharma, allowed him to travel back and forth three times without resolving his doubts. Guṇaprabha asked Devasena again, wishing to pay homage once more, but Devasena, disgusted by his pride, ignored him and did not reply. Since Guṇaprabha did not have his wish fulfilled, he harbored resentment and went into the mountain forests to practice meditation for the attainment of supernatural powers; however, because his pride was not eliminated, he did not realize the fruits of the Path.  Three or four *li* to the north of the Guṇaprabha monastery, there is a large monastery with over two hundred monks, all of whom study the teachings of the Lesser Vehicle (Hīnayāna). This is the place where the master of treatises Saṃghabhadra (眾賢 - *Saṃghabhadra*) passed away. The master of treatises was a man from the country of Kaśmīra (迦濕彌羅國 - *Kaśmīra*); he was intelligent and erudite, and from his youth he was renowned for his elegance, having studied the *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* (說一切有部毘婆沙論) with particular depth. At that time, there was the Bodhisattva Vasubandhu (世親 - *Vasubandhu*), who was single-mindedly devoted to the profound Path and sought to understand the meaning beyond the words. He refuted the positions held by the masters of the *Vibhāṣā* and composed the *Abhidharmakośa-śāstra* (阿毘達磨俱舍論), in which the language and meaning were skillful and the principles were lofty and refined. Saṃghabhadra (眾賢) read it and was moved to action. Thereupon, he delved deeply into study and research for twelve years, composing the *Hailstone on the Kośa* (俱舍雹論) in twenty-five thousand verses, totaling eight hundred thousand words. It was said that his words were profound and his reach far, exhausting the hidden and penetrating the subtle. He told his disciples, "With my outstanding talent and upholding my correct arguments, I shall drive back Vasubandhu (世親) and blunt his sharp edge, so that the old man may no longer enjoy a monopoly on pre-eminent fame." Thereupon, three or four of his most talented disciples took the treatise he had written and went to seek out Vasubandhu. At that time, Vasubandhu was in the city of Sākala (奢羯羅城) in the country of Takka (磔迦國). Word was sent from afar that Saṃghabhadra was arriving. Upon hearing this, Vasubandhu immediately began to pack his belongings. His disciples, filled with doubt, came forward to remonstrate, saying, "Great Master, your virtue surpasses that of former sages and your fame is unrivaled in the present age; among students near and far, there are none who do not defer to you. Now, hearing of Saṃghabhadra, why are you so flustered? If you must yield to him, we will be deeply ashamed." Vasubandhu replied, "I am traveling far away now, not to avoid this man. It is just that in this country, there are no longer any discerning scholars. Saṃghabhadra is a younger scholar whose sophistry flows like a river; I am old and frail and cannot engage in debate. I wish to defeat his heterodox views with a single word and lead him to Central India to face the eminent and learned scholars, so that they may discern truth from falsehood and examine right and wrong." He immediately ordered his companions to pack their book-satchels and set out on the long journey. The Master of Treatises Saṃghabhadra (眾賢) arrived at this monastery one day later, when he suddenly felt his vitality failing. He then composed a letter to apologize to Vasubandhu (世親), saying: "Since the Thus-Come One passed into extinction, the disciples have held to their own sectarian views, each transmitting their own school's learning, each specializing in their own field, favoring those who share their path and disparaging those of different schools. In my ignorance and dullness, I rashly received these traditions. Upon reading the *Abhidharmakośa-śāstra* (阿毘達磨俱舍論) that you composed, which refutes the great principles of the Vaibhāṣika masters, I—without measuring my own strength—spent years in deep study and composed this treatise to uphold the orthodox school. My wisdom was small but my ambition was great, and now death is approaching. You, Bodhisattva, expound the subtle words and propagate the supreme truth; if you do not disparage my convictions and allow my writings to be preserved, I shall be fortunate indeed, and what regret could I have in death?" He then selected from among his disciples those who were eloquent and told them: "I am truly a junior scholar who has rashly insulted a senior master; such is my fate, what can be done? I am about to pass away. You must take this letter and the treatise I have composed, apologize to that Bodhisattva, and repent on my behalf." No sooner had he finished dictating these words than he suddenly passed away. The disciples took the letter to Vasubandhu and delivered the message, saying: "Our master Saṃghabhadra has already abandoned his life. He left a final letter to reproach himself and apologize for his faults. That his name not be forgotten is not something we would dare to hope for." Bodhisattva Vasubandhu read the letter and examined the treatise, and after pondering for a long time, he said to the disciples: "The Master of Treatises Saṃghabhadra was a clever junior; although his reasoning was insufficient, his rhetoric was more than enough. I now wish to refute Saṃghabhadra’s treatise, and it will be as easy as pointing to the palm of my hand." "However, considering his dying request and valuing his challenging words, if it serves the great principles, I shall preserve his original intention; furthermore, this treatise clarifies my own school." He then changed the title to the *Abhidharma-nyāyānusāra-śāstra* (Treatise Following the Correct Principles). His disciples remonstrated, saying: "While Saṃghabhadra was still alive, the Master withdrew far away; now that you have obtained his treatise, you even change its title for him—how can all the students face the shame of this?" Bodhisattva Vasubandhu, wishing to remove their doubts, spoke a verse: "Like a lion king, avoiding a boar and going far away, the wise should know the victory or defeat of the two powers." After Saṃghabhadra died, they cremated his body and collected his bones. In the Āmra (mango) grove, two hundred paces northwest of the monastery, they erected a stūpa, which still exists today. Beside the Āmra grove is a stūpa containing the remains of the master Vimalamitra (in Tang language, "Stainless Friend"). The master was a man of the country of Kaśmīra (迦濕彌羅國) and had renounced the household life in the Sarvāstivāda school. He extensively studied the various scriptures and researched heterodox treatises. He traveled through the five Indias, studied the profound texts of the Tripiṭaka, and having established his reputation and completed his work, he was about to return to his home country. Passing by the stūpa of the master Saṃghabhadra, he patted it and sighed, saying: "The master possessed such noble magnanimity and refined character, expounding the great principles; just as he was about to defeat the heterodox sects and establish the legacy of his own school, how is it that his years were not prolonged! I, Vimalamitra, humbly follow in his footsteps; I have long admired his righteousness and have cherished his virtue across the ages." "Although Vasubandhu (世親) has passed away, his school's teachings are still transmitted. I shall exhaust all my knowledge to compose various treatises, causing the scholars of Jambudvīpa (贍部洲) to abandon the name of the Mahāyāna and to efface the fame of Vasubandhu; this shall be my immortal achievement, fulfilling my long-held ambition." Having spoken these words, his mind became deranged, five tongues emerged from his mouth, and hot blood gushed forth. Knowing that his life was surely coming to an end, he composed a letter of repentance, saying: "The Mahāyāna teachings are the ultimate discourse within the Buddha-dharma. Their names and meanings are profound and absolute, and their principles are subtle and mysterious. Because of my ignorance, I lightly refuted these advanced teachings; the karmic retribution is clear, and it is fitting that my body should be destroyed. I dare to warn all students: take this as a lesson, guard your intentions, and do not harbor doubts." The great earth shook, and his life then ended. At the place where he died, the ground sank into a pit. His traveling companions cremated his corpse, collected the remains, and built a memorial over them. At that time, an Arhat (羅漢) saw this and sighed, saying: "Alas! How painful! This master of treatises, following his own emotions and holding to his views, slandered and disparaged the Mahāyāna, and has fallen into the Avīci (無間) hell."

en_revised: In the Great Snow Mountains to the north of this country lies the kingdom of Suvarṇagotra (translated into Chinese as the "Gold Clan"). It produces superior gold, and is named accordingly. It is long from east to west and narrow from north to south; this is the Eastern Women's Kingdom. For generations, the country has been named after women. The husband is also called king, but he does not manage state affairs; the men's only duties are warfare and farming. The soil is suitable for winter wheat, and there is an abundance of sheep and horses. The climate is cold and harsh, and the people are impetuous and violent. To the east it borders the kingdom of Tubo, to the north it borders the kingdom of Khotan, and to the west it borders the kingdom of Sampaha.

issues: note （中印度境） merged into the running text ("which is within the borders of Central India") → bracketed note; Vilaśāṇa follows variant 刪 (CBETA 毘羅那拏), name kept
en_revised: From here, traveling east for two hundred sixty or seventy li and crossing the Ganges (Gaṅgā) River, one arrives south at the country of Vilaśāṇa (毘羅那拏國) (within the borders of Central India). The country of Vilaśāṇa is over two thousand li in circuit. The capital city of the country is over ten li in circuit. The climate and soil conditions are the same as those of the country of Ahicchatrā (堊醯掣呾邏國). The customs of the people are fierce and violent, yet they are knowledgeable in the arts. They revere and believe in non-Buddhist paths and have little respect for the Buddha-Dharma. There are two monasteries with three hundred monks, all of whom study the teachings of the Great Vehicle. There are five Deva temples where followers of various non-Buddhist paths live together. Inside an old monastery in the great city, there is the base of a stūpa which, although dilapidated, is still over one hundred feet high; it was built by King Aśoka. This is the place where the Tathāgata in the past spent seven days preaching the *Skandhadhātvāyatana-sūtra* (蘊界處經). Beside it are the seats and traces of the walking paths of the four past Buddhas.

issues: One who truly manifests is one who perceives that all phenomena are empty → 夫善現者 善現 is Subhūti's name: 'Subhūti, contemplating the emptiness of dharmas, has seen the Dharma-body' (recurs from earlier review); tens of thousands of laypeople → 淨人 'monastery servants' (recurs); Devāvatāra (三寶階) → 'three precious stairways' (recurs); *mūla-gandha-kuṭī* (精舍) → plain 精舍 'vihāra' (recurs); Subhūti note rendered as "Original note: In Tang language, 'Subhūti' means…" and 須菩提 given as "Subuti" → normal gloss form
en_revised: More than twenty *li* west of the city is a large monastery, its construction magnificent and its craftsmanship exquisite; the sacred forms and venerable images are adorned with the utmost solemnity. There are several hundred monks who study the teachings of the Saṃmitīya school, and tens of thousands of monastery servants (淨人) reside in its vicinity. Within the great wall of the monastery are the three precious stairways (三寶階), arranged from north to south and facing east, where the Tathāgata returned from the Trāyastriṃśa heaven. In the past, the Tathāgata rose from the Jetavana (勝林) and ascended to the heavenly palace, where he resided in the Hall of Good Dharma (Sudharmā-sabhā) to preach the Dharma for his mother. After three months had passed, he intended to descend. Śakra, the Lord of Devas, then exercised his divine power to establish a precious stairway: the middle step was of gold, the left of crystal, and the right of silver. The Tathāgata rose from the Hall of Good Dharma and, followed by a host of deities, stepped down the middle stairway; the Great Brahmā King, holding a white whisk, walked on the silver stairway to attend on the right; Śakra, the Lord of Devas, holding a precious canopy, stepped on the crystal stairway to attend on the left; the heavenly host hovered in the void, scattering flowers and praising his virtues. Several hundred years ago, the stairs still existed, but by the present time, they have completely sunk into the earth. The kings of various countries, lamenting that they could not see them, stacked bricks and stones and decorated them with precious gems upon the original foundation to imitate the ancient precious stairway. It is over seventy feet high, and a *vihāra* (精舍) is built upon it. Inside is a stone Buddha image, and on the stairs to the left and right are images of Śakra and Brahmā, modeled after the original appearance, still in a descending posture. Beside it is a stone pillar, over seventy feet high, erected by King Aśoka (無憂王). Its color is dark blue and lustrous, its substance hard and fine-grained. At the top is a lion, crouching and facing the stairway, with strange forms carved and engraved around its four sides; according to the merit or demerit of the person, shadows appear within the pillar. Not far from the precious stairway is a stūpa, which is the site of the traces where the four past Buddhas sat and performed walking meditation. Beside it is a stūpa where the Tathāgata formerly bathed. Beside that is a *vihāra* (精舍), which is the place where the Tathāgata entered into meditation. Beside the *vihāra* is a large stone, fifty paces long and seven feet high, which is the place where the Tathāgata performed walking meditation. The footprints he trod upon all have lotus patterns. To the left and right of the base are small stūpas, built by Śakra (帝釋) and Brahmā (梵王). In front of the stūpas of Śakra and Brahmā is the place where the bhikṣuṇī Utpalavarṇā (蓮華色), wishing to be the first to see the Buddha, transformed herself into a wheel-turning king. When the Tathāgata returned from the heavenly palace to Jambudvīpa, at that time Subhūti (蘇部底) (in the Tang language, Shanxian, 'Good Manifestation'; formerly called Xufuti [須扶提] or Xuputi [須菩提], translated as Shanji [善吉], 'Good Auspicious', all of which are erroneous) was sitting in meditation in a stone chamber and thought to himself: "Now the Buddha is descending, guided and followed by humans and devas. As for someone like me, what is appropriate to do? I have heard the Buddha say that to know all phenomena are empty and to realize the nature of all phenomena is to behold the Dharma-body with the eye of wisdom." At that time, the bhikṣuṇī Utpalavarṇā, wishing to be the first to see the Buddha, transformed herself into a wheel-turning king, guided by the seven treasures and guarded by the fourfold army, and upon arriving at the place of the World-Honored One, she returned to her form as a bhikṣuṇī. The Tathāgata replied, "You are not the first to see me. Shanxian (Subhūti), contemplating the emptiness of all phenomena — it is he who has seen the Dharma-body." Within the enclosure of the sacred traces, miraculous signs occurred one after another. To the southeast of the great stūpa, there is a dragon pond, and the dragon constantly protects the sacred traces. Because there is this unseen protection, they are difficult to violate lightly; though they have decayed naturally over the long years, no person has been able to destroy them. Traveling southeast from here for less than two hundred li, one arrives at the country of Kanyakubja (羯若鞠闍國) (in the language of Tang, the Kingdom of the Hunchbacked Maiden City; it is within the borders of Central India).

en_revised: The country of Kanyākubja (羯若鞠闍國) is over four thousand li in circumference. The capital city borders the Gaṅgā (殑伽河) to the west; it is over twenty li in length and four to five li in breadth. The city moats and ramparts are solid and steep, with towers and pavilions facing one another, and flower groves and ponds that are bright and clear as mirrors. Rare goods from distant regions are mostly gathered here. The inhabitants are prosperous and happy, and their households are wealthy and abundant. Flowers and fruits are plentiful, and crops are sown in their proper seasons. The climate is harmonious and mild, and the customs are honest and simple. The people are refined in appearance and wear bright and elegant clothing. They are devoted to learning and skilled in the arts, and their discourse is clear and profound. Regarding the two paths of the heterodox and the orthodox, the number of believers is about equal. There are over one hundred saṅghārāmas and more than ten thousand monks, who study both the Great and Small Vehicles with equal diligence. There are over two hundred deva temples, and several thousand followers of heterodox paths.  In the age when the people of the country of Kanyākubja enjoyed long lives, the old capital city was called Kusumapura (拘蘇磨補羅) (Original note: In the language of the Tang, this means "Flowery Palace"). The king was named Brahmadatta (梵授); he possessed the accumulated merits of wisdom and virtue, was fully accomplished in both civil and military affairs, his power intimidated Jambudvīpa, and his fame shook neighboring countries. He had a full thousand sons, who were wise, brave, magnanimous, and resolute; he also had one hundred daughters, who were beautiful in appearance and refined in manner.  At that time, there was a rishi living by the side of the Gaṅgā who concentrated his spirit in meditative absorption for tens of thousands of years until his form resembled a withered tree. Migratory birds perched and gathered there, dropping a nyagrodha fruit upon the rishi's shoulder; as summers went and winters came, it cast a shade and grew to the size of an arch. After many years had passed, he rose from his meditation and wished to remove the tree, but fearing he might overturn the birds' nests, he desisted. The people of the time praised his virtue and called him the "Rishi of the Big Tree." The rishi cast his eyes along the riverbank and wandered through the thickets, where he saw the king’s daughters playing together. Desire for the world of the senses arose, and a heart of attachment was born; he then went to the magnificent palace, wishing to make a formal request. When the king heard the rishi had arrived, he went to welcome him in person and greeted him, saying, "The great rishi dwells in spirit beyond the material world; what has prompted this sudden visit?" The rishi said, "I have dwelt in the forest and marshes for many years. Emerging from meditation to wander, I saw the king’s daughters, and a heart of attachment was born; I have come from afar to make a request." Hearing these words, the king was at a loss for a plan and said to the rishi, "Return now to your dwelling; please wait for an auspicious day." The rishi heard this command and returned to the forest and marshes. The king then asked each of his daughters in turn, but none would consent to the marriage. Fearing the rishi’s power, the king became sorrowful and haggard. His youngest daughter, waiting for a break in the king’s affairs, calmly asked, "Father, you have a full thousand sons and ten thousand nations admire your transformation; for what reason are you so sorrowful, as if you are in fear?" The king said, "The Rishi of the Big Tree (Mahāvṛkṣa-ṛṣi) has deigned to seek a marriage alliance, yet none of you sisters are willing to obey. An immortal possesses great power and can bring about either disaster or fortune; if his heart’s desire is not met, he will surely fall into a rage, destroying the kingdom, ending our ancestral sacrifices, and bringing shame upon the late kings. Deeply contemplating this calamity, I am truly afraid." The youngest daughter replied, "To have caused this deep sorrow is our fault. I am willing to offer my humble self to preserve the prosperity of the state." Hearing this, the king was overjoyed; he ordered a carriage to be prepared and sent her to him. Upon arriving at the hermit’s hut, the king thanked the hermit, saying, "The great hermit has condescended from his transcendent state to show concern for worldly affairs; I dare to offer my young daughter to serve you by sweeping and cleaning." The hermit saw her and was displeased, saying to the king, "You slight this old man by matching me with one so unattractive." The king replied, "I have asked all my daughters, and none were willing to obey. Only this young one is willing to serve as a maid." The hermit, harboring anger, uttered a wicked curse: "May the ninety-nine daughters all have their waists bent at once; their forms being thus ruined and spoiled, they shall have no marriage for their entire lives." The king sent someone to verify this, and indeed, their backs were already hunched. From that time on, it has been called the City of the Hunchbacked Maidens (Kanyakubja).  The present king is of the Vaiśya caste, and his name is Harṣavardhana (translated into Chinese as "Increment of Happiness"). He rules over the land, the third king of two generations. His father’s name was Prabhākaravardhana (translated into Chinese as "Increment of Light"), and his elder brother’s name was Rājyavardhana (translated into Chinese as "Increment of the Kingdom"). Rājyavardhana succeeded to the throne as the eldest and governed with virtue. At that time, King Śaśāṅka (translated into Chinese as "Moon") of the kingdom of Karṇasuvarṇa (translated into Chinese as "Golden Ear") in East India often said to his ministers, "To have a virtuous ruler in a neighboring state is a misfortune for one's own country." Thereupon, he lured and invited him, and at the meeting, he killed him. Once the people had lost their ruler, the country fell into chaos. At that time, the high minister Bhaṇi (translated into Chinese as "Eloquent and Wise"), whose position and reputation were of great weight, said to the officials and the populace, "The great plan for the country must be decided this day." "The son of the former king and younger brother of the deceased monarch is benevolent by nature and filial by heart; he is truly close to the virtuous, and I wish for him to succeed to the throne. What do you think of this matter? Each of you, speak your mind." The assembly all looked up to his virtue, and there was never any dissenting opinion. Thereupon, the assistant ministers and officials all exhorted him to take the throne, saying: "May the prince listen to us; the late king accumulated merits and cultivated virtues, gloriously possessing the mandate of the state. The succession reached Rājyavardhana, and we expected him to live out his full span of years; but his assistants were not good, and he abandoned his life at the hands of an enemy—this is a great shame for the country and the fault of us, your humble servants. Public opinion and the rumors of the time truly point to your brilliant virtue. If you were to grace the land and the territory, avenge your kin upon the enemy, wash away the shame of the country, and glorify the legacy of your father, what merit could be greater than this? We hope you will not decline!"  The prince said, "The matter of national succession has been a difficult one from ancient times to the present; the establishment of one in the position of a sovereign must be considered with great prudence. I am truly lacking in virtue, and now that my father and elder brother have been taken from me, if I were to be pushed to succeed to the great throne, would I be able to succeed in my duties? Although public opinion deems it appropriate, how could I forget my own insignificance? Now, on the bank of the Gaṅgā (殑伽河) river, there is an image of the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara (觀自在菩薩) which is highly responsive; I wish to go there to seek guidance."   He immediately went before the Bodhisattva's image and fasted to make his request. The Bodhisattva, moved by his sincerity, manifested his form and asked, "What do you seek, that you are so diligent and earnest?" The prince said, "I have only accumulated disasters; my benevolent father has passed away, and to add to this cruel punishment, my virtuous elder brother has been murdered. Reflecting on myself, I am lacking in virtue, yet the people of the country honor me and urge me to succeed to the great throne to glorify my father's legacy." "I am foolish and ignorant; how dare I hope for the holy decree!" The Bodhisattva replied, "In your former life, you were an āraṇyaka-bhikṣu (練若苾芻) in this forest, and you were diligent and unremitting. By the power of that merit, you have become this prince. Since the King of Karṇasuvarṇa (金耳國王) has destroyed the Buddha-dharma, you, in succeeding to the throne, should revive it; let compassion be your aim and sympathy dwell in your heart, and you will soon be the ruler of the five regions of India. If you wish to extend the prosperity of the state, you must follow my instructions; then, through hidden blessings, you will have no powerful enemies in the neighboring lands. Do not ascend the lion throne, and do not assume the title of Great King."  Thereupon, having received these instructions, he withdrew and assumed the throne, calling himself "The Prince" and taking the title Śīlāditya (尸羅阿迭多) (in the language of Tang, this means "Sun of Precepts"). He then said to his ministers, "The vengeance for my brother has not been requited, and the neighboring countries have not submitted; I shall not have a moment to eat with my right hand. Let all you officials be of one mind and exert your strength." He then gathered the national troops and trained his soldiers. He had 5,000 elephant troops, 20,000 cavalry, and 50,000 infantry, and from the west to the east, he campaigned against those who would not submit. Without the elephants being unsaddled or the men removing their armor, he brought the five regions of India into submission within six years. Having expanded his territory, he further increased his military forces, reaching 60,000 elephant troops and 100,000 cavalry. For nearly thirty years, the weapons of war were not raised, and the government and teachings were peaceful. He devoted himself to frugality, cultivated merit and goodness, and forgot both sleep and food. He ordered that no meat be eaten throughout the five regions of India, and if anyone took a life, they would be executed without pardon. Along the banks of the Ganges (gaṅgā), he erected several thousand stūpas, each over one hundred feet high. In the cities, villages, thoroughfares, and crossroads of the five regions of India, he established hospices (精廬) stocked with food, drink, and medicine to be distributed to travelers and the poor, providing for them without ceasing. At every site of a sacred relic, he built a monastery (saṅghārāma). Every five years, he held a great pan-charity assembly (pañcavārṣika), emptying the royal treasury to bestow gifts upon all beings, withholding only the weaponry from his charitable offerings. Every year, he gathered śramaṇas from various countries for a meeting lasting twenty-one days, during which he provided them with the four requisites, grandly decorated the Dharma seats and discussion halls, and had them engage in debate to assess their relative merits, praise the virtuous and criticize the evil, and demote the ignorant while promoting the enlightened. Those whose observance of the precepts was steadfast and whose moral character was profound were invited to ascend the lion seat, and the king would receive the Dharma from them in person. Those whose precepts were pure but whose learning was not grounded in the classics were merely treated with respect to show his veneration. Those who had no discipline and whose corrupt conduct was manifest were driven out of the country, as he did not wish to see or hear of them. If the minor rulers and assistant ministers of neighboring countries cultivated merit without ceasing and sought goodness without weariness, the king would take them by the hand to sit together and call them his "virtuous friends." If they were otherwise, he would not meet them face-to-face, and if there were matters to discuss, he would communicate only through the exchange of envoys. He toured the regions to inspect the customs of the people and did not have a fixed residence, building temporary huts wherever he stopped. Only during the three months of the rainy season did he cease traveling due to the heavy rains. At his temporary palaces, he would daily prepare fine meals to feed one thousand monks and five hundred Brahmins of various schools. He divided each day into three periods: one period for managing affairs and governing, and two periods for cultivating merit and practicing virtue. He was diligent and tireless, feeling that the day was never long enough. Initially, I had accepted an invitation from King Kumāra to travel from the country of Magadha (摩揭陀國) to the country of Kāmarūpa (迦摩縷波國). At that time, King Śīlāditya (戒日王) was on a tour of inspection in the country of Kajuṅghira (羯朱嗢祇羅國) and commanded King Kumāra, saying: "You should come quickly with the guest śramaṇa from Nālandā (那爛陀) to attend the assembly." Thereupon, I went with King Kumāra to meet him. After King Śīlāditya had offered greetings, he asked: "From what country have you come, and what is it that you seek?" I replied: "I have come from the Great Tang (大唐國) to seek the Buddha-Dharma." The king asked: "In what direction does the Great Tang lie? What is the extent of the route, and how far is it from here?" I replied: "It lies more than several tens of thousands of *li* to the northeast of here; it is what you in India call the country of Mahācīna (摩訶至那國)." The king said: "I have heard that in the country of Mahācīna there is a Son of Heaven, the Prince of Qin (秦王天子), who was perceptive and wise in his youth and has become divinely martial in his maturity. In the past, when the previous dynasty fell into chaos, the land was divided and collapsed, weapons of war arose on all sides, and the masses were poisoned by suffering. The Prince of Qin, however, early on cherished far-reaching strategies, aroused great compassion, rescued all sentient beings, and pacified the world. His civilizing influence reached far and wide, and his virtuous grace extended to distant places; strange lands and foreign regions admired his transformation and declared themselves his subjects. The people, having received his protection and nurturing, all sing the 'Music of the Prince of Qin Breaking the Ranks' (秦王破陣樂). I have heard these elegant hymns for a long time now. Is the reputation of his magnificent virtue truly as it is said? Is the Great Tang this country?" I replied, 'It is. Cīna (至那) was the name of the country under former kings; Great Tang is the title of my sovereign's realm. Before he ascended the throne, he was called the Prince of Qin; now that he has assumed the succession, he is titled the Son of Heaven. When the fortune of the previous dynasty ended, the masses were without a master, weapons of war arose in chaos, and living beings were cruelly harmed. The Prince of Qin, endowed by Heaven with vast magnanimity, felt compassion in his heart; his majestic influence stirred and spread, the various violent factions were exterminated, the eight directions were pacified, and ten thousand nations came to pay tribute. He loves and nurtures the four forms of birth, reveres and honors the Three Jewels, lightens taxes and levies, and reduces punishments; yet the state’s resources are abundant, and the common people have no need for hidden shelters. His civilizing influence and great transformation are difficult to fully describe.' King Śīlāditya (戒日王) said, 'Magnificent! The living beings of that land are blessed to be moved by such a holy lord.'  At that time, King Śīlāditya was about to return to the city of Kanyākubja (曲女城) to hold a religious assembly, followed by hundreds of thousands of people on the southern bank of the Ganges (殑伽河). King Kumāra (拘摩羅王) followed with tens of thousands of people, residing on the northern bank. They divided the river between them and advanced by both land and water. The two kings led the way, escorted by the four divisions of the army; some sailed in boats, others rode elephants, beating drums, blowing conches, and playing string and wind instruments. After ninety days, they reached the city of Kanyākubja, located in the Great Flower Wood to the west of the Ganges. At that time, more than twenty kings of various countries, having previously received the summons, arrived with the eminent śramaṇas, brahmans, officials, and soldiers of their respective kingdoms to gather for the great assembly. The King had previously built a large monastery (saṃghārāma) on the west side of the river. To the east of the monastery, he erected a precious terrace over one hundred feet high, in which was a golden Buddha image equal in size to the King’s own body. To the south of the terrace, he built a precious altar as a place to bathe the Buddha image. Fourteen or fifteen li to the northeast of this, he constructed a separate temporary palace. It was then the month of the middle of spring. From the first day of the month until the twenty-first, he provided delicious food to all the śramaṇas and brahmans. From the temporary palace to the monastery, pavilions were built along the sides of the road, decorated with every ornament, where musicians remained stationed, playing elegant music in succession.  The King brought out a golden image from the temporary palace, hollow and embossed, over three feet in height; it was loaded onto a large elephant and covered with a precious canopy. King Śīlāditya (戒日王), dressed in the attire of Indra (帝釋), held a precious canopy and attended on the left, while King Kumāra (拘摩羅王) assumed the guise of Brahmā (梵王), holding a white fly-whisk and attending on the right. Five hundred elephant-mounted soldiers on each side, clad in armor, provided a protective escort, while a hundred great elephants preceded and followed the Buddha image, carrying musicians who played music and beat drums. King Śīlāditya scattered pearls, various jewels, and gold and silver flowers at every step as an offering to the Three Jewels. First, they proceeded to the precious altar to bathe the image with perfumed water; then the King personally carried the image and escorted it to the western terrace, offering tens of hundreds of thousands of jewels and kauśeya garments as offerings. At that time, only twenty-some śramaṇas were permitted to follow, while the various kings served as guards. Once the meal was finished, he gathered the various heterodox scholars to discuss subtle doctrines and clarify profound principles. As the sun approached dusk, the King returned to his temporary palace. In this manner, he escorted the golden image daily, with the procession following as before, until the day of the dispersal. Suddenly, a fire broke out on the great terrace, and smoke and flames began to rage at the gatehouse of the monastery. The King said: "I have exhausted the treasures of the nation to build this monastery in honor of my late father, so as to manifest his magnificent achievements; yet my lack of virtue has left me without protection, resulting in such a disaster—with such an omen of calamity, what is the use of living!" He then burned incense, made a respectful petition, and took a vow, saying: "By the grace of my past good deeds, I have become a king over all India; may the power of my merit extinguish this fire, and if there is no spiritual response, I shall lose my life from this moment forth!" He immediately exerted himself, leaped across the threshold of the gate, and as if by some force extinguishing it, the fire died out and the smoke vanished. The various kings witnessed this miracle and their awe and reverence increased. Afterward, the King’s expression remained unchanged and his speech was as usual; he asked the various kings: "Suddenly this disaster has occurred, burning and destroying the finished work; what is in your hearts, and what are your thoughts?" The various kings prostrated themselves, weeping in sorrow, and replied: "This magnificent achievement was hoped to be passed on to future generations; now that it is reduced to ashes in an instant, how can we not be grieved? Furthermore, the various heterodox scholars are rejoicing in their hearts!" The King said: "Viewing it from this perspective, what the Tathāgata said is true. The heterodox scholars and those of different doctrines cling to the view of permanence, whereas only our Great Master teaches impermanence. However, my giving and renunciation have already been completed, and my heart’s desire has been fulfilled. Encountering this destruction, I have come to know once again the truthful teaching of the Tathāgata; this is a great good, and there is no reason for deep sorrow." Thereupon, he followed the various kings to the east to ascend the great stūpa to view the surroundings. Just as he was descending the steps, a strange man suddenly appeared holding a blade to confront the King. The King, in that moment of peril, retreated up the steps, bent down to seize the man, and handed him over to his officials. At that time, the officials were in a state of panic and did not know how to advance to rescue him. The various kings all requested that this man be executed, but King Śīlāditya (戒日王) showed no sign of anger and merely ordered that he not be killed. The King personally asked, "What have I done to wrong you that you would commit such a violent and evil act?" He replied, "Your Majesty’s virtuous grace is impartial, and both within and without the realm, all are indebted to you. However, I am mad and foolish; without considering the grander scheme, I was moved by a single word from the heretics to become an assassin and plot this treasonous murder." The King asked, "For what reason did the heretics harbor such evil intentions?" He replied, "Your Majesty has assembled the various nations and emptied the treasury to provide offerings to the śramaṇas and to cast Buddha images, yet the heretics, who were summoned from afar, have not been granted an audience; they truly feel ashamed and humiliated. This led me, in my madness and folly, to dare to commit this violent deception." Thereupon, the King investigated the followers of the heretics. There were five hundred Brahmins, all of them men of high talent, who had assembled by royal command; envious of the śramaṇas receiving the King's respect and honors, they shot fire-arrows to burn the precious terrace, hoping that in the ensuing chaos as people rushed to put out the fire, they could kill the Great King. Having found no other opportunity, they hired this man to rush into the narrow passage and carry out the assassination. At that time, the various kings and ministers requested that the heretics be executed, but the King only punished the ringleaders, left the remaining partisans unpunished, and banished the five hundred Brahmins from the borders of India. Thereupon, he returned to the capital.  To the northwest of the city is a stūpa built by King Aśoka (無憂王). In the past, the Tathāgata spent seven days here preaching various wonderful Dharmas. Beside it are the traces of where the four past Buddhas sat and walked. There are also small stūpas containing the hair and nails of the Tathāgata.  To the south of the preaching stūpa, overlooking the Ganges (殑伽河) river, there are three monasteries (saṃghārāma) sharing the same wall but having separate gates; the Buddha images are magnificent and beautiful, the monastic community is solemn and respectful, and they employ several thousand households of monastery servants (淨人). In the precious casket of the *vihāra* (精舍) is a tooth of the Buddha, over an inch and a half long, of extraordinary luster and changing colors, shifting from morning to evening. People from near and far flock there, and the gentry and commoners gather in great numbers, daily numbering a hundred thousand, to perform acts of veneration. Because the overseers were troubled by the noise and confusion, they provisionally established a heavy tax, announcing to those near and far: "Those who wish to see the Buddha's tooth must pay a large sum of gold." Nevertheless, the number of those coming to pay homage remained vast, and they were happy to compete in their hearts to pay the gold tax. On every fast day, it is brought out and placed on a high seat; hundreds of thousands of people burn incense and scatter flowers, and although the flowers pile up, the tooth casket is never submerged.  To the left and right in front of the monasteries, there is a *vihāra*, each over a hundred feet high, with stone foundations and brick chambers; the Buddha images within are adorned with various jewels, some cast in gold or silver, others smelted from brass (鍮石). In front of each of the two *vihāra*s is a small monastery. Not far to the southeast of the monastery, there is a large *vihāra* (精舍) with stone foundations and brick chambers, over two hundred feet in height. Inside is a standing image of the Tathāgata, over thirty feet high, cast in brass (鍮石) and adorned with various wonderful jewels. On the stone walls surrounding the *vihāra*, the deeds experienced by the Tathāgata while practicing the bodhisattva path are carved and painted, fully and exhaustively engraved. Not far to the south of the stone *vihāra*, there is a temple to the Sun God (Āditya-deva). Not far to the south of that temple, there is a temple to Maheśvara (大自在天). Both are polished with blue stone and are equally exhaustive in their carvings; their scale and dimensions are the same as the Buddha’s *vihāra*. Each has a thousand households assigned to sweep and clean them, with drums, music, and singing continuing day and night without cessation. Six or seven li to the southeast of the great city, on the south bank of the Gaṅgā (殑伽河), there is a stūpa over two hundred feet high, built by King Aśoka (無憂王). In the past, the Tathāgata spent six months here speaking on the impermanence, suffering, emptiness, and impurity of the body. Beside it are the sites of the seats and walking paths of the four past Buddhas. There are also small stūpas containing the hair and nails of the Tathāgata; when people are afflicted with illness, if they circumambulate them with utmost sincerity, they will certainly be cured and receive their blessings.

issues: Buddhadeva → 佛陀馱婆 with the note 唐言覺使 'Buddha's servant' = Buddhadāsa (Buddhadeva would be 佛陀提婆 覺天); misread name, recurs from earlier review (Mizutani emends 婆 to 娑, Buddhadāsa; CBETA has 婆 – transliteration inexact, the gloss decides); note garbled as '(唐言覺使 - Original note: …)' → render as bracketed note; 北至 now correctly 'arrives north at' (earlier error fixed)
en_revised: From here, traveling east for more than three hundred li and crossing the Ganges River (gaṅgā), one arrives north at the kingdom of Ayamukha (阿耶穆佉國) (within the borders of Central India). The kingdom of Ayamukha is two thousand four or five hundred li in circuit. The capital city of the kingdom borders the Ganges River and is more than twenty li in circuit. Its climate and soil conditions are the same as those of the kingdom of Ayodhyā (阿踰陀國). The people are honest and simple in their customs, diligent in study, and fond of meritorious deeds. There are five monasteries with over one thousand monks, who study the teachings of the Sāmmitīya school of the Lesser Vehicle. There are more than ten Deva temples, where followers of various sects live together. Not far to the southeast of the city, on the bank of the Ganges River, there is a stūpa built by King Aśoka, over two hundred feet high, which is the place where the Tathāgata formerly preached the Dharma for three months. Beside it are the sites of the seats and walking paths of the four past Buddhas. There is also a stūpa of blue stone containing the hair and nails of the Tathāgata. Beside it is a monastery with over two hundred monks; the Buddha images are adorned and majestic, as if he were still present. The towers and pavilions are magnificent, with unique structures rising high; this is where the master of treatises Buddhadāsa (佛陀馱婆) (in the language of the Tang, "Servant of the Buddha") formerly composed the *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* of the Sarvāstivāda school.

they have sought to make offerings to it, all claiming to have obtained the true image → 遂圖供養，俱言得真 'they had copies (圖) made for worship, each claiming its copy is true to the original'; the original is this image (recurs from earlier review; Mizutani: 模写の像を作り); *mūla-gandha-kuṭī* (精舍) → vihāra (recurs), and 'the sandalwood image (mūla-gandha-kuṭī)' is a garbled gloss; note on Udayana: (唐言出愛; formerly inaccurately called King Youtian) → gloss left untranslated and Chinese name missing: 鄔陀衍那王 (in the Tang language, 'Giving Rise to Love'; formerly called 優填王, which is erroneous)
en_revised: From here, traveling southwest into a great forest, one encounters ferocious beasts and wild elephants that attack travelers in herds; unless one has a large party, it is difficult to pass through. After traveling more than five hundred *li*, one arrives at the country of Kauśāmbī (憍賞彌國) (formerly called the country of Kausāmbi, which is incorrect; it is within the borders of Central India). The country of Kauśāmbī is over six thousand *li* in circumference. The capital city is over thirty *li* in circumference. The soil is described as fertile, the land is rich in produce, and there is much *śāli* rice and abundant sugarcane. The climate is hot, and the customs of the people are fierce and impetuous. They are fond of learning and the arts, and they esteem and cultivate merit and goodness. There are more than ten *saṃghārāmas*, which are dilapidated and overgrown, with over three hundred monks who study the teachings of the Lesser Vehicle. There are more than fifty *deva* temples, and the followers of non-Buddhist paths are very numerous. Within the old palace in the city, there is a large *vihāra* (精舍) over sixty feet high, housing a sandalwood Buddha image with a stone canopy suspended above it, which was made by King Udayana (鄔陀衍那王) (in the language of the Tang, "Giving Rise to Love"; formerly called King Youtian (優填王), which is erroneous). Miraculous signs appear from time to time, and divine light shines forth occasionally. Kings of various countries, relying on their strength, have wished to move it, but although they brought many people, none could shift it. Consequently, they have had copies made for worship, each claiming to have obtained the true likeness; when one speaks of their origin, it is indeed this very image. Initially, after the Tathāgata attained perfect enlightenment, he ascended to the heavenly palace to preach the Dharma for his mother, and for three months he did not return. The king, longing for him, wished to have his likeness made. He then requested the Venerable Maudgalyāyana to use his supernatural powers to transport an artisan to the heavenly palace to personally observe the Buddha's marvelous features and carve an image from sandalwood. When the Tathāgata returned from the heavenly palace, the sandalwood image rose to greet the World-Honored One, who consoled it, saying: "Have you been weary from the work of converting and guiding others? You are truly the hope for guiding those in the final age." More than one hundred paces to the east of the monastery are the sites containing the traces of where the four past Buddhas sat and walked. Not far to the side are a well and a bathhouse used by the Tathāgata; the well still provides water for drawing, but the bathhouse has fallen into ruin.

issues: formerly transcribed as Jushiluo → the old form is 瞿師羅 (Qushiluo); Jushiluo is the new form 具史羅 itself; Chinese name missing; Buddhist temple (mūla-gandha-kuṭī) → 佛精舍 'Buddha-vihāra' (recurs); *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-śāstra* → 唯識論 just 'treatise on consciousness-only' (recurs from earlier review); *Abhidharmasamuccaya-śāstra* → 顯揚聖教論 = *Āryaśāsanaprakaraṇa* (recurs); bathroom → bathhouse
en_revised: In the southeast corner of the city are the remaining foundations of an old residence, which was the former home of the elder Ghoṣila (具史羅) (formerly called Qushiluo (瞿師羅), which is erroneous). Within it are a Buddha-*vihāra* (佛精舍) and a stupa containing hair and nail relics. There are also old foundations that were the bathhouse of the Tathāgata. Not far to the southeast of the city is an old monastery, which was the former garden of the elder Ghoṣila. Within it is a stupa built by King Aśoka, over two hundred feet high. The Tathāgata preached the Dharma here for several years. Beside it are the seats of the four past Buddhas and the sites of their walking meditation, as well as another stupa containing the hair and nail relics of the Tathāgata. In a brick chamber on an upper story to the southeast of the monastery, the Bodhisattva Vasubandhu once resided and composed a treatise on consciousness-only (唯識論) to refute the Lesser Vehicle and challenge various non-Buddhist schools. In an Āmra (mango) grove to the east of the monastery are old foundations where the Bodhisattva Asaṅga composed the *Āryaśāsanaprakaraṇa* (顯揚聖教論). Eight or nine *li* to the southwest of the city is the stone cavern of a poisonous dragon. In the past, the Tathāgata subdued this poisonous dragon and left his shadow within it; although this is recorded in the chronicles, it cannot be seen today. Beside it is a stupa built by King Aśoka, over two hundred feet high. Nearby are the sites of the Tathāgata’s walking meditation and a stupa containing his hair and nail relics; those suffering from illnesses who pray there are often healed. When the Dharma of Śākyamuni reaches its end, this country will be the last to remain; therefore, from the sovereign above down to the common people, all who enter the borders of this country naturally feel a sense of sorrow, and there is no one who does not weep and return home with sighs of lamentation.
