en_revised: Traveling northward from here for one hundred and seventy or eighty li, one arrives at the country of Viśākhā (鞞索迦國) (索 is read 山格反) (within the borders of Central India). The country of Viśākhā is over four thousand li in circuit. The capital city is sixteen li in circuit. The crops are abundant, and flowers and fruits are plentiful. The climate is temperate and pleasant, and the customs are honest and simple. The people are fond of learning without fatigue and are unswerving in their pursuit of merit. There are more than twenty saṃghārāmas and over three thousand monks, all of whom study the teachings of the Sāṃmitīya school of the Lesser Vehicle. There are more than fifty deva temples, and there are many followers of non-Buddhist paths. To the left of the road south of the city, there is a large saṃghārāma. In the past, the Arhat Devaśarman (提婆設摩) composed the *Vijñānakāya-śāstra* (識身論) here, which argues that there is no self or person; the Arhat Gopa (瞿波) composed the *Treatise on the Essential Truth of the Sacred Teaching* (聖教要實論), which argues that there is a self and a person. Because of this difference in doctrinal adherence, they engaged in deep debate. Furthermore, it was here that the Bodhisattva Dharmapāla (護法) defeated one hundred masters of the Lesser Vehicle in seven days. Beside the saṃghārāma is a stūpa, over two hundred feet high, built by King Aśoka. In the past, the Tathāgata spent six years here preaching the Dharma and guiding the people. Beside the place where he preached is a marvelous tree, six or seven feet high; as spring and autumn succeed one another, it remains constant, neither increasing nor decreasing. It is said that the Tathāgata once cleaned his teeth here and discarded the twig, which then took root and has remained lush to this day. Various people of wrong views and followers of non-Buddhist paths have vied to cut it down, but it immediately grows back as it was before. Not far from there is the site of the seats and walking paths of the four past Buddhas. There is also a stūpa containing the hair and nails of the Tathāgata. The spiritual foundations are connected at the corners, and the woods and ponds reflect one another. Traveling northeast from here for more than five hundred li, one arrives at the country of Śrāvastī (室羅伐悉底國) (formerly called Shewei, which is an error; it is within the borders of Central India).

issues: Old transcriptions in the notes mis-romanized: 'Posinì' → 波斯匿 Bosini; 'Bojeboti' → 波闍波提 Bozhebotí; 'Yangjumolu' → 央掘摩羅 Yangjuemoluo. Notes otherwise correct and bracketed. Earlier errors (捨邪, 故宮城, 善施 = Sudatta, 歸命) do not recur
en_revised: The country of Śrāvastī (室羅伐悉底國) is over 6,000 li in circuit. The capital city is desolate and ruined, and its boundaries are not clearly defined. The old foundations of the palace city are over 20 li in circuit; although it is largely ruined and overgrown, there are still inhabitants. The grain crops are abundant, and the climate is temperate. The customs are honest and simple, and the people are devoted to learning and fond of merit. There are several hundred monasteries, most of which are in ruins, and the number of monks is small; they study the Sammatiya (正量部) school. There are one hundred deva temples, and there are many followers of non-Buddhist paths.  This was the capital city governed by King Prasenajit (鉢邏犀那恃多王; in Chinese, Shengjun [Victorious Army]; the old term, Bosini (波斯匿), is a corruption and abbreviation) during the time the Tathāgata was in the world. Within the old palace city, there are old foundations, which are the remaining traces of the palace of King Prasenajit. Not far to the east, there is an old foundation upon which a small stupa is built; this was the Great Dharma Hall that King Prasenajit formerly built for the Tathāgata. Not far from the side of the Dharma Hall, there is a stupa on old foundations; this is the nunnery of the Buddha’s maternal aunt, Prajāpatī (鉢邏闍鉢底; in Chinese, Shengzhu [Lord of Life]; the old term, Bozhebotí (波闍波提), is a corruption), which was built by King Prasenajit. To the east of this is a stupa, which is the former residence of Sudatta (蘇達多; in Chinese, Shanshi [Well-Bestowing]; the old term, Xuda, is a corruption). Beside the residence of the elder Sudatta, there is a large stupa; this is the place where Aṅgulimāla (鴦窶利摩羅; in Chinese, Zhiman [Finger-Garland]; the old term, Yangjuemoluo (央掘摩羅), is a corruption) abandoned his evil ways. Aṅgulimāla was a violent man of Śrāvastī. He harmed living beings and committed atrocities in the city and the country, killing people to take their fingers and wearing them on his head as a garland. He was about to kill his mother to complete the count of his fingers. The World-honored One, moved by compassion, set out to guide and transform him. Seeing the World-honored One from afar, he secretly rejoiced and said, "I am now certain to be reborn in heaven. My former teacher gave me instructions, and his legacy is here: by killing a Buddha and killing one's mother, one shall be reborn in the Brahmā heaven." He said to his mother, "Old lady, stay here for now; I must first kill that great śramaṇa." He immediately took up his sword and went to intercept the World-honored One. The Tathāgata then retreated at a slow pace, yet the wicked Aṅgulimāla could not catch up even though he ran fast. The World-honored One said to him, "Why do you persist in your base intentions, abandoning the root of goodness and stirring up the source of evil?" At that time, Aṅgulimāla heard this instruction and realized that his actions were wrong; he then took refuge, sought to enter the Dharma, practiced diligently without slackening, and attained the fruit of an Arhat.

en_revised: Five or six *li* south of the city is the Jetavana (逝多林; in the language of the Tang, "Victory Grove"; the old term "Qituo" (祇陀) is a corruption), which is the Anāthapiṇḍada-ārāma (給孤獨園). The minister Sudatta (善施) of King Prasenajit (勝軍王) built a vihāra (精舍) for the Buddha; it was formerly a monastery, but now it lies in ruins. To the left and right of the east gate stand stone pillars over seventy feet high; the left pillar is topped with a carved wheel, and the right pillar is surmounted by the figure of a bull, both of which were erected by King Aśoka (無憂王). The buildings have collapsed, leaving only the old foundations, save for a single brick chamber that stands alone and intact, containing an image of the Buddha. Formerly, after the Tathāgata had ascended to the Trāyastriṃśa heaven to preach the Dharma for his mother, King Prasenajit heard that King Udayana (出愛王) had carved a sandalwood image of the Buddha, and he thereupon had this image made. The Elder Sudatta was benevolent and intelligent; he accumulated wealth only to distribute it, rescuing the needy, relieving the poor, and showing compassion to the orphaned and the aged. People of the time praised his virtues and called him Anāthapiṇḍada ("the Giver to the Orphaned and Solitary"). Having heard of the Buddha’s merits, he developed a deep sense of reverence and wished to build a vihāra and invite the Buddha to descend. The World-Honored One commanded Śāriputra to accompany him to survey the land, and they found that only the garden of Prince Jeta (逝多太子) was high and dry. He immediately went to the Prince and explained his intentions in full. The Prince jokingly said, "If you cover the ground with gold, I will sell it." Upon hearing this, Sudatta’s heart was filled with joy; he immediately brought out his hidden gold and covered the ground as he had said. There was a small portion left uncovered, and the Prince requested to keep it, saying, "The Buddha is truly a fertile field; it is fitting to plant good seeds there." He then built the vihāra on the vacant land. The World-Honored One went there and said to Ānanda, "The garden ground was purchased by Sudatta (善施), and the trees were donated by Jeta (逝多); the two men were of one mind, and thus they jointly established this meritorious work. From now on, this place shall be called the Jetavana-anāthapiṇḍikārāma (逝多林給孤獨園)."  To the northeast of the Jetavana-anāthapiṇḍikārāma is a stūpa, which is the place where the Tathāgata washed a sick bhikṣu. Formerly, when the Tathāgata was in the world, there was a sick bhikṣu who was suffering and living alone. The World-Honored One saw him and asked, "What is your suffering? Why do you live alone?" He replied, "I am by nature lazy and cannot endure nursing the sick; therefore, I am now afflicted with illness, and there is no one to look after me." At that time, the Tathāgata felt compassion and said to him, "Good man, I will now nurse you." He stroked him with his hand, and his illness and suffering were all healed. He helped him out of the room, changed his bedding, personally washed him, and put new clothes on him. The Buddha said to the bhikṣu, "You should be diligent and exert yourself." Hearing this instruction, he felt gratitude, and his heart was joyful and his body at ease.  To the northwest of the Jetavana-anāthapiṇḍikārāma is a small stūpa, which is the place where Maudgalyāyana (沒特伽羅) exercised his supernatural power to lift Śāriputra’s (舍利子) robe and belt, but could not move them. Formerly, when the Buddha was at Lake Anavatapta (無熱惱池), humans and devas had all gathered, but only Śāriputra did not arrive at the assembly in time. The Buddha ordered Maudgalyāyana to go and summon him to join the gathering. Maudgalyāyana accepted the command and went; Śāriputra was mending his dharma-robe. Maudgalyāyana said, "The World-Honored One is now at Lake Anavatapta and has ordered me to summon you." Śāriputra (舍利子) said, "Wait a moment; I must finish mending this, and then I will go with you." Maudgalyāyana (沒特伽羅) said, "If you do not go quickly, I shall use my supernatural power to lift your stone chamber and take it to the great assembly." Śāriputra then untied his robe and belt, placed them on the ground, and said, "If you can lift this belt, my body might move." At that time, Maudgalyāyana exerted his great supernatural power, but he could not lift the belt, and the earth shook because of it. He then used his supernatural foot-power to return to the place of the Buddha, where he saw that Śāriputra was already seated in the assembly. Maudgalyāyana bowed his head and sighed, saying, "Only now do I know that the power of supernatural abilities is not equal to the power of wisdom."  Not far from the stupa of the belt, there is a well. When the Tathāgata (如來) was in the world, water was drawn from it for the Buddha’s use. Beside it is a stupa built by King Aśoka (無憂王), which contains relics of the Tathāgata. The sites of his walking meditation and the places where he preached the Dharma are all marked with signs and have stupas built upon them. Dark spirits guard and protect them, and miraculous signs appear from time to time; sometimes heavenly music is played, and sometimes divine incense is smelled. The auspicious omens of these blessings are difficult to describe in full.  Not far behind the monastery is the place where the non-Buddhist ascetics (外道梵志) murdered a courtesan to slander the Buddha. The Tathāgata possesses the ten powers, the fearlessnesses, and the omniscience of all modes; he is revered by humans and devas, and honored by sages and worthies. At that time, the various non-Buddhists consulted together, saying, "We should employ deceit and slander him in the midst of the assembly." They then enticed and hired a courtesan, pretending she was coming to listen to the Dharma, and once this was known to the assembly, they secretly murdered her, buried her corpse beside a tree, and complained to the king, claiming injury. The king ordered a search, and her body was found in the Jetavana (逝多園). At that time, the non-Buddhists loudly proclaimed: "The great śramaṇa Gautama (喬答摩) always praises precepts and patience; now he has had illicit relations with this woman and killed her to silence her. Having committed both lechery and murder, where are his precepts and where is his patience?" The devas in the sky responded in unison, saying: "The wicked non-Buddhists have fabricated this slander."  More than one hundred paces to the east of the monastery is a large, deep pit; this is the place where Devadatta (提婆達多), intending to harm the Buddha with poison, fell alive into hell. Devadatta (in Chinese, "Heaven-bestowed") was the son of King Droṇodana (斛飯王). He practiced diligently for twelve years and had already memorized the eighty thousand sections of the Dharma-store. Later, for the sake of profit, he sought to learn supernatural powers and associated with evil friends, consulting with them: "My physical marks are thirty; they are not much less than the Buddha's. With the great assembly surrounding me, how am I different from the Tathāgata?" Having thought this, he proceeded to cause a schism in the Sangha. Śāriputra (舍利子) and Maudgalyāyana (沒特伽羅子), following the Buddha’s instructions and relying on the Buddha’s majestic spiritual power, preached and admonished them, and the Sangha was reconciled. Devadatta did not abandon his evil heart; he placed a deadly poison under his fingernails, intending to harm the Buddha while performing an act of homage. As he was carrying out this plot, coming from afar and arriving at this spot, the earth suddenly split open, and he fell alive into hell. To the south of this, there is another large pit where the Bhikṣu Kokālika (瞿伽梨) fell alive into hell for slandering the Tathāgata. More than eight hundred paces to the south of the pit of Kokālika, there is a large, deep pit, which is the place where the Brahmin woman Ciñcā (戰遮) fell alive into hell for slandering the Tathāgata. When the Buddha was preaching the essentials of the Dharma to humans and devas, a disciple of an external path saw from afar the great assembly paying homage to the World-Honored One and thought to herself, "I must humiliate Gautama (喬答摩) today and ruin his good reputation, so that my teacher alone may possess a fragrant name." She then concealed a wooden basin tied to her body and went to the Jetavana (給孤獨園), where she cried out in a loud voice amidst the great assembly, "This preacher has had illicit relations with me, and the child in my womb is of the Śākya clan." Those of evil views all believed it to be true, while those who were steadfast knew it to be a slander. At that time, Śakra Devānām Indra (天帝釋), wishing to dispel the doubt, transformed into a white mouse and gnawed through the cord holding the basin. The sound of the cord snapping startled the great assembly, and all who saw and heard it felt their joy increase. One person in the assembly stood up, held the wooden basin, and showed it to the woman, saying, "Is this your child?" At that moment, the earth split open of its own accord, and she fell into it, her whole body sinking into the Avīci (無間) hell to suffer the full consequences of her actions. These three pits are bottomless; during the heavy rains of autumn and summer, when ditches and pools overflow, no water ever remains in these deep hollows. Sixty or seventy paces to the east of the monastery, there is a vihāra (精舍) over sixty feet high, in which there is an image of the Buddha seated facing east. In the past, the Tathāgata debated with various heretics here. To the east, there is a deva temple equal in size to the monastery. When the sun rises and sheds its light, the shadow of the deva temple does not cover the monastery; when the sun is about to set, the shadow of the monastery covers the deva temple. Three or four li to the east of the Shadow-covering Vihāra (影覆精舍), there is a stūpa, which is the place where the Venerable Śāriputra debated with the heretics.  Initially, the elder Sudatta (善施長者) purchased the garden of Prince Jeta (逝多太子) and wished to build a monastery for the Tathāgata. At that time, the Venerable Śāriputra accompanied the elder to survey the site. The teachers of the six heretical schools sought to compete in supernatural powers, but Śāriputra converted them according to the circumstances and subdued them in response to their challenges. Beside it, in front of a vihāra, a stūpa has been built; here the Tathāgata defeated the various heretics and also accepted the invitation of Mother Viśākhā.  To the south of the stūpa where he accepted the invitation is the place where King Virūḍhaka (毘盧釋迦王) (formerly called King Piliuli (毘琉離主), which is incorrect) raised an army to slaughter the Śākya clan, and where he saw the Buddha and turned his troops back. After King Virūḍhaka ascended the throne, he pursued his resentment over a previous humiliation, raised an army, and mobilized the masses. Once the deployment was complete, he issued the order to march. At that time, a bhikṣu heard of this and informed the Buddha. The World-Honored One then sat beneath a withered tree. King Virūḍhaka saw the World-Honored One from afar, dismounted to pay his respects, stood back, and said, "Lush trees are spreading and thick; why do you not sit under them, but instead stay by a withered stump and rotten branches?" The World-Honored One replied, "One's own kin are like the branches and leaves. When the branches and leaves are in danger, where is the shade?" The King said, "The World-Honored One is doing this for his kinsmen; I may turn back my carriage." Thereupon, seeing the Holy One and feeling moved, he returned his army to his country. Beside the place where the army turned back, there is a stūpa, which is the place where the Śākya women were slaughtered. When King Virūḍhaka (毘盧釋迦王) had conquered the Śākyas, he selected five hundred women to fill his palace. The Śākya women were filled with indignation and, speaking resentful and insolent words, cursed the King, saying, "You are the son of a domestic servant." When the King heard this, he became enraged and ordered them to be slaughtered. The executioners obeyed the King’s command, severed their hands and feet, and threw them into a pit. At that time, the Śākya women, enduring their suffering, called upon the Buddha. The World-Honored One, with his holy insight, perceived their bitter agony and commanded the bhikṣus to gather their robes and go there. He preached the subtle Dharma to the Śākya women, explaining how they were bound by the five desires, wandering through the three evil paths, separated from those they loved, and caught in the long cycle of birth and death. When the Śākya women heard the Buddha’s instruction, they cast off the dust and removed the stains, attained the pure Dharma-eye, and at that same moment passed away and were all reborn in the heavens. At that time, Śakra Devānām Indra transformed himself into a Brahmin, collected their remains, and cremated them; later generations have commemorated this. Not far from the stūpa of the slaughtered Śākyas, there is a large dried-up pond, which is the place where King Virūḍhaka sank into the earth and fell into hell. After the World-Honored One had observed the Śākya women, he returned to the Jetavana (給孤獨園) and told the bhikṣus, "Seven days from now, King Virūḍhaka will be consumed by fire." When the King heard the Buddha’s prophecy, he was filled with great fear and anxiety. When the seventh day arrived, he was safe and without danger. The king, feeling jubilant, ordered the palace maidens to go to the riverside to enjoy themselves with music and wine. Still fearing that a fire might break out, he rowed upon the clear currents and drifted along with the waves. Suddenly, a blazing fire erupted, consuming the light boat; the king’s body fell, and he entered the Avīci Hell to undergo all manner of suffering.

en_revised: From here, traveling southeast for more than five hundred *li*, one arrives at the country of Kapilavastu (劫比羅伐窣堵國) (formerly called Jialuowei (迦羅衛國), which is incorrect; it is within the borders of Central India). The country of Kapilavastu is over four thousand *li* in circuit. There are more than ten empty cities, which are extremely desolate and overgrown. The royal city is in ruins, and its exact dimensions are unknown. The inner palace city is fourteen or fifteen *li* in circuit; it was built of piled bricks, and its foundations remain high and solid. Having been desolate for a long time, the inhabited villages are sparse and wide apart. There is no great monarch; each city has its own ruler. The land is fertile and rich, and crops are sown at the proper times. The climate is regular, and the customs are harmonious and pleasant. There are more than a thousand old foundations of *saṃghārāmas*, and beside the palace city is one *saṃghārāma* with more than three thousand monks who study the teachings of the Hīnayāna Saṃmitīya school. There are two *deva* temples; followers of different sects live intermixed.  Inside the palace city are the old foundations of the main hall of King Śuddhodana. A vihāra (精舍) has been built upon it, containing a statue of the king. Not far to its side are the old foundations of the bedchamber of Queen Mahāmāyā (which in Chinese means "Great Illusion"). A vihāra has been built upon it, containing a statue of the queen. The vihāra beside it is the place where the Bodhisattva Śākya descended into his mother’s womb; inside is a statue of the Bodhisattva descending into the womb. The Sthavira school holds that the Bodhisattva descended into his mother’s womb on the night of the thirtieth day of the month of Uttarāṣāḍhā, which corresponds to the fifteenth day of the fifth month here; the other schools hold that he descended into his mother’s womb on the night of the twenty-third day of that month, which corresponds to the eighth day of the fifth month here. To the northeast of the place where the Bodhisattva’s spirit descended, there is a stūpa at the site where the rishi Asita (阿私多) examined the physiognomy of the prince. On the day the Bodhisattva was born, auspicious signs converged. At that time, King Śuddhodana (淨飯王) summoned the various physiognomists and said to them: "This child has been born; what is his fortune, good or evil? You must examine him thoroughly and speak clearly in your reply." They said: "According to the records of the ancient sages and examining the auspicious omens, if he remains in household life, he will become a wheel-turning sage king (cakravartin); if he leaves the household life, he will attain equal and correct enlightenment (samyaksambodhi)." At this time, the rishi Asita arrived from afar and knocked at the gate to request an audience. The king was very joyful, personally welcomed and paid homage to him, and invited him to take a precious seat, saying: "I did not expect the great rishi to visit today." The rishi said: "I was dwelling in peace and sitting at ease in the heavenly palace when I suddenly saw the hosts of devas dancing. I then asked them: 'Why are you so extremely joyful?' They replied: 'Great rishi, you should know that in Jambudvīpa, the first wife of the Śākya King Śuddhodana has now given birth to a prince who shall attain *saṃbodhi* (三菩提) and perfect the light of all-knowing wisdom.' Having heard these words, I came to pay my respects. What I lament is my decrepitude, that I shall not encounter his holy transformation." At the south gate of the city, there is a stūpa; this is the place where the prince competed in strength with the other Śākyas and threw an elephant. The prince was highly skilled in many arts, standing alone and peerless. King Śuddhodana, feeling joy, was about to return when a servant was driving an elephant, just as they were about to exit the city. Devadatta, who had long prided himself on his great strength, was entering from outside and asked the driver, "You have prepared this elephant; who is to ride it?" He replied, "The prince is about to return, so I am going to serve as his driver." Devadatta, in a fit of anger, pulled the elephant, struck its forehead, and kicked its chest, causing it to fall dead and block the road, obstructing the path so that it could not be moved, and the crowd became congested. Nanda arrived later and asked, "Who killed this elephant?" They replied, "Devadatta." He immediately dragged it aside to clear the path. When the prince arrived, he also asked, "Who committed this evil act and killed this elephant?" They replied, "Devadatta killed it to block the gate, and Nanda dragged it away to open the path." The prince then lifted the elephant and flung it high, over the city moat. Where the elephant fell to the ground, it formed a large, deep pit, which local tradition calls the Pit of the Fallen Elephant. In a vihāra (精舍) beside it, a statue of the prince has been made. Beside that is another vihāra, which was the bedchamber of the prince's consort; inside are statues of Yaśodharā and Rāhula. In the vihāra beside the palace, a statue has been made in the posture of receiving instruction; this is the original site of the prince’s schoolroom. At the southeast corner of the city is a vihāra containing a statue of the prince riding a white horse through the air, marking the spot where he leaped over the city wall. Outside each of the four city gates is a vihāra containing statues of an old man, a sick man, a dead man, and a *śramaṇa*. These represent the prince’s excursions, where, upon seeing these signs, his anxiety increased and he became deeply weary of the mundane world; it was here that he was awakened [to renunciation] and ordered his servant to turn the carriage back.

en_revised: From here, traveling east through a wilderness and desolate forest for more than two hundred *li*, one arrives at the country of Rāmagrāma (藍摩國) (within the borders of Central India). The country of Rāmagrāma has been desolate for a long time; its borders are undefined, its cities and towns are in ruins, and its inhabitants are few and scattered. To the southeast of the old city, there is a brick *stūpa* slightly less than one hundred feet high. Formerly, after the Tathāgata entered *parinirvāṇa*, the former king of this country obtained a share of the relics, brought them back to his own country, and duly honored them by building [this structure]. Miraculous signs appeared from time to time, and divine light shone occasionally. Beside the *stūpa* is a clear pool; the dragon often emerges to wander, changing its form into that of a snake, circling the *stūpa* to the right in winding movements. Herds of wild elephants come to gather flowers and scatter them [as offerings]; this spiritual influence keeps watch, and there has never been any interruption. Formerly, when King Aśoka (無憂王) was distributing [relics] to build *stūpas*, those built by the seven [other] kingdoms had all been opened. When he arrived in this country and was about to begin the work, the dragon of this pool, fearing they would be seized and taken away, transformed into a Brahmin, approached the elephant, and said: "Your Majesty’s devotion flows toward the Buddha-dharma, and you have widely planted fields of merit; I venture to ask you to deign to visit my abode." The King said: "Where is your home? Is it near or far?" The Brahmin said: "I am the Dragon King of this pool. Having heard that Your Majesty wishes to build superior merit, I have ventured to come and invite you." The King accepted his invitation and thereupon entered the dragon palace. After sitting for a long time, the dragon approached and said: "Because of my evil karma, I have received this dragon body. I make offerings to the relics, hoping to eliminate my sins and faults. I wish for the King to go in person to observe and pay homage." When King Aśoka (無憂王) saw them, he said with trepidation: "All these implements of offering are not things of the human world." The dragon said: "If that is so, I hope you will not destroy or damage them." King Aśoka judged that his own power was not a match for theirs, and so he did not open them. The place where he emerged from the pool now has a marker.  Not far from the side of the stupa (窣堵波) is a monastery (伽藍); the community of monks is small, and the place is pure, solemn, and bright, with a novice (沙彌) in charge of all the affairs of the community. When monks from afar arrive, they are treated with great respect; they are always kept for three days and provided with the four requisites.  According to ancient records, there were once bhikṣus who, having invited one another, came from afar to pay homage at the stupa. They saw herds of elephants coming and going; some used their tusks to clear away grass, others used their trunks to sprinkle water, and each held different flowers to make offerings together. When the group saw this, they were moved to sadness and reflection. One bhikṣu then renounced his full precepts, wishing to remain and make offerings. He said to the group: "I have had much good fortune, but I have merely left traces among the sangha; years and months have passed quickly, yet my practice has no record. This stupa contains the Buddha’s relics, and his holy virtue reaches into the unseen, causing herds of elephants to tread and sprinkle it. To leave my body in this place and be willing to join this group, to be able to finish the remainder of my life here, would truly be a blessing." The group said to him: "This is a magnificent undertaking. We are heavy with defilements, and our wisdom does not reach this far. Take good care of yourself at all times, and do not fall short in this excellent work." Having parted from the group, he reaffirmed his sincere vow, lived alone in joy, and held the determination to remain there until the end of his days. He then thatched a hut for a dwelling, diverted a stream to form a pond, gathered seasonal flowers, and sprinkled and swept the burial area. As the years and months passed, his devotion never faltered. The kings of neighboring countries heard of this and held him in high esteem; they vied with one another to donate treasures to jointly build a monastery, and subsequently invited him to deign to oversee the monastic affairs. Since then, this tradition has been followed in succession so as not to let his original merit be forgotten, and a śrāmaṇera (沙彌) is always appointed to manage the affairs of the monastery.

en_revised: Three or four *li* to the northwest of the city, one crosses the Ajitavatī River (阿恃多伐底河) (in the Tang language, "Invincible"; this is merely the common name in this world. The old name, Alilobati River (阿利羅跋提河), is a corruption. The classical language calls it the Hiraṇyavatī River, which translates as "River of Gold"). Not far from the west bank, one reaches the Sāla (娑羅) grove. The trees resemble the oak, but their bark is greenish-white and their leaves are very glossy and smooth. Four trees are particularly tall; this is the place where the Tathāgata attained extinction (parinirvāṇa). In the large brick vihāra (精舍) is an image of the Tathāgata in the state of *nirvāṇa*, lying with his head to the north. Beside it is a *stūpa* built by King Aśoka; although the base has collapsed and sunken, it is still over two hundred feet high. In front of it stands a stone pillar recording the event of the Tathāgata’s extinction; although there is an inscription, it does not record the year or month. I have heard from ancient records that the Buddha entered *parinirvāṇa* at the age of eighty on the fifteenth day of the second half of the month of Vaiśākha, which corresponds to the fifteenth day of the third month. The Sarvāstivāda school, however, holds that the Buddha entered *parinirvāṇa* on the eighth day of the second half of the month of Kārttika, which corresponds to the eighth day of the ninth month. Since the Buddha’s *nirvāṇa*, the various schools have held differing opinions: some say more than 1,200 years have passed, some say more than 1,300 years, some say more than 1,500 years, and others say more than 900 but less than 1,000 years. Not far from the side of the vihāra is a *stūpa* marking the place where the Tathāgata, when practicing the Bodhisattva path, acted as the king of a flock of pheasants to save them from a fire. Formerly, there was a great, dense forest in this place, where feathered and furred creatures nested and lived in burrows. Sudden winds arose from all directions, and the fierce flames surged rapidly. At that time, there was a pheasant who, moved by compassion, soaked its wings in a clear stream and flew into the air to sprinkle the water. The Heavenly Emperor Śakra (天帝釋) looked down and said to it, "Why are you so foolish, exhausting your wings in vain? A great fire has broken out, burning the forest and the wilderness; how could your tiny body possibly extinguish it?" The pheasant replied, "Who is it that speaks?" He said, "I am the Heavenly Emperor Śakra." The pheasant said, "Today, the Heavenly Emperor possesses great merit and power, and there is no desire he cannot fulfill; to relieve disasters and rescue those in distress should be as easy as pointing to one's own palm. Yet you instead question my lack of success—where does the blame truly lie? The fierce fire is currently raging; do not speak further!" It then flew off again to head toward the flowing water. The Heavenly Emperor then scooped up water with his hands and sprinkled it over the forest; the fire was extinguished and the smoke vanished, the lives of all creatures were saved, and thus it is now called the Fire-extinguishing Stūpa (救火窣堵波).  Not far from the side of the place where the pheasant extinguished the fire, there is a stūpa marking the place where the Tathāgata, while practicing the Bodhisattva path, saved lives as a deer. In the remote past, there was a great forest here; a fire broke out in the wilderness, and the birds and beasts were driven to desperation, facing the peril of a swift current in front and the hardship of a raging fire behind, such that none escaped drowning or losing their lives. The deer, moved by compassion, positioned its body across the current, its skin pierced and bones broken, forcing itself to rescue the drowning. A lame hare arrived last, and the deer, enduring its fatigue and pain, rescued it as well. When its strength was exhausted, it drowned and died. The devas gathered its remains and erected a stūpa. Not far to the west of where the deer rescued the drowning, there is a stūpa. This is the place where Subhadra (蘇跋陀羅) (in the Tang language, "Good and Virtuous" [善賢]; formerly called Xubatuoluo [須跋陀羅], which is incorrect) entered into extinction. This Good and Virtuous one was originally a Brahmin teacher. He was one hundred and twenty years old, an elder of great wisdom. Hearing that the Buddha was about to enter extinction, he arrived at the twin trees and asked Ānanda, "The Buddha, the World-honored One, is about to enter extinction. I have doubts and hesitations, and I wish to ask him questions." Ānanda said, "The Buddha is about to enter nirvāṇa; please do not disturb him." He replied, "I have heard that it is difficult to encounter a Buddha in the world and difficult to hear the true Dharma. I have deep doubts and fear that I will have no one to ask." Subhadra then entered and first asked the Buddha, "Are there various other groups who call themselves teachers, each having different doctrines, handing down instructions to guide the laity—can Gautama (formerly called Qutan [瞿曇], which is a corruption and abbreviation) know them all?" The Buddha said, "I have thoroughly investigated them all," and then he expounded them for him. Having heard this, Subhadra’s mind was purified and he gained faith and understanding. He requested to enter the Dharma and receive the full ordination. The Tathāgata said to him, "Are you able to do so? For those of other paths and different schools who wish to practice the holy life, they must be tested for four years. By observing their conduct and examining their nature—if their deportment is tranquil and their speech is truthful—then they may practice the holy life in my Dharma. It depends on the person's conduct; how could this be difficult?" Subhadra said, "The World-honored One is compassionate and merciful, bestowing salvation without partiality. If one is tested for four years, the three karmas will then be in accord." The Buddha said, "I have already said that it depends on the person's conduct!" Thereupon, Subhadra (善賢) renounced the household life, immediately received the full precepts, and diligently practiced with a courageous body and mind. Before long, he had no doubts regarding the Dharma and personally attained realization. Before the night was far advanced, he attained the fruit of an Arhat; all his outflows were exhausted, and his holy life was established. Unable to bear seeing the Buddha enter mahānirvāṇa, he entered the fire-element samādhi (火界定) amidst the assembly, manifested supernatural powers, and entered nirvana first. This was the Tathāgata's final disciple, who attained extinction first; he is the one who, in the past, was the hare that crossed the river last. Beside the spot where Subhadra entered nirvana, there is a stūpa; this is the place where the Vajra-holder (執金剛) fell to the ground.  The Greatly Compassionate World-honored One, having appeared to benefit beings according to their capacities, finished his work of transformation and entered the joy of extinction, lying down with his head to the north between the twin trees. When the Vajra-holding deity, the Guhyapāda Malla (密迹力士), saw the Buddha enter nirvana, he cried out in bitter grief: "The Tathāgata has forsaken me and entered mahānirvāṇa; I have no refuge and no protection; the poisoned arrow has struck deep, and the fire of sorrow burns fiercely!" He cast aside his vajra-club and fell to the ground in a swoon. After a long time, he rose again, filled with sorrow and longing, and they said to one another: "In the great ocean of birth and death, who will serve as the boat and oar? In the long night of ignorance, who will serve as the lamp and torch?" Beside the spot where the Vajra-holder fell to the ground, there is a stūpa; this is the place where the Tathāgata was venerated for seven days after his nirvana. When the Tathāgata was about to enter nirvana, a brilliant light shone everywhere. Humans and devas gathered in full, all feeling deep sorrow and emotion, saying to one another: "The Great Awakened World-Honored One is now about to enter nirvana; the merit of sentient beings is exhausted, and the world is left without a refuge." The Tathāgata lay on his right side on a lion-couch and addressed the great assembly: "Do not say that the Tathāgata has entered final nirvana. The Dharma-body is eternally abiding and free from all change. You should abandon sloth and seek liberation early." The bhikṣus sobbed and grieved. At that time, Aniruddha (阿泥𢫫陀) (𢫫 is read 盧骨反, i.e. *lu[t]*; formerly called Analü [阿那律], which is incorrect) told the bhikṣus: "Stop, stop! Do not grieve; the devas will mock and wonder at you." When the Malla people had finished their offerings and wished to lift the golden coffin to proceed to the cremation ground (涅疊般那), Aniruddha said: "Wait! The devas wish to keep it for seven days to make offerings." Thereupon, the host of devas held exquisite heavenly flowers, wandered through the void, praised the holy virtues, and each exhausted their sincere hearts to join in making offerings. Beside the place where the coffin rested, there is a stūpa; this is the spot where Lady Mahāmāyā wept for the Buddha. After the Tathāgata had entered nirvana and the encoffining was completed, Aniruddha ascended to the heavenly palace and informed Lady Mahāmāyā, saying: "The Great Holy Dharma King has now entered nirvana." Upon hearing this, Mahāmāyā was choked with grief and fainted. She went with the assembly of devas to the space between the twin trees, where she saw the saṃghāṭi (monastic robe), the pātra (alms bowl), and the khakkhara (pewter staff). Stroking them, she wailed in agony, fainting and then regaining her voice to cry out: "The merit of humans and devas is exhausted, and the Eye of the World is extinguished! Now these objects are empty and without a master." By the holy power of the Tathāgata, the golden coffin opened of its own accord, emitting a great light; he sat up with palms joined and consoled his compassionate mother: "You have descended from a great distance! All conditioned things are by nature such; I pray you, do not grieve so deeply." Ānanda, suppressing his sorrow, asked the Buddha: "If future generations ask me, how shall I answer them?" He replied: "Say that after the Buddha had entered nirvana, his compassionate mother Mahāmāyā descended from the heavenly palace to the space between the twin trees, and for the sake of unfilial sentient beings, the Tathāgata rose from his golden coffin and preached the Dharma with his palms joined."

issues: 'The scriptural texts call it' → 典言 'in the classical language (Sanskrit) it is called' | Chinese 阿恃多伐底河 missing on first occurrence | 'translated into Chinese as' → 唐言 'in the Tang language' (fine)
en_revised: Three or four li to the northwest of the city, one crosses the Ajitavatī River (阿恃多伐底河) (translated into Chinese as "Invincible"; this is merely the name commonly used in the world. It was formerly called the Alirabati River, which is an error. In the classical language it is called the Hiraṇyavatī River, which translates as "River Possessing Gold").

issues: fanqie note （女黠反） for 痆 dropped, and Chinese 婆羅痆斯國 missing | 'the great settlement of Mahāgrāma (大邑聚)' → 大邑聚 is 'a large town', not a name | 'to wash his vessels' → 滌器 'wash [my] vessels' (not specifically the Buddha's)
en_revised: Traveling two hundred-odd *li* southwest from the relic stūpa, one arrives at a large town (大邑聚). There was a brāhmaṇa there, a man of great wealth and high standing, whose lineage was pure and unmixed, who had mastered the five sciences (pañcavidyā), and who deeply revered the Three Jewels. Adjacent to his residence, he established a monastery, exhausting his resources to provide it with every adornment. Whenever members of the saṅgha traveled along that road, he would earnestly invite them to stay, offering them his wholehearted support, whether they stopped for a single night or for as long as seven days. Later, when King Śaśāṅka (設賞迦王) destroyed the Buddha-dharma, the saṅgha was dispersed and the years passed quickly, yet the brāhmaṇa remained filled with sincere sorrow. While walking in meditation, he saw a śramaṇa with bushy eyebrows and white hair approaching, leaning on a staff. The brāhmaṇa hurried to welcome him, asked where he had come from, and invited him into the monastery, where he prepared every kind of offering, including a morning meal of porridge cooked with pure milk. The śramaṇa accepted it, but after tasting only a morsel, he set down his bowl and sighed deeply. The brāhmaṇa, holding the food, knelt and asked, "Great Virtuous One, whose wisdom and merit follow conditions, I am fortunate to have your presence; were you uncomfortable during the night, or was the porridge not to your taste?" The śramaṇa replied with compassion, "I grieve that the merit and blessings of sentient beings are gradually thinning. Let that matter rest for now; I will speak after I have eaten." Once the śramaṇa had finished eating, he adjusted his robes and spoke. The brāhmaṇa said, "You previously promised to speak; why are you silent now?" The śramaṇa replied, "I have not forgotten. What I have to discuss is not easy, and the matter may invite doubt. If you truly wish to hear it, I shall now speak of it briefly." "What I sighed about just now was not to disparage your porridge. For several hundred years, I have not tasted such a flavor. Long ago, when the Tathāgata was in the world, I was in his retinue at the Bamboo Grove Monastery (Veṇuvana-vihāra) in the city of Rājagṛha, where I would lean over the clear stream to wash the vessels, or use the water for rinsing and bathing. Alas! The rich milk of today cannot compare to the plain water of old; this is because the merit of humans and devas has been exhausted." The brāhmaṇa asked, "In that case, does the Venerable One mean that you personally saw the Buddha?" The śramaṇa replied, "Indeed. Have you not heard of the Buddha’s son, Rāhula? I am he. To protect the True Dharma, I have not yet entered final extinction." Having said these words, he suddenly vanished. The brāhmaṇa then anointed and swept the room where he had stayed, set up an image with solemn ceremony, and paid his respects as if he were still present. Traveling further through the great forest for more than five hundred li, one arrives at the country of Vārāṇasī (婆羅痆斯國) (痆 is read 女黠反; formerly called Poluonai, which is incorrect. It is in the region of Central India).

issues: note on 梅呾麗耶: 'the old term *Mile* is a phonetic abbreviation' → 訛略也 'an erroneous abbreviation' (the 'erroneous' is dropped); earlier error (三佛經行 'the Buddha') does not recur
en_revised: Beside the place where the three Buddhas walked in meditation, there is a stūpa marking the spot where the Bodhisattva Maitreya (梅呾麗耶; in Tang language *Ci* [Loving], which is his surname; formerly called *Mile* [彌勒], which is an erroneous abbreviation) received the prediction of his future Buddhahood. Long ago, the Tathāgata, while at Vulture Peak (Gṛdhrakūṭa) near the city of Rājagṛha, told the bhikṣus: "In a future age, when the land of this Jambudvīpa is level and even, and the human lifespan is eighty thousand years, there will be a Brahmin’s son named Maitreya. His body will be the color of pure gold, shining with brilliant light. He will leave his home to attain perfect enlightenment and will widely preach the Dharma for sentient beings in three assemblies. Those whom he saves will all be beings who planted roots of merit under my own dispensation. Whether lay or monastic, whether they kept the precepts or broke them, all who hold deep respect and a single mind toward the Three Jewels will receive his guidance and attain the fruit of liberation. Within these three assemblies of preaching, he will first save those who are followers of my dispensation, and only then will he transform those who are fellow-travelers with whom he shares a karmic connection." At that time, the Bodhisattva Maitreya, having heard these words of the Buddha, rose from his seat and said to the Buddha: "I vow to become that Maitreya, the World-Honored One." The Tathāgata replied: "As you have said, you shall attain this fruit. All that has been described above is the manner of your teaching and transformation." To the west of the place where the Bodhisattva Maitreya received his prediction, there is a stūpa marking the spot where the Bodhisattva Śākya received his own prediction. In the Bhadrakalpa, when the human lifespan was twenty thousand years, the Buddha Kāśyapa appeared in the world, turned the wheel of the wonderful Dharma, and opened the way for sentient beings to be transformed, bestowing upon the Bodhisattva Prabhāpāla (護明菩薩) the prediction: "This Bodhisattva, in a future age when the lifespan of sentient beings is one hundred years, shall attain Buddhahood and be named Śākyamuni." Not far to the south of the place where the Bodhisattva Śākya received his prediction, there are the traces of the four past Buddhas walking to and fro. The site is over fifty paces long and about seven feet high, built of piled bluestone, and upon it is an image of the Tathāgata in the act of walking. The appearance of the image is extraordinary and solemn; from the top of the uṣṇīṣa, hair uniquely emerges, its spiritual features are fully revealed, and its divine intelligence is clearly evidenced. Within its enclosure, there are many sacred sites, including several hundred *vihāras* (精舍) and *stūpas*; I have briefly mentioned two or three, as it is difficult to describe them in detail.

issues: 'externally, you are both his subjects and ministers' → 外則既君且臣 'externally, he is your lord and you his subjects' (Mizutani: 外では君臣の関係)
en_revised: Two or three li to the southwest of the monastery, there is a stupa over three hundred feet high; its base is broad and imposing, adorned with lustrous and rare gems. It has no tiered niches on top, but is surmounted by an inverted bowl; although a central pillar was erected, it lacks the usual rings and bells. Beside it is a small stupa, marking the place where the five men, including Ājñāta-Kauṇḍinya (阿若憍陳如), abandoned their restraint to welcome the Buddha.  Previously, after the Prince Sarvārthasiddha (薩婆曷剌他悉陀; in Tang language, "Accomplished in All Meanings"; formerly called Siddhārtha, which is an abbreviated and inaccurate rendering) had climbed over the city wall, he dwelt in mountain valleys, forgetting his own body in his devotion to the Dharma. King Śuddhodana then commanded three members of the royal clan and two from the maternal side, saying: "My son, Accomplished in All Meanings, has left home to practice and learn; he wanders alone through mountains and marshes and dwells in isolation among the woods and thickets. Therefore, I order you to follow him and keep track of his whereabouts. Internally, you are his uncles and maternal uncles; externally, he is your lord and you are his subjects. In all his movements, you should know when to advance and when to stop."  The five men accepted the command and kept watch over him, providing protection. Consequently, they practiced diligently, hoping to attain liberation. They often said to one another, "Is the path to enlightenment attained through suffering, or is it attained through ease?" Two of them said, "Ease is the path." Three of them said, "Hardship and suffering are the path." The two and the three argued with each other, unable to reach a clear conclusion. Thereupon, the Prince contemplated the ultimate truth and, in order to subdue the non-Buddhist ascetics, he restricted himself to a few grains of hemp and rice to sustain his body. Those two men saw this and said, "What the Prince is practicing is not the true Dharma." "The Way is to be realized through ease; now he practices diligent suffering, so he is not one of our kind." They abandoned him and fled to a distance, contemplating the realization of the fruit. The Prince practiced asceticism for six years without realizing enlightenment; wishing to verify that asceticism was not the truth, he accepted milk gruel and attained the fruit. These three men heard of this and sighed, saying, "His merit was on the verge of completion, yet now he has retreated. Six years of asceticism, and in one day he has cast away his merit!" Thereupon, they followed one another to seek out the two men. Having met, they sat upright and engaged in lofty discourse, discussing further: "Formerly we saw the Prince, Sarvārthasiddha (一切義成), leave the royal palace, go to the desolate valleys, discard his precious garments, and don deerskin. He applied himself with diligent resolve and painstaking integrity to seek the profound and wonderful Dharma, aspiring to the supreme fruit. Now he has accepted milk gruel from a cowherd girl, ruining his path and compromising his resolve; I know him well, he is capable of nothing." Those two men said, "Why are you so late in seeing this? This is merely a reckless person. Dwelling in the deep palace, secure in his exalted status, he could not calm his mind; he fled to the mountain forests, abandoned the position of a wheel-turning king, and performed the acts of a base and lowly person—what is there to think about? Speaking of him only increases one's sorrow!" The Bodhisattva bathed in the Nairañjanā (尼連河) River, sat under the Mahā-bodhi (菩提樹) tree, attained perfect enlightenment, and was titled the Teacher of Gods and Humans. Remaining in silent tranquility, he observed those ready for deliverance and said, "That Udraka Rāmaputra (欝頭藍子) has realized the meditative state of neither perception nor non-perception and is capable of receiving the wonderful Dharma." The devas in the sky heard his voice and replied, "It has been seven days since Udraka Rāmaputra (欝頭藍子) passed away." The Tathāgata sighed with regret, "How unfortunate that he did not encounter this, for he was on the verge of hearing the wonderful Dharma, yet he has suddenly undergone transformation!" He observed the world again, seeking someone to teach, and found Ārāḍa Kālāma (阿藍迦藍), who had attained the meditative state of nothingness and could be taught the ultimate truth. The devas said again, "He passed away five days ago." The Tathāgata sighed once more, pitying his meager fortune. He observed carefully again: who was fit to receive instruction? Only the five men in the Deer Park (鹿林) could be guided first. At that time, the Tathāgata rose from the Mahā-bodhi (菩提樹) tree and headed for the Deer Park; his deportment was serene, his divine light shone brilliantly, his brow-hair possessed the luster of jade, and his body was the color of genuine gold as he proceeded composedly to guide those five men. When these five men saw the Tathāgata from afar, they said to one another, "Sarvārthasiddha (一切義成) is the one coming there. Much time has passed, he has not realized the holy fruit, and his aspirations have retreated, so he is coming to seek us. We should each remain silent and not rise to greet or pay homage to him." As the Tathāgata gradually approached, his divine power moved them; the five men, forgetting their resolve, bowed to welcome him with greetings and attended to him according to etiquette. The Tathāgata gradually guided them, revealing the wonderful truth to them, and after two retreats, they finally attained the realization of the fruit.

issues: Chinese name missing on first occurrence: Aviddhakarṇa (阿避陀羯剌拏) Monastery; 'no monks with pierced ears (Avitakarṇa)' → the bracketed 'Avitakarṇa' is DM's invention and means the opposite ('unpierced'); dropped
en_revised: Going eastward from the great city for more than two hundred li, one reaches the Aviddhakarṇa Monastery (阿避陀羯剌拏僧伽藍) (which in the language of the Tang means "Unpierced Ears"). Its surrounding walls are not extensive, but the carvings and decorations are most exquisite; the flower ponds reflect one another, the terraces and pavilions stand with connected roofs, the monks are solemn and grave, and the community conducts its rituals in an orderly manner.  According to the records of former times: Long ago, in the country of Tukhāra (覩貨邏國) north of the Great Snowy Mountains, there were śramaṇas who delighted in learning. In their leisure time after chanting and recitation, two or three like-minded companions would often say to one another, "The wonderful principles are profound and mysterious, and cannot be fully investigated through mere talk; the sacred sites are clearly manifest, and can be sought out by the soles of one's feet. We should consult with those of like mind and personally visit the sacred sites."  Thereupon, these two or three friends took up their staves and traveled together. Upon arriving in India, they lodged at various monasteries, but because they were looked down upon as being from a borderland, no one would provide them with shelter. Exposed to the wind and dew outdoors and burdened by hunger and thirst within, their complexions became haggard and their bodies grew emaciated.  At that time, the king of this country was traveling in the suburbs and, seeing these visiting monks, was surprised and asked, "From what region are you mendicants? For what reason have you come? Your ears are not pierced, and your robes are dirty and tattered."  The śramaṇas replied, "We are people from the country of Tukhāra. Respectfully upholding the legacy of the teachings, we have transcended worldly dust. I led my like-minded companions to visit and pay homage to the sacred sites. Regrettably, due to our meager merit, we have been forsaken by all; the Indian monks show no concern for us travelers. We wish to return to our native land, but our pilgrimage is not yet complete; although we are pressed by hardship, our hearts are reluctant to give up." Upon hearing their account, the king’s pity and sorrow were further increased. He immediately established a monastery at this excellent site and, writing a decree on white cotton cloth, declared: "That I dwell as the most honored in the world and the noblest among men is entirely due to the spiritual protection of the Triple Gem. Since I am a king of men and have received the Buddha’s entrustment, I shall provide relief and aid to all those who wear the dyed robes. This monastery has been constructed to provide hospitality for travelers. From this time forward, no monks with pierced ears shall be allowed to stay in this monastery of mine." Because of these events, it was so named.

issues: fanqie note （昌葉反） after 呫 dropped; '(Lichchhavi; formerly called Lichezi…)' → the 'Lichchhavi' is a stray spelling, and the Chinese 栗呫婆子 is missing
en_revised: Traveling fifty or sixty li to the northwest of the great city, one reaches a great stūpa at the place where the Licchavis (栗呫婆子; 呫 read with the initial of 昌 and the final of 葉; formerly called Lichezi [離車子], which is an error) bade farewell to the Tathāgata. When the Tathāgata was proceeding from the city of Vaiśālī toward the country of Kuśinagara, the Licchavis, hearing that the Buddha was about to enter parinirvāṇa, followed him, wailing and lamenting as they saw him off. Seeing that their sorrow and longing were so deep as to be beyond words, the World-honored One used his supernatural powers to create a great river with steep, precipitous banks and a rapid, rushing current. The Licchavis were stopped there in their bitter grief, and the Tathāgata left his almsbowl as a memento for them.

issues: note on 鴦輸伐摩: '(唐言光胄, "Light-Vestment" in Tang language)' → Chinese name missing, 唐言 left untranslated; 光胄 'Light-Helmet' (胄 = helmet; Mizutani: 光冑)
en_revised: From here, traveling northwest for one thousand four or five hundred li, crossing mountains and entering valleys, one reaches the country of Nepāla (尼波羅國) (in the region of Central India). The country of Nepāla is over four thousand li in circuit and is situated within the Snow Mountains (Himālaya). The capital city is over twenty li in circuit. The mountains and rivers are connected; the land is suitable for grain and produces many flowers and fruits. It yields red copper, yaks, and jīvañjīvaka birds. For currency, they use red copper coins. The climate is cold and severe. The customs are treacherous and uneven; the people’s nature is stubborn and fierce, and they are fickle in matters of faith and righteousness. They lack formal learning and arts, but possess technical skill. Their appearance is ugly and coarse, and they believe in both heterodox and orthodox teachings. Monasteries and deva temples are adjacent and share corners. There are over two thousand monks, who study both the Great and Lesser Vehicles with equal diligence. The number of non-Buddhist heterodox practitioners is not known. The king is of the Kṣatriya Licchavi clan. His aspirations for learning are noble and lofty, and he is purely devoted to the Buddha-Dharma. In recent times, there was a king named Aṃśuvarman (鴦輸伐摩; in the language of the Tang, "Light-Helmet" [光胄]). He was a man of great learning and intelligence who authored the *Śabdavidyā-śāstra*. He valued learning and respected virtue, and his fame was known far and near. To the southeast of the capital city is a small pool; when a person throws fire into it, the water immediately bursts into flames, and if other objects are thrown in, they also turn into fire. From here, I returned to the country of Vaiśālī (吠舍釐國) and, crossing the Gaṅgā (殑伽河) to the south, reached the country of Magadha (摩揭陀國) (formerly called Mojiatuo or Mojieti, both of which are erroneous transcriptions; in the region of Central India).

issues: recurs from earlier review: 'saying, "This is the marriage tree"' → 謂女聲樹也 is a gloss: the pāṭalī is called a tree of feminine gender (女聲 = grammatically feminine; Mizutani: 女性名詞の木); notes: 'Original note:' inserted in the 拘蘇摩補羅 note; the 阿輸迦 note is attached to the first 'King Aśoka' (無憂王) instead of 阿輸迦 and both the Aśoka and Bimbisāra notes keep the Chinese '唐言…' untranslated instead of giving the transcription (阿輸迦, 頻毘婆羅); 'My prime of life is passing' → 盛色方剛 'I am in the full vigour of youth'
en_revised: To the south of the Ganges (Gaṅgā) River is an old city, over seventy li in circuit; although it has long been deserted, its foundations still remain. In the past, when the human life span was immeasurable, it was called the city of Kusumapura (拘蘇摩補羅; in the language of the Tang,  "Fragrant Flower Palace City"). The royal palace had many flowers, and thus it was so named. When the human life span reached several thousand years, the name was changed to Pāṭaliputra (波吒釐子城; it was formerly called the city of Balianfu, but that is an error).  Initially, there was a Brahmin of high talent and broad learning who had several thousand disciples receiving instruction from him. As the students were traveling together for recreation, there was one young scholar who paced back and forth, looking melancholy. His companions asked him, "Why are you so worried?" He replied, "I am in the full vigour of youth, yet I am a traveler wandering in the shadows; years have accumulated, yet my studies remain unaccomplished. Reflecting on this, my heart is filled with deep distress."  Thereupon, the students jokingly said to him, "We shall now seek a marriage match for you." They then designated two people to act as the groom's parents and two as the bride's parents, and seated him under a Pāṭalī tree, for it is called the tree of feminine gender (*strī-liṅga*). They gathered seasonal fruits, drew from the clear stream, set forth the sequence of the marriage rites, and requested a date for the happy union. At that time, the man acting as the bride's father plucked a flowering branch and handed it to the scholar, saying, "This is your fine spouse; I hope you will not decline." The scholar’s heart was joyful and content; when evening came and it was time to return, he remained behind, filled with longing. The students said, "Our previous words were merely a joke! You should come back with us; we fear that wild beasts in the forest might harm you." The scholar then remained, pacing back and forth beside the tree. After the sun had set, a strange light illuminated the wilderness, and the sounds of elegant pipes and strings arose as curtains and canopies were displayed. Presently, an old man was seen approaching with a staff to offer greetings, followed by an old woman leading a young maiden, with the road filled with attendants in splendid attire playing music. The old man then pointed to the maiden and said, "This is your wife." They indulged in singing and feasting for seven days. The students, suspecting he had been harmed by wild beasts, went to search for him and found him sitting alone in the shade of the tree, as if entertaining an honored guest. They urged him to return with them, but he declined their request. Later, he went into the city himself to visit his relatives and friends and told them the whole story. Those who heard were astonished and went with his friends into the forest, where they all saw that the flowering tree had become a grand mansion, with servants and attendants hurrying to and fro, while the old man received them with composure, laying out a feast and playing music, with all the etiquette between host and guests fully observed. His friends returned to the city and reported the details to everyone, far and near. After one year, a son was born. The scholar said to his wife, "I now wish to return home, yet I cannot bear to be separated; but if I continue to stay here, I am merely lodging in the open, exposed to the elements." Upon hearing this, his wife reported it all to her father. The old man said to the scholar, "In human life, one seeks pleasure; why must it be in one's native village? I shall now build a house for you, so you should have no other intentions." Thereupon, the laborers were set to work, and the task was completed in a few days. The old city of Kusumapura (拘蘇摩補羅) was moved to this location. Because of that son, the spirits built the city, and from then on, it was named the city of Pāṭaliputra (波吒釐子城). To the north of the old palace of the king is a stone pillar, several tens of feet high; this is the place where King Aśoka (無憂王) established a hell. One hundred years after the Parinirvāṇa of Śākya Tathāgata, there was King Aśoka (阿輸迦; in the language of the Tang, "No Sorrow"; formerly called Ayu [阿育], which is an error), the great-grandson of King Bimbisāra (頻毘婆羅; in the language of the Tang, "Firm Shadow"; formerly called Pinposuo [頻婆娑], which is an error). He moved his capital from Rājagṛha to Pāṭaliputra and built an outer wall that encircled the old city. As the ages have long since passed, only the old foundations remain. Of the hundreds of sites of saṃghārāmas, deva temples, and stūpas, only two or three still exist. Only to the north of the old palace, bordering the Gaṅgā river, is a small city containing over a thousand families.  Initially, after King Aśoka succeeded to the throne, his conduct was harsh and tyrannical; he established a hell to harm living beings. Lofty walls rose steeply on all sides, with watchtowers standing tall at the corners; there were furnaces of fierce fire and sharp-edged weapons, and all manner of torture instruments were prepared in imitation of the underworld, while a savage man was recruited to be the jailer. At first, criminals from throughout the kingdom, regardless of the severity of their offenses, were all cast into the fire and ash. Later, anyone who happened to pass by the prison was seized and executed; all who arrived there died, and thus the evidence was destroyed. At that time, there was a śramaṇa who had newly joined the monastic order; while making his rounds in the neighborhood to beg for food, he happened upon the gate of the prison, and the cruel jailer seized him, intending to do him harm. The śramaṇa was terrified and requested permission to perform repentance. Suddenly, he saw a man brought in bound to the prison, his hands and feet severed and his body torn apart; in the blink of an eye, his limbs were scattered and pulverized. Having witnessed this, the śramaṇa was filled with profound grief and pity, developed a contemplation on impermanence, and attained the fruit of the arhat (aśaikṣa). The jailer said, "You may now die." Having attained the holy fruit, the śramaṇa’s mind was indifferent to life and death; although he was cast into a cauldron of boiling water, it felt as if he were in a clear pond, with a great lotus flower serving as his seat. The prison warden was terrified and sent a messenger to inform the King. The King then came to observe in person and deeply praised this miraculous protection. The warden said, "Great King, you must die." The King asked, "Why?" He replied, "Your Majesty previously issued a decree ordering me to oversee the prison, stating that all who reach the prison walls are to be executed, and it did not say that if the King enters, he alone should be exempt from death." The King said, "The law has already been fixed, and in principle, it cannot be changed again. When I first issued the order, did it exclude your own person? That you have lived so long in error is my fault." He immediately ordered the jailer to cast him into the great furnace. Once the warden was dead, the King was able to leave; he then demolished the walls, filled in the moats, abolished the prison, and lightened the punishments.

en_revised: Not far from the side of the Vihara of the Buddha’s Footprints, there is a large stone pillar over thirty feet high. The inscription is incomplete, but its general meaning is: "King Aśoka’s (無憂王) roots of faith were firm and solid; he thrice offered Jambudvīpa to the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Sangha, and thrice redeemed it with various precious treasures." This is the general gist of the text.  To the north of the old palace is a large rock chamber; from the outside it appears like a high mountain, and inside it is several zhang wide. It was built by King Aśoka for his younger brother who had left home to become a monk, by employing spirits and ghosts.  Originally, King Aśoka had a younger brother by the same mother named Mahendra (摩醯因陀羅; in the language of Tang, "Great Emperor"). Born into the nobility, he wore clothing that usurped royal regulations and was extravagant, indulgent, and violent, causing the masses to harbor resentment. An old minister who assisted the state remonstrated with the King, saying, "Your arrogant brother’s exercise of power has already become too excessive. When government is equitable, the state is well-ordered; when the people are harmonious, the ruler is secure. This is an ancient maxim that has existed for a long time. I hope you will uphold the state laws and hand him over to the authorities."  King Aśoka wept and said to his brother, "I have inherited the foundation of the ancestors and provide shelter to all living beings; how could I forget the affection for you, my own flesh and blood? Yet, because I did not guide you earlier, you have already fallen into the trap of criminal law. Above, I fear the ancestral spirits; below, I am pressured by the public consensus."  Mahendra bowed his head and apologized, saying, "I did not conduct myself with prudence and dared to violate the national constitution. I pray you grant me a new lease on life by allowing a seven-day respite." Thereupon, he was placed in a secluded chamber, strictly guarded, and provided with fine delicacies and superior food, served without fail. The guard called out, "One day has passed; six days remain." When the sixth day had ended, having felt deep anxiety and fear, he further exerted his body and mind, whereupon he attained the fruit of enlightenment, ascended into the void, and manifested divine miracles; soon after, he left the secular world to dwell far away in a rocky valley. King Aśoka (無憂王) went in person and said to him, "Formerly, I was bound by state law and intended to impose a severe punishment. Who would have thought you would transcend so purely and attain the holy fruit? Since you are no longer burdened by attachments, you may return to the country." The younger brother replied, "Formerly, I was fettered by the net of desire, my mind racing after sights and sounds; now that I have escaped the city of danger, my will finds joy in the mountain valleys. I wish to abandon the human world and dwell forever among the hills and ravines." The king said, "To quiet the mind and thoughts, must one necessarily seek a secluded cliff? I shall follow your will and build a retreat for you." He then summoned the spirits and deities and told them, "On a coming day I shall prepare a grand feast of delicacies; you shall lead one another to gather at my assembly, each bringing a large stone to serve as your own seat." The spirits received the command and gathered in full by the appointed time. When the assembly had ended, the king said to the spirits, "The stone seats are scattered about; you should stack them up yourselves. Without laboring over the work, pile them into a chamber." The spirits received the command and completed it in a few days. King Aśoka went in person to invite him to stay in this mountain hut. North of the old palace and south of the hell, there is a large stone trough; it was through the divine labor of King Aśoka’s craftsmen that this vessel was created to store food when providing meals for the monks. To the southwest of the old palace is a small rocky mountain. Within its surrounding cliffs and valleys are several dozen stone chambers, which King Aśoka (無憂王) had built by employing spirits for the sake of the arhat Upagupta (近護) and others. Beside them is an old terrace with stone foundations remaining. There is a pond with rippling water, clear and limpid like a mirror; people from neighboring countries and distant lands call it the "holy water," and if one drinks from it or washes in it, one’s sins and defilements are eradicated.  To the southwest of the mountain are five stupas. Their lofty foundations have subsided, yet the remaining sites are still high; viewed from afar, they appear like lush mounds, each side measuring several hundred paces. People of later generations have built small stupas atop them. The *Record of India* (印度記) states: "In the past, after King Aśoka had built eighty-four thousand stupas, there remained five *dou* of relics; therefore, he specially constructed these five stupas, with a design surpassing all other places, where miracles occur from time to time to represent the fivefold Dharma-body (五分法身) of the Tathāgata." Those of shallow faith have secretly speculated that this was a treasury built by the former King Nanda (難陀王) to store the seven treasures. Later, there was a king who was not very sincere in his faith; hearing these earlier speculations, he gave free rein to his greed and desire. He mobilized his army and generals and came in person to excavate them. The earth shook and the mountains tilted, clouds darkened and the sun was obscured, and a great sound like thunder shook from within the stupas. The soldiers fell down stiff, and the elephants and horses fled in terror. Ever since then, no one has dared to covet them. Some say: "Although there are many public opinions, they are not definitive conclusions; by following the ancient records, one can obtain the truth."
