en_revised: To the southeast of the old city is the Kukkuṭārāma (屈吒阿濫摩; 屈 read with the initial of 居 and the final of 勿; in the language of the Tang, "Rooster Garden" [鷄園]) monastery; it was built by King Aśoka (無憂王). When King Aśoka first gained faith in the Buddha-dharma, he followed the teachings to build this monastery and cultivate the seeds of merit; he summoned a thousand monks, both ordinary and holy, providing them with the four requisites and a complete supply of daily necessities. It has long been in ruins, but the foundations still remain. Beside the monastery is a large stūpa named Āmalaka. This is the name of a medicinal fruit in India. King Aśoka fell ill and was on the verge of death; knowing his life could not be saved, he wished to give away his treasures to cultivate a field of merit. However, powerful ministers held the reins of government and warned him not to follow his desires. Later, during a meal, he kept an āmalaka fruit and toyed with it until it was half-rotten; then, clutching the fruit and sighing deeply, he asked his ministers, "Who is now the lord of Jambudvīpa?" The ministers replied, "Only the Great King." The King said, "That is not so. I am no longer the lord. Only this half-fruit is under my control. Alas! The wealth and honor of the world are more precarious than a candle in the wind. Though I occupy the realm and hold a high title, at the end of my life I am destitute, constrained by powerful ministers. The world is no longer mine; only this half-fruit remains!" He then commanded an attendant, saying, "Take this half-fruit to that Rooster Garden, offer it to the assembly of monks, and speak these words: 'The former lord of Jambudvīpa, now the king of half an āmalaka fruit, bows his head before the monks of great virtue and prays that you will accept his final offering. All that I possessed has been lost; only this half-fruit remains, over which I have a little freedom. May you have compassion for the destitute and increase the seeds of merit." The senior monk of the assembly spoke thus: "King Aśoka (無憂大王) long cherished the vow of universal salvation, but now he is afflicted by illness, treacherous ministers have usurped his authority, and the accumulated treasures are no longer his; he offers this half-fruit as alms. We have received the King’s command to distribute it to the entire assembly of monks." He then summoned the steward to boil it all in the soup. They collected the fruit’s pit and erected a stupa. Having received this great kindness, they honored his final request.  To the northwest of the Āmalaka Stupa (阿摩落伽窣堵波), in an old monastery, there is a stupa called "Sound of Striking the Ghaṇṭā" (建揵稚聲). Formerly, there were hundreds of monasteries within this city; the monks were solemn and respectful, their academic pursuits were lofty and pure, and the non-Buddhist scholars kept silent and held their tongues. Later, the monks passed away one after another, and the younger generation failed to continue the practices of their predecessors. The non-Buddhist teachers and disciples passed down their training until they had mastered their arts; they then summoned their companions by the thousands and tens of thousands to assemble at the monastery, shouting aloud: "Strike the ghaṇṭā (揵稚) to summon the scholars!" The ignorant crowd joined in, and they mistakenly struck it. They then reported to the King, requesting a debate to determine who was superior. The non-Buddhist masters were of high talent and great learning, while the monks, though numerous, were shallow in their arguments and discourse. The non-Buddhists said, "Our arguments have prevailed. From this day forward, no monastery shall strike the ghaṇṭā to assemble its members." The King granted their request and issued a decree based on the previous debate. The community of monks, having suffered this shame, endured the insults and withdrew, and for twelve years they did not strike the ghaṇṭā. At that time, in Southern India, there was the Bodhisattva Nāgārjuna (那伽閼剌樹那; in the language of the Tang, Longmeng [龍猛, "Dragon-Valiant"]; the old translation Longshu [龍樹, "Dragon-Tree"] is wrong), who from his youth was renowned for his elegance and in his maturity possessed a great reputation. He abandoned desire and attachment, left the household life to cultivate learning, deeply investigated the subtle principles, and attained the stage of the first bhūmi. He had a great disciple named Deva, who was wise, bright, and quick-witted, with a sharp and alert mind. He said to his teacher, "The scholars of the city of Pāṭaliputra have been defeated in debate by the non-Buddhists and have not struck the ghaṇṭā; time has passed swiftly, and it has been twelve years. I dare to wish to crush the mountain of wrong views and light the torch of the true Dharma." Nāgārjuna said, "The non-Buddhists of Pāṭaliputra are erudite, and you are no match for them; I shall go myself." Deva said, "To crush rotten grass, why must one overturn a mountain? I dare to accept your instruction to dismiss these heterodox teachings. May the Master establish the arguments of the non-Buddhists, and I shall refute them point by point; let us examine their strengths and weaknesses, and then I shall plan my journey." Nāgārjuna then upheld the non-Buddhist arguments, and Deva proceeded to refute his logic. After seven days, Nāgārjuna lost his position, and he sighed, saying, "Fallacious words are easily defeated, and false doctrines are difficult to maintain. You may go now; you will certainly crush them!" Bodhisattva Deva had long enjoyed a great reputation; when the non-Buddhists of Pāṭaliputra heard of him, they immediately assembled and hurried to inform the King, saying, "Your Majesty previously condescended to listen to us and prohibited the monks from striking the ghaṇṭā. We pray that you will issue a decree." "Order the gatekeepers not to allow any strange monks from neighboring territories to enter the city, for fear that they might form a faction and recklessly overturn the previous regulation." The King agreed to their request and strictly increased the surveillance. When Deva (提婆) arrived, he was unable to enter the city. Hearing of the restrictive order, he changed his clothes, folded his saṃghāṭī (僧加胝) robe and placed it inside a bundle of straw, then lifting his skirts and hurrying along, he entered while carrying the bundle on his head. Once inside the city, he discarded the straw and put on his robe, then came to this monastery (saṃghārāma) seeking a place to rest. As he knew few people and no one would offer him lodging, he spent the night on the ghaṇṭā (揵稚) platform. At dawn, he struck it loudly. When the crowd heard it and investigated, they found it was a traveling bhikṣu. All the monasteries echoed the sound in response. When the King heard of this and made inquiries, he could not find the culprit until he reached this monastery, where everyone pointed to Deva. Deva said, "The ghaṇṭā is struck to assemble the community. If one has it but does not use it, why hang it up?" The King’s men replied, "In the past, the monastic community lost a debate, and it was decreed that it should not be struck; it has been twelve years." Deva said, "Is that so? Today, I shall sound the Dharma-drum once more." He sent word to the King, saying, "A strange śramaṇa wishes to wash away the previous shame." The King then summoned the scholars and established a decree, saying, "Whoever loses the debate and abandons their original school shall forfeit their life as an apology." Thereupon, the non-Buddhists vied to display their banners and drums, clamoring with their divergent doctrines, each showing off the sharpness of their rhetoric. Once the Bodhisattva Deva had ascended the debate seat, he listened to the other side speak first, then analyzed and refuted their arguments point by point. In less than twelve days, he had crushed all the heterodox schools. The king and his ministers were filled with joy and built this spiritual foundation to commemorate his supreme virtue. To the north of the stūpa of striking the ghaṇṭā (建擊揵稚窣堵波) is an old foundation, which was formerly the dwelling place of the "Demon-Eloquent Brahman."  Formerly, there was a Brahman in this city who built a hut in a desolate thicket, withdrew from the world, worshipped spirits to seek blessings, and consorted with demons. He engaged in profound discussions and intense debates, his elegant words responding to all inquiries; when people challenged him, he would answer from behind a lowered curtain. Among the scholars and men of talent of that time, none could surpass him, and the gentry and commoners alike looked up to him as if he were a sage.  There was a Bodhisattva named Aśvaghoṣa (阿濕縛窶沙; in the language of the Tang, "Horse-neighing" [馬鳴]), whose wisdom encompassed all things and whose teachings spread through the Three Vehicles. He often said to others, "This Brahman has no teacher for his learning and no ancient precedent for his arts; yet, living in seclusion and solitude, he enjoys a high reputation all to himself. If he were not reliant on ghosts and spirits or possessed by demons, how could he be thus? When eloquence is granted by demons, one cannot speak face-to-face with others, and once their words are heard, they can never be repeated. I shall now go there to observe his conduct."  He then went to the Brahman’s hut and said to him, "I have long admired your great virtue. I hope you will be willing to raise the curtain, as I dare to express a long-held wish." Yet the Brahman remained arrogant and haughty, responding from behind the lowered curtain and refusing to speak face-to-face. Aśvaghoṣa (馬鳴) knew in his heart that it was a demon, yet he was very confident. After taking his leave and withdrawing, he said to the people, "I have already understood it; I shall certainly defeat him." He then went to inform the king, "I only hope you will grant me permission to engage that householder in a rigorous debate." Hearing this, the king was alarmed and said, "What kind of person is this! If one has not realized the three knowledges (三明) and acquired the six supernatural powers (六通), how can one debate with him?" The king ordered his carriage to attend in person to observe the debate in detail. At that time, Aśvaghoṣa discussed the subtle words of the Tripitaka (三藏) and expounded the great principles of the five sciences (五明); his marvelous eloquence was unrestrained, and his lofty arguments were profound and far-reaching. After the Brahman had finished stating his case, Aśvaghoṣa spoke again, saying, "You have missed the gist of my argument; you should state it again." At that moment, the Brahman remained silent and kept his mouth shut. Aśvaghoṣa scolded him, saying, "Why do you not resolve the difficulty? The demon you serve should quickly provide you with words!" He then swiftly lifted the curtain to look at and observe the strange creature. The Brahman was terrified and said, "Stop! Stop!" Aśvaghoṣa withdrew and said, "This fellow’s reputation has collapsed this morning; a false name does not last long—this is what is meant by that." The king said, "If not for a man of great virtue, who could discern the heterodox path? Such wisdom in knowing men is unparalleled in the past and future; the country has established laws, and we should honor such genuine substance."

en_revised: More than thirty *li* to the northwest of the mountain, in a mountain recess, there is a monastery. It rests against a ridge with a lofty foundation, and its pavilions stand upon sparse cliffs. There are more than fifty monks, all of whom study the teachings of the Mahāyāna. This is the place where the Bodhisattva Guṇamati (瞿那末底; in the language of the Tang, "Virtue-Wisdom" [德慧]) defeated a non-Buddhist.  Formerly, there was a non-Buddhist in this mountain named Mādhava, who took the Sāṃkhya (僧佉) school as his ancestor and practiced its path. His learning exhausted both internal and external doctrines, his words reached the limits of emptiness and existence, his reputation stood above his contemporaries, and his virtue was esteemed at the time. The king cherished and respected him, calling him the "treasure of the country," and the ministers and commoners revered him, all calling him their "family teacher." Scholars from neighboring countries, hearing of his influence and admiring his virtue, ranked him among the foremost, truly a man of broad attainment. He was supported by the income of two cities, which surrounded his residence as a fief.  At that time, the Bodhisattva Guṇamati of South India was quick-witted from his youth; he excelled early in the subtle and profound, his learning mastered the Tripiṭaka, and his reasoning exhausted the Four Noble Truths. Hearing that Mādhava’s theories were extremely profound and subtle, he harbored the intent to blunt his sharp edge. He ordered a disciple to write a letter saying: "I respectfully inquire whether Mādhava is well and at peace. You should forget your weariness and toil, and diligently study your old learning; three years from now, I shall destroy your fine reputation."  In the second and third years, he sent messengers to notify him in this manner. When he was about to set out, he wrote another letter saying: "The time limit has expired; how is your study progressing? I am arriving now; you should be aware of this." Mādhava was filled with great fear and warned his disciples and the inhabitants of his town: "From this day forward, you must not provide lodging to any śramaṇas or followers of heterodox paths; spread this word among yourselves and do not violate this command." At that time, the Bodhisattva Guṇamati (德慧) came carrying his staff and arrived at the town of Mādhava. The people kept their agreement, and no one would offer him lodging. The Brahmins further reviled him, saying, "With your shaven head and strange robes, what strange kind of man are you? You should leave quickly; do not stay here!" The Bodhisattva Guṇamati, wishing to defeat the heterodox teachings and hoping to lodge in the town, spoke with a compassionate heart and humble words, saying, "You all practice the pure conduct of worldly truth, while I practice the pure conduct of the ultimate truth; since our pure conduct is the same, why do you reject me?" The Brahmins would not speak to him, but only sought to drive him away. They drove him out of the town and into a great forest. In the forest, packs of fierce beasts acted with violence. A man of pure faith, fearing he might be harmed by the beasts, bound together a torch and took up a staff, saying to the Bodhisattva, "There is a Bodhisattva Guṇamati of South India whose reputation has spread far and wide, and who intends to come here for a debate; therefore, the lord of this town, fearing the loss of his good name, has strictly decreed that no śramaṇa be allowed to stay. Fearing you might be harmed by the creatures, I have come to assist you. Go now and be at peace; have no other worries." Guṇamati said, "I must tell you, pure believer, that I am Guṇamati." Having heard this, the pure believer showed even deeper respect and said to Guṇamati, "Since it is as you say, you should depart quickly." He then left the deep forest and rested in an empty marsh. The pure believer lit a fire and held his bow, patrolling around him; when the night had ended, he said to Guṇamati, "You may go now, for I fear people may hear of this and come to harm you." Guṇamati thanked him, saying, "I shall not forget your kindness." Thereupon he departed. Arriving at the royal palace, he said to the gatekeeper, "There is a śramaṇa who has come from afar; he requests the king's gracious permission to debate with Mādhava (摩沓婆)." Hearing this, the king was surprised and said, "This is a delusional man." He immediately ordered an envoy to go to Mādhava’s residence to proclaim the royal decree, saying, "An extraordinary śramaṇa has come seeking a debate; the debate hall has now been cleansed and prepared, and an announcement has been sent out far and near; we await your arrival and hope you will grace us with your presence." Mādhava asked the king's envoy, "Is it not the Śāstra Master Guṇamati (德慧) of South India?" The envoy replied, "It is." Upon hearing this, Mādhava was very displeased, but as the matter was difficult to decline, he proceeded to the debate hall. The king, ministers, scholars, commoners, and noble families all gathered to listen to the profound discourse. Guṇamati first established his thesis, and by the time the sun had set, Mādhava excused himself on the grounds of his advanced age and the dullness of his wit in responding quickly, requesting to return home to reflect so that he might respond to the challenge later. Every point was met with a request to return home, and when he ascended the seat the next morning, he ultimately offered no counter-arguments. On the sixth day, he vomited blood and died. As he was about to expire, he looked at his wife and commanded, "You possess great talent; do not forget this shame!" After Mādhava died, his death was concealed and not announced; his wife changed into his fine, colorful robes and came to the debate hall. The crowd broke into a hubbub, saying to one another, "Mādhava is conceited about his own talent and is ashamed to face Guṇamati, so he has sent his wife instead; the difference in their caliber is now clear." Guṇamati Bodhisattva (德慧菩薩) said to his wife, "The one who could control you, I have already subdued." Mādhava’s wife, realizing the difficulty, withdrew. The King asked, "What was that secret conversation, that she became silent?" Guṇamati replied, "Alas, Mādhava is dead! His wife intended to come and debate with me." The King asked, "How did you know this? I wish you would explain it to me." Guṇamati said, "When his wife came, her face bore the look of mourning and her voice was filled with grief and resentment; therefore, I knew that Mādhava was dead. 'The one who could control you' referred to her husband." The King ordered an envoy to go and observe, and it was indeed as discussed. The King then apologized, saying, "The Buddha-Dharma is profound and mysterious; brilliant sages follow in succession. By practicing the Way through non-action, all sentient beings are moistened by its transformation. According to the ancient laws of the state, there is a constant practice of praising virtue." Guṇamati said, "Though I am ignorant, I embody the Way and dwell in purity. If one maintains integrity and seeks to benefit others, then to promote and guide them, one must first crush their arrogance. As for using expedient means to gather and transform them, now is the time. I only wish that Your Majesty would assign the descendants of the households in Mādhava’s fief to serve the monastery (saṃghārāma) for a thousand generations, so as to leave a warning for future ages and spread this beauty boundlessly. And may that man of pure faith who protected me have his blessings extended to his descendants, and may his food and provisions be the same as the monks', so as to encourage the pure-hearted and praise profound virtue." Thereupon, this monastery was built to commemorate this remarkable event. Initially, after Mādhava was defeated in debate, some ten or more Brahmins fled to a neighboring country to escape the disgrace. They reported the humiliation to various heretics (tīrthikas) and recruited talented individuals to come and wash away their previous shame. Since the king esteemed and respected Guṇamati (德慧), he went in person to request him, saying: "Now these heretics, overestimating their own strength, have formed a clique and dared to sound the drum of debate; I only wish that the Great Master would crush these heterodox sects." Guṇamati said: "It is appropriate to assemble the debaters." Thereupon, the heretical scholars comforted one another with joy, saying: "Today, we are certain to be victorious over him." When the heretics began to expound their doctrines, Guṇamati Bodhisattva said: "These heretics fled the disgrace and went far away; according to the king's prior decree, they are all outcasts, so how can I engage in a debate with them?" Guṇamati had a seat-carrier (a servant who carried his portable seat) who had long listened to his debates and was quite familiar with the subtle meanings; he stood by his side, listening to their lofty discourse. Guṇamati patted his seat and said: "Seat, you may debate with them." The assembly was entirely shocked and found his command strange. At that time, the seat-carrier immediately launched his challenge; profound meanings gushed forth like a spring, and his clear eloquence responded to every point. After three rounds, the heretics lost their tenets; their sharpness was severely blunted, and their wings were broken. Ever since they were defeated in debate, they were established as the households of the monastery (saṃghārāma).

en_revised: More than twenty *li* southwest of the Guṇamati (德慧) monastery, one arrives at an isolated hill (孤山). There is a monastery here that was built by the master Śīlabhadra (尸羅跋陀羅) (in the Tang language, Jiexian 戒賢, 'Precept-Worthy') after he won a debate; he donated his village to establish it. A single precipitous peak rises up like a stūpa, and within it are placed relics of the Buddha. The master was of the royal lineage of the country of Samataṭa (三摩呾吒國) and of the Brāhmaṇa caste. In his youth, he was fond of learning and possessed a noble character; he traveled throughout the various regions of India, inquiring after the wise and sagacious. Upon arriving at the Nālandā (那爛陀) monastery in this country, he met the Bodhisattva Dharmapāla (護法), and upon hearing the Dharma, he developed faith and understanding. He requested to don the dyed robes, consulted him on the ultimate goal, and asked about the path to liberation. Having exhausted the highest truths and investigated the subtle words, his fame dominated the era and his reputation was high in foreign lands.  In South India, there was a non-Buddhist who explored the obscure and searched for the hidden, exhausting the profound and penetrating the subtle. Hearing of Dharmapāla’s high fame, he conceived deep arrogance and jealousy, and undeterred by mountains or rivers, he beat the drum to demand a debate, saying: "I am a man of South India. I have heard that there is a great master of debate within this kingdom; although I am not clever, I wish to discuss matters with him in detail." The king said: "It is so; it is truly as you say." He then ordered an envoy to invite Dharmapāla, saying: "A non-Buddhist from South India has come from a distance of a thousand *li* to seek a debate; I only hope you will condescend to attend the assembly at the debate ground." Having heard this, Dharmapāla gathered his robes and prepared to go. His disciple Śīlabhadra, who was the most outstanding among the younger generation, stepped forward and requested: "Why must you go so hastily?" Dharmapāla (護法) said: "Since the Sun of Wisdom has withdrawn its light and the Lamp of the Dharma has ceased its illumination, heretics have gathered like ants and heterodox schools have swarmed like wasps; therefore, I now intend to demolish their arguments." Śīlabhadra (戒賢) said: "I have respectfully heard your arguments; I dare to demolish the heterodox path." Dharmapāla knew that he was a man of outstanding talent and therefore granted his consent. At that time, Śīlabhadra was just thirty years old, and the assembly slighted his youth, fearing he would be unable to shoulder the task alone. Dharmapāla, knowing the dissatisfaction of the assembly, explained to them: "What is valued is brilliance and wisdom, not one's age; from what I see now, he is certain to defeat them."  When the day of the debate arrived, people from far and near flocked to the scene, and both young and old gathered together. The heretic expounded his great principles, exhausting their profound subtleties; Śīlabhadra followed reason to demand the truth, reaching the depths of the abstruse. The heretic’s arguments were exhausted, and he retreated in shame. The king, wishing to reward his virtue, bestowed this city upon him. The Master of Shastras declined, saying: "A man in dyed robes finds his support in contentment and maintains himself in purity; what use has he for a city?" The king said: "The Dharma King has hidden his traces and the Boat of Wisdom has sunk; if there is no recognition, there is nothing to encourage future students. For the sake of propagating the True Dharma, I hope you will compassionately accept it." The Master of Shastras, unable to refuse, accepted the city. He then built a monastery (saṃghārāma), exhausting all the rules of construction, and dedicated the households of the city to provide for its maintenance.

issues: note (舊曰那提迦葉，訛也。洎諸迦葉，例無波字，略也): 'formerly called Nadi-Kāśyapa' loses the point (the old form 那提迦葉 lacks 波); 'the omission of the pa character is a simplification' → 'for all the Kāśyapas the character 波 is regularly missing, an abbreviation'; Gayā-śīrṣa is an addition not in the Chinese (kept as a gloss)
en_revised: Five or six *li* to the southwest of the city, one arrives at Mount Gayā (伽耶山; Gayā-śīrṣa). The ravines and valleys are dark and deep, and the peaks and cliffs are precipitous. In the customs of the country of India, it is commonly called the Spirit Mountain (靈山). Since ancient times, monarchs who have governed the universe and inherited the succession, whose civilizing influence has reached distant peoples, and whose virtues have surpassed those of previous generations, have all ascended this mountain to perform the *feng* sacrifice and announce their successes. On the summit of the mountain is a stone *stūpa* over one hundred feet high, which was built by King Aśoka (無憂王). Its spiritual efficacy is secretly felt, and divine light occasionally illuminates it; in the past, the Tathāgata expounded the *Ratnamegha* (寶雲) and other sutras here. To the southeast of Mount Gayā is a *stūpa* that marks the native village of Kāśyapa. To its south are two *stūpas*, which are the places where Gayā-Kāśyapa and Nadī-Kāśyapa (formerly called Natijiaye 那提迦葉, which is erroneous; in all the names with Kāśyapa (迦葉) the character 波 (pa) is regularly missing, an abbreviation) practiced fire worship.

en_revised: Traveling fourteen or fifteen *li* southwest from the mountain of Prāgbodhi (前正覺山), one arrives at the Mahā-bodhi (菩提樹). A surrounding wall of piled bricks is high, steep, and secure. It is long from east to west and narrow from north to south, measuring over five hundred paces in circumference. Rare trees and famous flowers interweave their shade and shadows; fine sand and exotic grasses form a lush, spreading carpet. The main gate opens to the east, facing the Nairañjanā River; the south gate connects to a large flower pond; the west side is closed off and strongly protected; and the north gate leads to a great monastery. Within the enclosure, sacred sites are adjacent to one another, some being stūpas and others being *vihāra*s (精舍). Kings, ministers, and noble families from all the countries of Jambudvīpa, reverently upholding the Buddha’s legacy, have built them as memorials.  In the center of the Mahā-bodhi enclosure is the Vajra Seat (金剛座). Long ago, when the Bhadrakalpa was first formed, it arose together with the great earth. It is situated in the center of the three-thousand great chiliocosm, reaching down to the golden wheel and up to the surface of the ground. It is composed of diamond and measures over a hundred paces in circumference. Because the thousand Buddhas of the Bhadrakalpa sit upon it to enter the diamond samādhi, it is called the Vajra Seat. It is the place where the holy path is realized, also called the *bodhimaṇḍa* (道場). When the great earth shakes, this place alone does not tremble or sway. For this reason, when the Tathāgata was about to realize perfect enlightenment, he traversed these four corners, and the ground shook everywhere; but when he later arrived at this spot, it was peaceful and did not tilt. Since entering the final age, the True Dharma has gradually faded, and it has become covered with sand and earth, no longer to be seen. After the Buddha’s *nirvāṇa*, kings of various countries, having heard of the dimensions of the Vajra Seat as described by the Buddha, used two statues of Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva to mark the northern and southern boundaries, facing toward the east. I have heard from the elders: "When the bodies of these Bodhisattva statues sink and disappear, the Buddha-Dharma will come to an end." Today, the Bodhisattva at the southern corner has sunk past its chest. The Mahā-bodhi tree (菩提樹) on the Vajra Seat is the pippala tree. When the Buddha was in the world, it was several hundred feet high; though it has been repeatedly cut down, it is still four or five zhang high. The Buddha sat beneath it and attained Perfect Enlightenment, and for this reason, it is called the Bodhi tree. Its trunk is yellowish-white, and its branches and leaves are emerald green; they do not wither in winter or summer, and their luster remains unchanged. Every year on the day of the Tathāgata’s *nirvāṇa*, the leaves all wither and fall, but after a short while, they return to their former state. On that day, the monarchs of various countries, along with clergy and laity from other regions, numbering in the tens of millions, gather without being summoned to water and wash the tree with scented water and milk; they then play music, arrange fragrant flowers, and keep lamps and torches burning day and night, vying with one another to present offerings.  After the Tathāgata’s *nirvāṇa*, when King Aśoka (無憂王) first ascended the throne, he believed in heretical doctrines and destroyed the sacred sites left by the Buddha, mobilizing troops and coming in person to cut the tree down. The roots, stems, branches, and leaves were chopped into small pieces and piled up several dozen paces to the west, where fire-worshiping Brahmins were ordered to burn them as a sacrifice to heaven; yet before the smoke and flames had subsided, two trees suddenly grew out from the midst of the fierce fire with luxuriant, verdant leaves, and were thus called the "Ash Bodhi Trees." King Aśoka witnessed this miracle and repented; he watered the remaining roots with scented milk, and by the time dawn approached, the tree had grown back as it was before. The king witnessed this miracle and was deeply overjoyed; he personally performed offerings, finding such delight that he forgot to return home. The queen, who had long believed in heretical teachings, secretly dispatched messengers after midnight to cut down the tree again. When King Aśoka (無憂王) went to pay his respects at dawn, he saw only a stump; deeply moved by grief, he prayed with utmost sincerity and irrigated it with fragrant milk, and within a few days it grew back to life. The king, deeply respecting this marvel, built a stone wall around it over ten feet high, which can still be seen today.  Recently, King Śaśāṅka (設賞迦王), a believer in heretical teachings who slandered and envied the Buddha-dharma, destroyed monasteries and cut down the Mahā-bodhi (菩提樹) tree; he dug down to the springs but could not exhaust the roots, so he set it on fire and soaked it with sugarcane juice, wishing to rot it and utterly destroy any remaining sprouts. Several months later, King Pūrṇavarman (補剌拏伐摩王; in Tang language, "Full Armor" [滿胄]) of the kingdom of Magadha (摩揭陀國), the last descendant of King Aśoka, heard of this and sighed, saying: "The sun of wisdom has already set, and only the Buddha-tree remains; now that it has been destroyed again, what will living beings look upon!" He threw his entire body to the ground, his sorrow moving all who saw him. He had the milk of several thousand cows collected to irrigate it, and within a night the tree grew back to a height of over one zhang. Fearing it might be cut down again in the future, he surrounded it with a stone wall twenty-four feet high. Therefore, the Mahā-bodhi tree is now hidden within a stone enclosure, rising more than one zhang above it.

en_revised: To the east of the Mahā-bodhi (菩提樹) is a vihāra (精舍), one hundred and sixty or seventy feet high, with a base more than twenty paces wide, built of blue bricks and plastered with lime. The tiered niches all contain golden images, and the four walls are carved with exquisite designs, some in the form of linked pearls, others as celestial beings. At the top is placed a golden-copper āmalaka fruit (also called a treasure vase, or a treasure terrace). The eastern side is connected to a multi-storied pavilion with eaves and roofs rising in three distinct tiers; the rafters, pillars, beams, doors, and windows are decorated with gold and silver carvings and inlaid with pearls and jade. The inner chambers and deep halls have three sets of connecting doors. On the left and right of the outer gate are niche chambers; on the left is an image of Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva (觀自在菩薩), and on the right is an image of Maitreya Bodhisattva (慈氏菩薩), both cast in white silver and over ten feet high. On the original site of the vihāra, King Aśoka (無憂王) first built a small vihāra, which was later expanded by a Brahmin. Initially, there was a Brahmin who did not believe in the Buddha’s teachings and worshipped Maheśvara (大自在天). Hearing that the deity resided in the Snow Mountains, he went there with his younger brother to seek the fulfillment of his vows. The deity said, "All wishes and prayers are fulfilled only when one has merit. What you pray for is not something I can grant." The Brahmin asked, "What merit should I cultivate to fulfill my heart's desire?" The deity replied, "If you wish to plant good seeds and seek a superior field of merit, the Mahā-bodhi is the place where the Buddha attained the fruit of enlightenment. You should return quickly, go to the Mahā-bodhi, build a great vihāra, dig a large water pond, and perform various offerings; then your wishes shall be fulfilled." The Brahmin, having received the divine command, conceived great faith and returned together; the elder brother built a vihāra (精舍) and the younger brother excavated a water pond. Thereupon, they performed grand offerings and diligently sought the fulfillment of their heart’s desires, which were eventually realized as they became high ministers to the king, and all the emoluments and rewards they received were given away as alms. Once the vihāra was completed, they sought to recruit craftsmen to fashion an image of the Tathāgata as he first attained Buddhahood. A long time passed, and no one responded to the call. After a while, a Brahmin came and told the assembly, "I am skilled at depicting the wondrous form of the Tathāgata." The assembly asked, "Now that we are to create the image, what do you require?" He replied, "Only scented clay. It should be placed inside the vihāra, along with a single lamp for illumination. Once I have entered, seal the door firmly; it may only be opened after six months." The monastic assembly followed his instructions. With four days still remaining before the six months were up, the assembly became alarmed and curious, and they opened the door to look inside. They saw the Buddha image inside the vihāra looking majestic, sitting cross-legged with the right foot on top, the left hand withdrawn, and the right hand hanging down, facing east and appearing as solemn as if it were alive. The pedestal was four feet two inches high and twelve feet five inches wide; the image was eleven feet five inches tall, with a distance of eight feet eight inches between the knees and six feet two inches between the shoulders. Its auspicious marks were complete and its compassionate face seemed real, except that the polishing above the right breast was not yet finished. Since the man was nowhere to be seen, they realized it was a divine manifestation, and the assembly sighed with sorrow and earnestly prayed to understand. There was a śramaṇa of simple and honest character who had a dream in which the former brahmin appeared and said to him, "I am Maitreya Bodhisattva (慈氏菩薩); fearing that the thoughts of craftsmen could not fathom the holy countenance, I came in person to depict the Buddha's image. As for the lowered right hand, formerly when the Tathāgata was about to realize the fruit of Buddhahood, the celestial Māra came to harass him, and an earth deity announced his arrival. One of them emerged first to help the Buddha subjugate the demon, but the Tathāgata told him, 'Do not be worried or afraid; I shall surely subjugate him through the power of forbearance.' The demon king asked, 'Who will be the clear witness?' The Tathāgata then lowered his hand and pointed to the ground, saying, 'This is the witness.' At that time, the second earth deity emerged to bear witness; therefore, the hand of the present image imitates that former posture of lowering." The assembly, knowing of this spiritual manifestation, was filled with sorrow and reverence. Consequently, where the area above the breast was not yet finished, they filled it with various precious substances, and adorned it with pearl necklaces, jeweled crowns, and rare treasures.  After King Śaśāṅka (設賞迦王) had felled the Mahā-bodhi (菩提樹) tree, he wished to destroy this image; however, once he beheld its compassionate countenance, his heart could not bear it, and as he turned his carriage to return, he commanded a high minister, saying, "You should remove this Buddha image and install a figure of Maheśvara (大自在天)." Having received the decree, the minister was afraid and sighed, saying, "If I destroy the Buddha image, I shall incur calamity for kalpas to come; yet if I disobey the King's command, I shall lose my life and have my clan exterminated. In such a dilemma, what is the proper course of action!" He then summoned men of faith to serve as laborers and built a brick wall across the front of the image; feeling ashamed that it would be in total darkness, he also placed a bright lamp inside, and on the front of the brick wall, he painted a picture of Maheśvara. When the work was completed, he reported back to the King. Upon hearing this, the King was terrified; his entire body broke out in pustules, his skin and flesh cracked and split, and before long, he died. The minister hurried back and destroyed the wall that had served as a barrier. Although many days had passed, the lamp was still not extinguished. The image remains to this day, and the divine craftsmanship is unimpaired. Since it is situated in a secluded chamber where lamps are kept burning in succession, one who wishes to behold the compassionate countenance cannot examine it clearly; one must hold a large, bright mirror in the morning to reflect light inside, and only then can the sacred image be seen. Those who see it naturally feel an increase in sorrow and reverence.  The Tathāgata attained perfect enlightenment on the eighth day of the second half of the Indian month of Vaiśākha, which corresponds to the eighth day of the third month in our calendar. According to the Sthavira school, however, he attained perfect enlightenment on the fifteenth day of the second half of the month of Vaiśākha, which corresponds to the fifteenth day of the third month. At that time, the Tathāgata was thirty years old; others say he was thirty-five.  To the north of the Mahā-bodhi (菩提樹) is the place where the Buddha walked in meditation. After the Tathāgata attained perfect enlightenment, he did not rise from his seat for seven days, remaining in silent meditation. When he arose, he went to the north of the Mahā-bodhi and walked in meditation for seven days, pacing back and forth from east to west for more than ten paces. Extraordinary flowers appeared in his footprints, numbering eighteen in total. Later generations built a brick foundation here, more than three feet high. I have heard from ancient records that this sacred foundation indicates the length of a person's life: if one first makes a sincere vow and then measures it, the number will increase or decrease according to the length of one's lifespan. To the north of the meditation foundation, on the right side of the path, upon a large rock, there is a great shrine (精舍) containing a Buddha image that is looking upward with its eyes raised. In the past, the Tathāgata spent seven days here gazing at the Mahā-bodhi tree (菩提樹) without once averting his eyes. He did this to repay the tree for its kindness, and thus he kept it in his view. Not far to the west of the Mahā-bodhi tree, in a great shrine (精舍), there is a brass Buddha image adorned with rare jewels, standing and facing east. In front of it is a blue stone with wonderful patterns and extraordinary colors; this is where, when the Tathāgata first attained perfect enlightenment, the Brahma King (Brahmā) built a hall of seven treasures and Lord Indra (Śakra) constructed a throne of seven treasures, upon which the Buddha meditated for seven days, emitting a wondrous light that illuminated the Mahā-bodhi tree. As the time since the Sage’s passing is long, the treasures have turned into stone.  Not far to the south of the Mahā-bodhi tree, there is a stūpa over a hundred feet high, built by King Aśoka (無憂王). When the Bodhisattva had bathed in the Nairañjanā River and was about to proceed to the Mahā-bodhi tree, he secretly pondered what he should use for a seat. He soon realized that he required clean grass. Lord Indra (天帝釋) transformed himself into a grass-cutter, carrying grass and following the path. The Bodhisattva said to him, "Could you bestow upon me some of the grass you are carrying?" The transformed being, hearing this request, respectfully offered the grass, which the Bodhisattva accepted, holding it as he proceeded forward.  Not far to the northeast of where he received the grass, there is a stūpa, which marks the place where bluebirds and herds of deer presented auspicious omens when the Bodhisattva was about to attain the fruit of Buddhahood. In India, such signs are considered favorable omens; therefore, the gods of the Pure Abodes (Śuddhāvāsa-deva) conformed to the ways of the world, and the flocks followed, flying and circling to manifest their spiritual power and reveal the holiness of the site. To the east of the Mahā-bodhi tree, on either side of the main road, there is a stūpa; these are the places where the King of Māras disturbed the Bodhisattva. When the Bodhisattva was about to attain the fruit of Buddhahood, the King of Māras urged him to accept the position of a Wheel-Turning King; when his entreaties failed, he returned in deep sorrow. The daughters of the King of Māras requested to go and seduce him, but through the Bodhisattva’s divine power, their beautiful appearances withered and changed; they withdrew supporting one another, frail and leaning on staves. To the northwest of the Mahā-bodhi tree (菩提樹), inside a shrine (精舍), there is an image of Kāśyapa Buddha; it is renowned for its spiritual efficacy and frequently emits a brilliant light. According to ancient records, if a person with utmost sincerity circumambulates it seven times, they will attain the knowledge of past lives in whatever place they are reborn. To the northwest of the Kāśyapa Buddha shrine are two brick chambers, each containing an image of an earth deity. In the past, when the Tathāgata was about to attain perfect enlightenment, one reported the arrival of Māra, and the other served as a witness for the Buddha. Later generations, mindful of their service, depicted their forms to honor their virtue. Not far to the west of the Mahā-bodhi tree enclosure, there is a stūpa called the Saffron (郁金香) Stūpa, over forty feet high, which was built by a merchant lord of the country of Jāguḍa (漕炬吒國). Formerly, in the country of Jāguḍa, there was a great merchant lord who worshiped heavenly deities and offered sacrifices to seek blessings, while holding the Buddha’s teachings in contempt and disbelieving in cause and effect. Later, he led a group of merchants to trade goods, sailing on the southern sea, when they encountered a storm and lost their way. Drifting on the waves for three years, their provisions were exhausted and they could not even secure enough food to survive. The people on the ship, unable to plan for the next day, joined their efforts and shared their resolve, calling upon the deities they served; yet, though their minds were weary with anxiety, their secret prayers were not answered. Suddenly, they saw a great mountain with towering cliffs and steep ridges, where two suns shone together, casting a brilliant, double light. At that time, the merchants comforted one another, saying, "We are fortunate; having passed this great mountain, we should stop here and find peace and happiness." The merchant leader said, "It is not a mountain, but a makara-fish. The towering cliffs and steep ridges are its whiskers and mane, and the two suns shining together are the light of its eyes." Before his voice had faded, the ship drifted toward it. Thereupon, the merchant leader told his companions, "I have heard that the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara can bestow peace and happiness in the midst of all dangers and difficulties; we should each, with utmost sincerity, call upon his name." They immediately joined their voices in unison, taking refuge and reciting his name. The towering mountain then vanished, and the two suns also disappeared. Suddenly, they saw a śramaṇa, dignified and composed, holding a staff and walking through the void, who came to rescue them from drowning; before long, they arrived at their own country.  Because of this, their faith became firm and steadfast, and they sought merit without wavering. They built a stūpa and performed offerings, coating it from top to bottom with saffron-scented mud. Having developed this faith, they led their companions to personally pay homage to the sacred sites and view the Mahā-bodhi tree. Before they had time to return home, a month had already passed. As the merchants traveled together, they said to one another, "The mountains and rivers are vast and our homeland is far away; since we are here, who is there to sweep and clean the stūpa we previously built?" Having said this, they circled around to this spot and suddenly saw the stūpa. Astonished at how this could be, they went forward to examine it and found it was the very stūpa built by their own country. Therefore, in India today, it is known by the name of Saffron. At the southeast corner of the wall surrounding the Mahā-bodhi (菩提樹), beside a banyan tree (nyagrodha), there is a vihāra (精舍) next to a stūpa, containing a statue of the Buddha in a seated posture. In the past, when the Tathāgata first attained the fruit of Buddhahood, the Great Brahmā King (Mahābrahmā-devarāja) here entreated him to turn the wheel of the wonderful Dharma. Within the enclosure of the Mahā-bodhi, there are large stūpas at each of the four corners. In the past, after the Tathāgata had received the auspicious grass (kuśa), he proceeded toward the Mahā-bodhi; he first passed by the four corners, and the great earth shook, only becoming still when he reached the Vajrāsana (金剛座). Within the enclosure of the tree, sacred sites are arranged like the scales of a fish, and it is difficult to enumerate them all.  Outside the enclosure of the Mahā-bodhi, to the southwest, there is a stūpa marking the former residence of the two milkmaids who offered the milk gruel. Beside it is a stūpa where the milkmaids boiled the gruel. Next to this stūpa is the place where the Tathāgata received the gruel. Outside the south gate of the Mahā-bodhi enclosure is a large pond, over seven hundred paces in circumference, with clear, mirror-like waves where dragons and fish dwell; it was excavated by two Brahmin brothers acting under the command of Maheśvara (大自在天). To the south of this is another pond; in the past, when the Tathāgata had first attained perfect enlightenment and wished to bathe, Śakra-devānām-indra (天帝釋) manifested this pond for the Buddha. To the west is a large stone; after the Buddha had washed his robes and wished to dry them, Śakra-devānām-indra brought it from the Great Snow Mountains (Himālaya). Beside it is a stūpa where the Tathāgata put on an old garment. Further to the south, in the forest, is a stūpa marking the place where the Tathāgata accepted the offering of an old garment from a poor elderly woman.
