en_revised: Outside the north gate of the Bodhi tree is the Mahābodhi Monastery (摩訶菩提僧伽藍), which was built by a former king of the country of Siṃhala (僧伽羅國). It has six courtyards and three-storied pavilions, surrounded by walls thirty to forty feet high; the workmanship is of the utmost ingenuity, and the painted decorations are exquisite. As for the Buddha images, they are cast in gold and silver, and all their adornments are inlaid with precious gems. The various stupas are lofty, spacious, and exquisitely decorated, containing the relics of the Tathāgata; the bone relics are as large as a finger joint, lustrous, pure white, and translucent inside and out. The flesh relics are like large pearls, with a color tinged with reddish-blue. Every year, on the full moon day of the month of the Tathāgata’s great spiritual manifestations, they are displayed to the public (Original note: This is the thirtieth day of the twelfth month in India, which corresponds to the fifteenth day of the first month here). At this time, they sometimes emit light or rain down flowers. The community of monks numbers nearly one thousand; they study the teachings of the Mahāyāna and the Sthavira school, their monastic discipline is pure and strict, and their conduct is upright and bright. Formerly, in the southern sea, there was the country of Siṃhala, whose king was purely devoted to the Buddha-dharma, a faith arising from his own nature. He had a younger cousin who became a monk and, longing to see the sacred sites of the Buddha, traveled far to India. He stayed in various monasteries, but all of them treated him with contempt as a border-dweller. He then returned to his own country, and the king personally went out to welcome him. The śramaṇa was sorrowful and distressed, as if he were unable to speak. The king said, "What burden do you carry that causes such deep melancholy?" The śramaṇa said, "Relying on the prestige of the state, I traveled to distant lands to inquire after the Way. Living as a stranger in foreign territories, I endured the cold and the heat, and at every turn I encountered humiliation and was mocked for my speech. Bearing such sorrow and shame, how could I be happy?" The king asked, "What do you mean by this?" He replied, "I sincerely wish that Your Majesty would take the field of merit to heart and establish a monastery (saṃghārāma) in India. This would both honor the holy sites and bring you great fame, while the resulting merit would support the late king and its blessings would reach your descendants." The king said, "This is a wonderful idea; why did I not hear of it sooner?" He then sent the treasures of his country as an offering to the King of India.  Having accepted the tribute and wishing to show kindness to those from afar, the King of India said to the envoy, "What should I now give as a return gift for your mission?" The envoy said, "The King of Siṃhala (僧伽羅) bows his head to the Great Auspicious King of India! Your majesty’s prestige and virtue extend far, and your benevolent grace reaches to distant places. The śramaṇas of our lowly land, admiring your influence and transformation, dared to travel to your superior kingdom to pay their respects at the holy sites. Yet, when they stayed in the monasteries, they were not provided with lodging; they suffered extreme hardship and returned home having endured shame. I humbly propose a far-reaching plan to set an example for future generations: to build this monastery in India so that traveling mendicants may have a place to rest, the two countries may enjoy friendly relations, and travelers may pass between them without end." The king said, "The Tathāgata’s subtle influence has passed, but his legacy remains; you may choose any one of the holy sites." The envoy accepted the command and returned to report the mission. The ministers offered their congratulations, and the king then gathered the śramaṇas to deliberate on the construction. The śramaṇas said, "The Mahā-bodhi (菩提樹) is the place where all Buddhas of the past and future attain holiness; having examined the various opinions, there is no better plan than this." Thereupon, the king gave up the treasures of his country and built this monastery, assigning monks from his own country to perform the offerings, and he engraved a copper plate as a record, which stated: "To provide for all without partiality is the supreme teaching of the Buddhas; to aid those with affinity through wisdom is the clear instruction of the ancient sages. Now I, this humble person, having inherited the great royal undertaking, have built this monastery to commemorate the holy site, so that the resulting merit may benefit my ancestors and its grace may extend to the common people. Only monks from my own country shall have authority here, and any of my countrymen shall be treated the same as the monks. May this be passed down to descendants, forever and ever without end." For this reason, this monastery is mostly occupied by monks from the country of Siṃhala (師子國).  More than ten li south of the Mahā-bodhi, holy sites are adjacent to one another, and it is difficult to list them all. Every year, when the bhikṣus conclude the rains retreat (vārṣika), clergy and laity from the four directions, numbering hundreds of thousands,, for seven days and seven nights, carry incense and flowers, play music, and travel throughout the forest to pay homage and make offerings. According to the holy teachings of the Buddha, the monks of India all enter the two-part rains retreat on the first day of the first half of the month of Śrāvaṇa, which corresponds to the sixteenth day of the fifth month here; they conclude the two-part rains retreat on the fifteenth day of the second half of the month of Aśvayuja, which corresponds to the fifteenth day of the eighth month here. The names of the Indian months are based on the stars and have remained unchanged from ancient times to the present; among all the schools, there is no discrepancy. It is because the local dialects were not fully reconciled and there were errors in translation regarding the division of time and the calculation of months that these discrepancies have arisen; therefore, the retreat is entered on the sixteenth day of the fourth month and concluded on the fifteenth day of the seventh month.

issues: upāsaka/upāsikā notes garbled: transliterations wrong ('yisaisai' for 伊蒱塞), the upāsikā note (舊曰優婆斯，又曰優婆夷，皆訛也) is moved outside the sentence as an invented 'Original note' and the Buddha's quotation is broken off before 皆先濟渡 → restored as two bracketed notes in place; (居勿反) pronunciation note dropped (minor); Chinese of 屈屈吒播陀山 missing
en_revised: Going east from the Mahā River, one enters a great forest wilderness and, after traveling over a hundred li, reaches Kukkuṭapāda Mountain (屈屈吒播陀山) (屈 pronounced 居勿反) (translated into Chinese as Jizu, "Cock's Foot"), also called Gurupāda Mountain (translated into Chinese as Zunzu, "Venerable Foot"). The high peaks are steep and the ravines infinitely deep; the caverns are boundless, and at the foot of the mountain by the mountain streams, tall trees fill the valleys, while ridges and cliffs are covered with lush grass. Three peaks rise sharply with sheer precipices standing at their sides, their atmosphere joining with the heavens and their forms merging with the clouds. Because the Venerable Mahākāśyapa later entered nirvana in its midst, people did not dare to refer to him directly by name, and thus it is called "Venerable Foot."  Mahākāśyapa (摩訶迦葉波) is a disciple of the Śrāvaka vehicle who attained the six supernatural powers and possesses the eight liberations. When the Tathāgata had finished his work of transformation and was about to enter nirvana, he told Kāśyapa: "Throughout vast eons I have diligently practiced austerities, seeking the supreme Dharma for the sake of all sentient beings. The vows I made in the past have now been fulfilled. I am now about to enter the great nirvana, and I entrust the entire treasury of the Dharma to you. Maintain and proclaim it; do not let it be lost or fall into ruin. The golden-threaded robe offered by my aunt is to be kept and passed on to Maitreya when he attains buddhahood. Among the practitioners within my bequeathed Dharma—whether they be bhikṣus, bhikṣunīs, upāsakas (鄔波索迦) (in the Tang language, 'laymen who serve'; formerly called yipusai 伊蒱塞, also youposai 優波塞, also youposai 優婆塞, all of which are erroneous), or upāsikās (鄔波斯迦) (in the Tang language, 'laywomen who serve'; formerly called youposi 優婆斯, also youpoyi 優婆夷, all of which are erroneous)—all of them are to be liberated first, causing them to depart from the cycle of transmigration." Kāśyapa accepted the command to uphold the True Dharma. Once the compilation was finished, in the twentieth year, he grew weary of the world and its impermanence and was about to enter final extinction. He then went to Mount Kukkutapāda (雞足山), ascended from the northern side of the mountain, and took a winding path to the southwest ridge. The mountain peaks were steep and obstructed, and the cliff paths were rugged; he struck them with his staff, and they split open as if cut. Once the mountain path was opened, he proceeded along the way, winding and turning through crisscrossing passages until he reached the summit and emerged on the northeast side. Having entered the midst of the three peaks, he stood holding the Buddha’s robe, and by the power of his vow, the three peaks closed over him, which is why the mountain now has three protruding ridges. When the future Maitreya, the World-Honored One, appears in the world and completes his three assemblies of preaching the Dharma, there will remain countless arrogant sentient beings who shall ascend this mountain and come to the place of Kāśyapa. When Maitreya snaps his fingers, the mountain peaks will open of their own accord; yet when those sentient beings see Kāśyapa, their arrogance will increase even further. At that time, the Great Kāśyapa will present the robe and deliver a discourse; once they have finished paying their respects, he will ascend into the void, manifest various spiritual transformations, transform into fire to consume his body, and thus enter final extinction. At that time, the assembly will gaze up in reverence, their arrogant minds will be dispelled, and through this realization, they will all attain the holy fruits. Therefore, a stūpa has been built on the mountain; on quiet nights, one may see a bright torch from afar, but upon ascending the mountain, nothing can be seen.

issues: (the yi and jie characters are reversed in pronunciation; ...) → note （移結反） is a fanqie for 洩: 'pronounced y(i) + (j)ie'; "Six out of every ten students who received his teachings were his disciples" (circular) → 受業門人，十室而六 'disciples receiving instruction came from six households out of ten' (recurs from earlier review); seven koṭis (in the Tang language, this means one hundred million) → note （唐言億） just gives 億 (yi), a value the text does not fix
en_revised: Traveling more than thirty *li* eastward through the empty valleys of Buddhavana Mountain (Skt. *buddha-vana*), one reaches Yaṣṭivana (洩瑟知林) (洩 is pronounced y[i] + [j]ie) (in the language of Tang, this means "Staff Forest"). The forest’s bamboo is tall and slender, covering the mountains and filling the valleys. Long ago, there was a Brahmin who heard that the body of the Buddha Śākyamuni was sixteen feet tall; he constantly harbored doubts and, unable to believe it, took a sixteen-foot bamboo staff, intending to measure the Buddha’s body. The staff always extended beyond the sixteen-foot mark at its tip; as it continued to grow taller in this way, he could never reach the truth of it, so he threw the staff away and departed, and it subsequently took root. Within the forest is a large *stūpa* built by King Aśoka. In the past, the Tathāgata spent seven days here manifesting great supernatural powers for the sake of gods and humans, and expounding the profound and subtle Dharma.  Recently, in the Staff Forest, there was an *upāsaka* named Jayasena (in the language of Tang, this means "Victorious Army"), who belonged to the Kṣatriya caste of Western India. His aspirations were for simplicity and ease, his heart delighted in the mountains and forests, and while his physical traces remained in this illusory realm, his mind roamed the boundaries of ultimate truth. He had thoroughly investigated the subtle mysteries of both internal and external scriptures, possessing noble eloquence and elegant manners. Śramaṇas, Brahmins, followers of non-Buddhist paths, heterodox scholars, kings, ministers, elders, and the wealthy and influential all flocked to visit him, bowing their heads to request instruction. Of every ten households, six had sent disciples to receive his instruction. Now approaching seventy years of age, he studied with tireless devotion; having abandoned all other arts, he practiced only the Buddhist scriptures, exerting his body and mind without ceasing day or night. According to the custom of India, scented powder is mixed into clay to make small stupas five or six inches high; scriptures are written and placed inside them, which are called Dharma relics. As the number gradually accumulates, a large stupa is built to house them all within, where offerings are constantly performed. Thus, the practice of Jayasena (勝軍) was as follows: his mouth would proclaim the wonderful Dharma to guide and encourage students, while his hands would make stupas to cultivate superior merit. At night, he would practice circumambulation, chanting, and seated meditation, never finding time for sleep or food, and working day and night without slackening. He reached one hundred years of age, yet his resolve and work did not decline. Over a period of thirty years, he made a total of seven koṭis (in the Tang language, *yi* [億]) of Dharma-relic stupas. Each time he completed one koṭi, he built a large stupa to house them all, where he grandly performed offerings and invited the monastic assembly to celebrate with a religious ceremony. At those times, a divine light would shine brilliantly as a manifest miracle, and from then on, it would emit light from time to time.

issues: the Isolated Hill (Vyāsa) / the Small Isolated Hill (Asura) → 孤山, 小孤山 carry no such names (recurs from earlier review); some curious individuals deeply skilled in magical arts who gathered their companions → 往有好事者，深閑呪術，顧儔命侶，十有四人 'a curious man versed in spells gathered companions, fourteen in all' – one magician, hence 唯彼術士 and 餘十三人 (recurs from earlier review); note (Original note: The older terms Asura, Ashulun, and Axiuluo are all erroneous) → 舊曰阿修羅，又曰阿須倫，又曰阿修羅，皆訛也 'formerly called axiuluo, also axulun, also axiuluo, all erroneous' – the main-text term is 阿素洛 (asura)
en_revised: Four or five li to the northeast of the Isolated Hill is the Small Isolated Hill. In the cliffside of the mountain is a stone chamber, vast and spacious, capable of seating over a thousand people; here the Tathāgata in the past preached the Dharma for three months. Above the stone chamber is a large flat rock where Śakra and Brahmā ground ox-head sandalwood to anoint the Buddha’s body; the lingering fragrance on the rock remains potent to this day. In the southwest corner of the stone chamber is a rocky grotto, which in India is called the palace of the *asura* (阿素洛) (formerly called *axiuluo* [阿修羅], also *axulun* [阿須倫], also *axiuluo*; all are erroneous). In the past, there was a curious man, deeply skilled in spells, who gathered companions, fourteen people in all, and having made a pact to share the same purpose, entered this grotto. After traveling thirty or forty li, it suddenly became brightly illuminated, and they beheld cities, towers, and pavilions, all made of gold, silver, and lapis lazuli. Once these people arrived, there were various young maidens standing by the gates who joyfully welcomed them and treated them with great courtesy. Proceeding gradually to the inner city gate, there were two maidservants, each holding a golden basin filled with flowers and incense, who came to greet them. They said to the group, "It is fitting to go to the pool to bathe, to apply perfumes and wear flower garlands, and only after that to enter; this would be most excellent. Only that sorcerer should proceed quickly." The other thirteen people then bathed, but as soon as they entered the pool, they felt as if they had forgotten everything, and they found themselves sitting in a rice paddy on a level plain to the north of this place, already thirty or forty li away. Beside the stone chamber is a plank road, more than ten paces wide and four or five li long. In the past, when King Bimbisāra (頻毘娑羅王) was about to go to the place of the Buddha, he had rocks cut to open the valley and cliffs leveled to fill the ravines; he either piled up stones or excavated the cliffs to create steps, in order to reach the place of the Buddha.

issues: Aśvajit (阿濕婆恃; in the language of Tang, Ma Sheng) → gloss untranslated: 唐言馬勝 'Horse Victory'; attained supreme enlightenment (samyaksambodhi) → 證三菩提 'realized saṃbodhi' (三菩提 transcribes saṃbodhi; recurs from earlier review in another form); (translated into Chinese as Shengmi [Victorious Secret]) – now a genuine note （唐言勝密）, fine; 'Pravaragiri' and 'threefold bodhi' of the earlier version no longer occur
en_revised: Traveling east from these great mountains for more than sixty li, one reaches the city of Kuśāgrapura (矩奢揭羅補羅城; in the language of Tang, the City of Superior Thatch Palaces). The City of Superior Thatch Palaces is located in the center of the kingdom of Magadha and was the capital of ancient kings; because it produces an abundance of excellent and auspicious fragrant thatch, it is called the City of Superior Thatch. Lofty mountains surround it, serving as an outer wall; to the west it connects to a mountain pass, and to the north a mountain gate opens. It is long from east to west and narrow from north to south, with a circumference of more than one hundred and fifty li. The remaining foundations of the inner city measure more than thirty li in circumference. *Karṇikāra* (羯尼迦) trees cover all the paths; their flowers contain a unique fragrance and their color is as brilliant as gold, so that in the month of late spring, the forests are all golden.  Outside the north gate of the palace city is a stūpa, marking the place where Devadatta, having become an intimate friend of King Ajātaśatru (未生怨王), released the intoxicated elephant Dhanapāla (護財) in an attempt to harm the Tathāgata. From the tips of the Tathāgata’s fingers, five lions emerged, and the intoxicated elephant was subdued and bowed down here. To the northeast of the place where the intoxicated elephant was subdued is a stūpa, marking the place where Śāriputra heard the bhikṣu Aśvajit (阿濕婆恃) (in the language of Tang, "Horse Victory" [馬勝]) preach the Dharma and attained the fruit of sainthood.   Formerly, when Śāriputra was a householder, he possessed high talent and elegant bearing, and was esteemed by his contemporaries; students and disciples came to him to receive instruction. At this time, he was about to enter the great city of Rājagṛha, and the bhikṣu Aśvajit was also just then begging for food. At that time, Śāriputra saw Aśvajit from afar and said to his disciples, "That person coming here is very composed and dignified; if he has not attained the holy fruit, how could he be so calm and tranquil?" "We should wait a moment and observe his demeanor." The bhikṣu Aśvajit had already attained the state of an arhat; his mind was at ease, his bearing was gentle and refined, and he approached with the ringing of his khakkhara. Śāriputra said, "Elder, are you well and at peace? Who is your teacher, and what Dharma have you realized, that you are so joyful?" Aśvajit replied, "Do you not know? The crown prince of King Śuddhodana, who renounced the position of a wheel-turning monarch, out of compassion for the six destinies, practiced austerities for six years, realized perfect enlightenment (*saṃbodhi*), and possesses omniscience—he is my teacher. As for the Dharma, it is neither existent nor non-existent; it is difficult to define or explain. Only a Buddha and a Buddha can fully describe it; how could one as ignorant as I discuss it in detail?" He then recited a verse in praise of the Buddha’s Dharma. Upon hearing this, Śāriputra attained the fruit.  Not far to the north of where Śāriputra attained the fruit, there is a large, deep pit with a stūpa built beside it; this is the place where Śrīgupta (室利毱多) (in the language of Tang, "Victorious Secret" [勝密]) attempted to harm the Buddha with a fire pit and poisoned food. This Śrīgupta followed the teachings of the non-Buddhists and was deeply attached to erroneous views. The various Brahmins said to him, "Gautama is respected by the people of the country, which has left our followers with nothing to rely on. You should now invite him to your home for a feast; dig a large pit at the gate, fill it with fire, bridge it with rotten wood, and cover it with dry earth. All the food and drink should be mixed with poison; if he escapes the fire pit, he will surely encounter the poisoned food." Śrīgupta accepted their command and prepared the poisoned feast. The people in the city all knew that Śrīgupta (勝密) harbored evil and harmful intentions toward the World-Honored One, and they all urged and pleaded with the Buddha not to go. The World-Honored One replied, "Do not harbor anxiety. The body of the Tathāgata cannot be harmed by anything." Thereupon, he accepted the invitation and went. As his foot stepped upon the threshold of the gate, the fire pit turned into a pool, its clear waters reflecting like a mirror and filled with blooming lotuses. Having seen this, Śrīgupta was filled with panic and confusion, and said to his disciples, "He used magic to escape the fire, but there is still the poisoned food." After the World-Honored One had finished his meal, he preached the wonderful Dharma for him; having heard this, Śrīgupta confessed his faults and took refuge.

issues: During the fifty years → 垂五十年 'for nearly fifty years' (recurs from earlier review)
en_revised: Traveling fourteen or fifteen *li* northeast from the palace city, one reaches Gṛdhrakūṭa Mountain (in the language of Tang, this means Vulture Peak, and it is also called Vulture Terrace; the old name, Qidujue Mountain, is incorrect). It adjoins the southern slope of the North Mountain and rises solitary and steep; it is a place where vultures dwell and it resembles a lofty terrace, with the verdant peaks reflecting against the sky in varying shades of color. For nearly fifty years, while the Tathāgata presided over the world, he resided mostly on this mountain, extensively expounding the subtle Dharma. For the sake of hearing the Dharma, King Bimbisāra mobilized laborers to build a path from the foot of the mountain to the summit, spanning valleys and scaling rocks, laying stones to form steps more than ten paces wide and five or six *li* in length. Midway along the path are two small stūpas: one is called "Dismounting," marking the spot where the king would proceed on foot; the other is called "Turning Back the Ordinary," marking the spot where he would screen out ordinary people and not allow them to accompany him further. The summit of the mountain is long from east to west and narrow from north to south.

issues: there were still remnants left over, which at that time emitted a light like a candle → 尚有遺餘，時燭光景 'remnants (of the relics) are still left, which from time to time give off light'
en_revised: To the east of the Kalandaka Bamboo Grove (迦蘭陀竹園) is a stūpa built by King Ajātaśatru (阿闍多設咄路王; translated in the Tang language as "Unborn Enemy" [未生怨], formerly called Ajāśatru [阿闍世], which is an erroneous abbreviation). After the Tathāgata entered nirvāṇa, the various kings divided the relics among themselves. King Ajātaśatru obtained his share and brought them back, where he formally observed the rites of construction and performed offerings. When King Aśoka (無憂王) developed faith, he opened the stūpa to retrieve the relics and built [new] stūpas; some relics still remain, and from time to time they shine with light.  In the stūpa of King Ajātaśatru, there are relics of half the body of the Venerable Ānanda. Formerly, when the Venerable One was about to enter parinirvāṇa, he left the country of Magadha (摩揭陀國) and headed toward the city of Vaiśālī (吠舍釐城). The two countries were in conflict and intended to raise an army. The Venerable One felt compassion and therefore divided his body; the King of Magadha received his portion and brought it back for veneration, and at this very sacred site, he formally performed the rites of construction. Beside it is a place where the Tathāgata walked in meditation. Not far from this is a stūpa, which is the place where Śāriputra (舍利子) and Maudgalyāyana (沒特伽羅子) and others resided during the rainy season.

issues: All others who are still in the stage of learning → 自餘果學 'the rest, whether holders of a fruit or learners' (recurs from earlier review); notes (Original note: The old term 'Sūtra' is incorrect) / ('Vinaya' is incorrect) → 舊曰修多羅，訛也 / 舊曰毘那耶，訛也: the rejected forms are the transcriptions xiuduoluo 修多羅 and pinaye 毘那耶, against 素呾纜 and 毘奈耶; as rendered the note condemns the terms themselves
en_revised: Traveling five or six li southwest from the Bamboo Grove (Veṇuvana), on the northern side of the South Mountain (Dakṣiṇagiri), in a great bamboo forest, there is a large stone chamber. This is where the Venerable Mahākāśyapa, together with nine hundred and ninety great arhats, compiled the Tripiṭaka after the Tathāgata’s nirvana. In front are the old foundations of a hall built by King Ajātaśatru (未生怨王) for the great arhats who were to compile the Dharma-treasury.  Initially, while Mahākāśyapa was sitting in meditation in the mountain forest, he suddenly saw a brilliant light and observed the earth quake. He said, "What omen is this, that it should be so extraordinary?" Using his heavenly eye to observe, he saw that the Buddha, the World-Honored One, had entered parinirvana between the twin trees, and he immediately ordered his followers to hasten to the city of Kuśinagara (拘尸城). On the road, he met a Brahman holding a heavenly flower in his hand. Mahākāśyapa asked, "Where do you come from? Do you know where my Great Teacher is now?" The Brahman replied, "I have just come from that city of Kuśinagara; I saw that your Great Teacher has already entered nirvana, and the multitudes of gods and men are all making offerings. The flower I hold was obtained from there."  Upon hearing this, Mahākāśyapa said to his followers, "The sun of wisdom has set, the world is in darkness, the excellent guide has departed, and sentient beings will fall into ruin." Lax monks congratulated one another, saying, "The Tathāgata has attained extinction, so we are now at ease. If we commit any offense, who will be able to rebuke or restrain us?" Hearing this, Mahākāśyapa was deeply saddened and thought to compile the Dharma-treasury to govern offenses according to the teachings. He then went to the twin trees to view the transformation and pay his respects. Soon after, the Dharma King passed away, leaving humans and gods without a guide, and the great arhats also entered parinirvāṇa. At that time, Mahākāśyapa thought to himself, "In obedience to the Buddha’s teachings, it is appropriate to compile the Dharma-treasury." Thereupon, he ascended Mount Sumeru (蘇迷盧山), struck the great ghaṇṭā (大揵稚), and proclaimed: "A Dharma assembly is about to be held in the city of Rājagṛha (王舍城); all those who have realized the fruits of the path should assemble here with haste!" The sound of the ghaṇṭā carried the teaching of Kāśyapa, reaching throughout the trichiliomegachiliocosm, and all who possessed supernatural powers heard it and gathered.  At that time, Kāśyapa addressed the assembly, saying, "The Tathāgata has entered extinction, and the world is empty. We must compile the Dharma-treasury to repay the Buddha’s kindness. Now, in compiling the Dharma, we must prioritize simplicity and quietude; how could we rely on a large crowd and fail to accomplish this noble task? Those who possess the three knowledges (三明), have attained the six supernatural powers (六通), are endowed with perfect retention (聞持) without error, and possess unobstructed eloquence (辯才)—such superior persons may participate in the compilation. All the rest, those who hold a fruit and those still in training, should return to their respective dwellings."  Thus, he obtained nine hundred and ninety people, excluding Ānanda, who was still in the stage of learning. Mahākāśyapa summoned him and said, "You have not yet exhausted the outflows (漏); you should leave the assembly of sages." Ānanda replied, "I have attended upon the Tathāgata for many years, and whenever there were discussions on the Dharma, I was never excluded. Now that the compilation is to take place, I am being expelled; the Dharma King has entered extinction, and I have lost my refuge." Kāśyapa told him, "Do not harbor sorrow or distress. Although you have personally attended upon the Buddha and are indeed learned, your attachments and delusions have not yet been exhausted, and your habitual bonds have not yet been severed." Ānanda, silenced, withdrew and went to a quiet, secluded place, desiring to attain the state of no-more-learning (aśaikṣa), but despite his diligent efforts, he did not attain it. Having become exhausted and weary, he intended to lie down for a moment; before his head had even touched the pillow, he attained the state of an Arhat. He went to the place of the assembly and knocked on the door to announce his arrival. Kāśyapa asked, "Have you exhausted your defilements? You should employ your supernatural powers and enter without using the door." Ānanda accepted the command, entered through the keyhole, paid homage to the monks, and then withdrew to sit down. This was on the fifteenth day, the beginning of the summer retreat.  Thereupon, Kāśyapa proclaimed aloud, "Reflect and listen carefully! Ānanda, who has heard and retained the teachings, and whom the Tathāgata praised, shall compile the Sūtra-piṭaka (素呾纜藏) (formerly called *xiuduoluo* [修多羅], which is erroneous). Upāli, who is clear and thorough in upholding the Vinaya and is recognized by the assembly, shall compile the Vinaya-piṭaka (毘奈耶藏) (formerly called *pinaye* [毘那耶], which is erroneous). I, Kāśyapa, shall compile the Abhidharma-piṭaka." After two or three months had passed, the compilation of the three piṭakas was completed. Because Mahākāśyapa was the senior elder (sthavira) among the monks, it was consequently called the Sthavira school (Sthaviravāda).  To the northwest of where Mahākāśyapa held the assembly, there is a stūpa; this is where Ānanda, having been rebuked by the monks and excluded from the assembly, came to sit in meditation and attained the fruit of Arhatship. Only after attaining this fruit was he permitted to participate.

issues: Jotipāla error of the earlier version fixed (now Jyotiṣka); the old translation "Śrotika" is incorrect → 舊曰樹提伽，訛也 'formerly called Shutijia (樹提伽), which is erroneous' – 'Śrotika' invented; (in Chinese, Wangshe) → gloss untranslated: 唐言王舍 'King's Abode'; the ministers' words 寒林者…當自謹護 are split, with the definition of the Cold Forest outside the quotation (style)
en_revised: Not far to the northeast of the stone pillar, one reaches the city of Rājagṛha (曷羅闍姞利呬城) (in the language of Tang, "King's Abode" [王舍]). The outer wall has already collapsed, and no remains of the ramparts are left; although the inner city is ruined, its foundations are still steep and high, measuring over twenty *li* in circumference, with one gate on each side.   Formerly, when King Bimbisāra (頻毘娑羅王) had his capital in the Upper Palace City, the households of the registered inhabitants frequently suffered from the calamity of fire. If one family was negligent, the neighbors on all four sides would suffer the disaster; the people had no time for anything but fire prevention, their properties and livelihoods were abandoned, and the masses lived in grievance and unrest. The king said, "Because of my lack of virtue, the common people suffer; what merit can I cultivate to avert this?" The ministers replied, "Your Majesty’s virtuous transformation is harmonious and peaceful, and your governance and teachings are clear and discerning. Now, these common people are not cautious, leading to these fires. It is appropriate to establish strict regulations to prevent future offenses. If a fire breaks out, investigate thoroughly to find who started it, punish the primary culprit, and banish them to the Cold Forest (寒林)."   The Cold Forest is a place where corpses are abandoned; it is commonly called an inauspicious place, and people avoid traveling there. "Now, to banish them there is the same as treating them like a corpse. Since they will be ashamed of such a lowly dwelling, they will naturally be cautious and protective." The king said, "Good; it should be announced everywhere to the residents." Shortly after, a fire broke out in the king’s own palace first. He said to his ministers, "I shall move." He then ordered the crown prince to oversee the affairs of the capital, and wishing to clarify the laws of the state, he moved his residence there. At that time, the King of Vaiśālī (吠舍釐王), hearing that King Bimbisāra was living in the open at the Cold Forest, assembled his troops with the intent to launch a surprise attack. The border guards reported this, and he then built a city. Because the king had first taken up residence here, it was called Rājagṛha (the City of the King’s Abode). The officials, the gentry, and the common people all moved their households there. Some say that it was not until King Ajātaśatru (未生怨王) that this city was built; once the crown prince Ajātaśatru succeeded to the throne, he then made it his capital. By the time King Aśoka (無憂王) moved the capital to Pāṭaliputra (波吒釐城), he bestowed Rājagṛha upon the brahmans; therefore, there are no longer any common people in the city, only fewer than a thousand brahman families. In the southwest corner of the palace city are two small saṃghārāmas where visiting monks from various countries stay when they come and go; this is the place where the Buddha formerly expounded the Dharma. To the northwest of this is a stūpa, the former birthplace of the elder Jyotiṣka (珠底色迦) (in the language of Tang, "Star Calendar" [星曆]; formerly called Shutijia [樹提伽], which is erroneous). Outside the south gate of the city, to the left of the road, there is a stūpa where the Tathāgata expounded the Dharma and converted Rāhula.

issues: The King said that in this original great monastery… → 帝曰本大伽藍者: read 帝日 = Śakrāditya, 'Śakrāditya's original great monastery now houses a Buddha image…' – no one is speaking (Mizutani: 帝日王の大伽藍) (recurs from earlier review); those who travel here under false pretenses are all treated with respect → 竊名而遊，咸得禮重 'those who travel about falsely claiming its name are everywhere treated with respect' (recurs); seventeen or eighteen out of every twenty → 十七八 'seven or eight in ten' (recurs); We came from that country → 我至那國也 'we have come from Cīna (至那國)' – Cīna lost (recurs in another form); Śakrāditya ("Sun of the Emperor") → 帝日 'Emperor Sun' (帝 = Indra/Śakra)
en_revised: From here, traveling north for more than thirty *li*, one arrives at the Nālandā (translated into Chinese as "Giving Without Weariness") monastery. I heard from the elders that in the mango grove to the south of this monastery there is a pond; a dragon named Nālandā lived there, and because the monastery was built beside it, it took its name from the dragon. According to the actual account, it is because the Tathāgata, in the past when practicing the bodhisattva path, was a great king who established his capital in this place. He felt compassion for sentient beings and delighted in giving generously; at the time, people praised his virtue and called him "Giving Without Weariness," and thus the monastery took this as its name. The land was originally a mango grove; five hundred merchants bought it with ten billion gold coins and offered it to the Buddha. The Buddha preached the Dharma here for three months, and the merchants all attained the fruits of sainthood. Not long after the Buddha’s nirvana, a former king of this country named Śakrāditya (translated into Chinese as "Emperor Sun" [帝日]) deeply respected the One Vehicle and honored the Triple Gem; he selected this auspicious site by divination and built this monastery. When the work first began, they pierced and injured the body of the dragon. At that time, there was a Nirgrantha outsider skilled in divination who saw this and predicted: "This is a superior site; if a monastery is built here, it will surely flourish and become the standard for the five Indias. It will grow even more prosperous after a thousand years, and later students will easily complete their studies here. However, there will be much coughing of blood, because the dragon was injured." His son, King Buddhagupta (translated into Chinese as "Protector of Awakening"), succeeded to the throne and, following the noble legacy, built another monastery to the south of this one. King Tathāgatagupta (translated into Chinese as "Thus-Come") earnestly followed the noble legacy and built another monastery to the east of this one. When King Bālāditya (translated into Chinese as "Young Sun") succeeded to the throne, he built another monastery to the northeast of this one. When the work was completed and the ceremonies finished, he held a celebratory feast of merit, expressing his sincerity to both the hidden and the manifest, and invited both the ordinary and the holy. At this assembly, monks from the five Indias gathered from ten thousand miles away. Once the assembly was seated, two monks arrived late and were led up to the third-story pavilion. Someone asked, "The King is holding this assembly and has invited the ordinary and the holy; from what place do you venerable ones come, that you arrive last?" They replied, "We have come from the country of Cīna (至那國); our teacher was suffering from an illness, so we departed only after he had eaten. Having received the King’s distant invitation, we have come to attend the assembly." The questioner was astonished and immediately reported this to the King. The King, knowing in his heart that they were sages, went in person to inquire of them, but when he arrived at the upper pavilion, he did not know where they had gone. The King’s faith deepened further, and he renounced his kingdom to become a monk. Once he had become a monk, he was ranked at the very end of the assembly, which left him constantly dissatisfied and uneasy, thinking: "I was once a king, occupying the highest and most honorable position; now that I have become a monk, I am ranked at the very end of the assembly." He soon went to inform the monks and recounted his situation. Thereupon, the assembly of monks reached a consensus, decreeing that those who have not yet received the full precepts shall be ranked according to their age; thus, this monastery alone possesses this rule. The King’s son, Vajra (translated into Chinese as "Diamond"), possessed a firm and steadfast faith; after succeeding to the throne, he built another monastery to the west of this site. Afterward, the King of Central India built another great monastery to the north of this one. Thereupon, the surrounding walls were raised high, and they were joined into a single gate; since successive kings have built them generation after generation, exhausting all the arts of carving and joinery, it is truly a magnificent sight. In the original great monastery of Śakrāditya (帝日), a Buddha image is now installed, and forty monks are dispatched from the assembly daily to eat here in order to repay the kindness of the donors. The number of monks is several thousand, all of whom are men of outstanding talent and high learning; those whose virtue is esteemed in the present age and whose fame has spread to foreign lands number more than several hundred. Their conduct in the precepts is pure and white, and their monastic discipline is refined and perfect; the monks have strict regulations, and the assembly is entirely upright and simple, such that all the countries of India look to them as a model. They seek instruction and discuss profound mysteries, finding the whole day insufficient; they remain vigilant and admonish one another day and night, with the old and young helping each other to perfection, and if there were any who did not discuss the subtle meanings of the Tripitaka, they would feel ashamed of their own shadows. Therefore, scholars from foreign lands who wish to spread their reputation all come here to resolve their doubts, and only then does their elegant fame flow forth. For this reason, even those who travel about falsely claiming its name are everywhere treated with respect. When those from distant regions and foreign lands wish to enter for discussion, the gatekeepers pose difficult questions, and many are forced to turn back; only those who are deeply learned in both ancient and modern studies are permitted to enter. Consequently, when visiting scholars and newcomers discuss their arts and abilities in detail, those who are forced to retreat are certainly seven or eight out of every ten. As for the few who are broadly learned, they are questioned in turn by the assembly, and there is none whose sharpness is not blunted and whose reputation is not diminished. As for those of eminent talent and broad learning, possessing strong memories and many abilities, these virtuous and wise men join their brilliance and follow in the footsteps of their predecessors. As for Dharmapāla (護法) and Candrapāla (護月), they stirred the fragrant dust of the Buddha’s legacy; Guṇamati (德慧) and Sthiramati (堅慧) spread their elegant reputations throughout their time; there were the refined discourses of Prabhāmitra (光友) and the lofty discussions of Jinamitra (勝友); Candrakīrti (智月) was clear and keen in his discernment; and Śīlabhadra (戒賢) possessed virtue that was sublime and profound. These superior men were known to all; their virtue excelled that of their predecessors, and their learning encompassed the ancient texts; each composed more than ten treatises and commentaries, which were widely circulated and highly valued by their contemporaries. Around the monastery, there are hundreds of sacred traces; I shall cite two or three of them as a brief summary.

issues: King Bimbisāra went to meet the Buddha and traveled more than twenty li to the southeast → 頻毘娑羅王迎佛東南行二十餘里 is a route statement: 'from (the place where) King Bimbisāra welcomed the Buddha, going southeast more than twenty li' – wrong subject (recurs from earlier review); (Original note: koṭi means one hundred million in the language of Tang) → （拘胝者，唐言億）'koṭi is, in the language of Tang, yi (億)'
en_revised: From the place where King Bimbisāra welcomed the Buddha, traveling more than twenty *li* to the southeast, one arrives at the town of Kālapināka (迦羅臂拏迦邑). In it is a stūpa built by King Aśoka. This is the native village of the Venerable Śāriputra, and the well still exists today. Beside it is a stūpa where the Venerable entered into extinction, which contains his bodily relics. The Venerable was of a great Brahmin lineage. His father was highly talented and broadly learned, with a deep insight into the subtle and profound; there was no classic or treatise that he had not thoroughly studied. His wife had a dream and told her husband in detail, saying: "Last night in my sleep, I dreamt of a strange man clad in armor and holding a vajra, who demolished all the mountains and then stood back beneath a single mountain." Her husband said: "This is a very auspicious dream. You will give birth to a son who will be learned and peerless in the world, who will defeat all the masters of debate and shatter their doctrines, but who will be inferior to only one person, to whom he will become a disciple." She was indeed pregnant, and the mother suddenly became brilliant, engaging in high-level discussions and intense debates with speech that was never obstructed. When the Venerable was eight years old, his fame spread to the four quarters; his nature was pure and simple, his heart was compassionate, he destroyed the bonds of defilement, and he attained wisdom. He and Maudgalyāyana (沒特伽羅子) had been friends since youth and were deeply weary of the dusty world, yet they had not found a place to turn. Thereupon, he and Maudgalyāyana went to the place of the non-Buddhist Sañjaya (珊闍耶) to study. They then said to each other: "This is not the ultimate principle, and it cannot exhaust the limits of suffering. Let us each seek a clear guide; whoever tastes the nectar first must share its flavor with the other." At that time, the great arhat Aśvajit (馬勝) held his alms bowl and entered the city to beg for food. Śāriputra (舍利子) saw his dignified and refined demeanor and immediately asked him, "Who is your teacher?" He replied, "The prince of the Śākya clan, who grew weary of the world, renounced household life, and attained equal and perfect enlightenment—he is my teacher." Śāriputra said, "What dharma does he teach? May I hear it?" He replied, "I have only recently received instruction and have not yet grasped the profound meaning." Śāriputra said, "I wish to hear what you have heard." Aśvajit then expounded it according to the occasion, and upon hearing it, Śāriputra immediately attained the first fruit. He then went with his two hundred and fifty disciples to the place of the Buddha. The World-Honored One saw them from afar and, pointing them out, told the assembly, "Among my disciples, he is the foremost in wisdom." Upon arriving, he bowed his head to the ground and wished to follow the Buddha’s dharma. The World-Honored One said, "Welcome, bhikṣu." Upon hearing these words, his precepts were fully perfected. More than half a month later, he heard the Buddha preaching to the Long-nailed Brahmacārin (長爪梵志), and upon hearing the remaining discourse, he was enlightened and attained the fruit of an arhat. Later, when Ānanda (阿難) received the Buddha’s announcement of the time of his extinction, the news was passed from one to another, and all were filled with sorrow and grief. Śāriputra’s longing and reverence deepened, and, unable to bear seeing the Buddha enter parinirvāṇa, he requested the World-Honored One to let him enter extinction first. The World-Honored One said, "You should know the time." He took leave of his disciples and went to his native village, where his attendant novice informed the entire city. King Ajātaśatru (未生怨王) and the people of his country all rushed there like the wind, gathering like clouds. Śāriputra (舍利子) preached the Dharma extensively, and having heard him, the people departed. During the last watch of the night, he focused his mind and entered the samādhi of cessation (nirodha-samāpatti); upon arising from that meditation, he entered final extinction. Four or five li to the southeast of the town of Kālapināka (迦羅臂挐迦邑), there is a stūpa at the place where the disciples of the Venerable Śāriputra entered nirvāṇa. Some say that when Kāśyapa Buddha (迦葉波佛) was in the world, three koṭis (*koṭi* is, in the language of Tang, *yi* [億]) of great arhats entered nirvāṇa without remainder at this same place.

issues: note （許贈反） after 亘 (pronunciation of 亘 as x[u] + [z]eng) dropped; which is the gradual teaching of the Lesser Vehicle → 小乘漸教也 'the Lesser Vehicle is the gradual teaching'; according to local custom → 聞諸土俗曰 'I heard from the local people'
en_revised: Going thirty-some *li* to the east of the stupa of the disciples of Śāriputra, one arrives at the mountain of Indraśailaguhā (Indra-śaila-guhā; in the language of Tang, "Cave of Śakra"). The mountain’s rocky valleys are deep and dark, and its flowering forests are lush and dense; on the ridge are two peaks that rise prominently and steeply. Between the southern cliffs of the western peak is a large stone chamber, wide but not high, where the Tathāgata once stayed. From time to time, the Heavenly Lord Śakra would carve forty-two questions of doubt onto the stone to ask [the Buddha], and the Buddha would explain them; those traces still remain. Today, an image has been made there to emulate the sacred appearance of the past, and those who enter to pay homage are all filled with awe and trepidation. On the mountain cliffs are the sites of the sitting and walking meditation traces of the four past Buddhas. On the eastern peak is a monastery; I heard from the local people that the monks there sometimes see, during the night, lamps and torches shining as constant illumination before the Buddha image in the stone chamber of the western peak. In front of the monastery on the eastern peak of Indraśailaguhā Mountain is a stupa called Haṃsa (亘娑) (亘 is pronounced x[u] + [z]eng) (in the language of Tang, "Goose"). Formerly, this monastery practiced the Lesser Vehicle; the Lesser Vehicle is a gradual teaching, and therefore permitted the consumption of the three pure meats, a practice this monastery followed and did not abandon. Later, the three pure meats were not always obtainable. A monk who was walking in meditation suddenly saw a flock of geese flying by and jokingly said, "Today the midday meal for the monks is insufficient; the Mahāsattvas should know the time." Before his words had ceased, one goose flew back, landed before the monk, and cast its body down to die. After the bhikṣu saw this, he reported it fully to the assembly of monks. Those who heard were moved with grief and said to one another, "The Tathāgata established the Dharma to guide and entice according to the capacity of the individual; we have clung to our ignorance and followed the gradual teachings. The Mahāyāna is the true principle; we should change our former attachments and strive to follow the holy will. This goose has handed down a warning and is truly a bright guide; we should commemorate its great virtue and transmit this record for all eternity." Thereupon, they built a stūpa to manifest its heroic legacy, burying the dead goose beneath it.
